---
title: "Wapishana"
subtitle: "Brazil"
region: "Latin America"
tags: [ethnography, latin-america]
---

## Overview

The Wapishana — also written Wapichan, Wapisiana, Wapitxana, Vapidiana and Wapixana — are an Indigenous people of the Roraima area straddling the Brazil–Guyana border. In Brazil they live in the state of Roraima, north and east of Boa Vista, concentrated in the Serra da Lua (Moon Ridge) region between the Branco River and its affluent the Tacutu, with mixed Wapishana–Macushi villages on the lower Uraricoera. In Guyana they occupy the southern Rupununi savannas between the Takutu, Rupununi and Kwitaro rivers, bordering Macushi territory at the Kanuku Mountains to the north and Wai-Wai land to the south. Population estimates give about 9,441 in Brazil (2014), 6,000 in Guyana (1990) and 37 in Venezuela (2011). Their language is Arawakan — the only surviving Arawakan language of the circum-Roraima area. For folk culture they matter above all for cassava processing technology and the basketry and handspun cotton that serve it.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The museum objects shown here document two textile lines — handspun cotton weaving by women, and the men's basketry that dominates the collection.

**Hammock (*shrimék*)** — A double-woven hammock of spindle-spun cotton; the Museum of Ethnography example made at Sand Creek measures 290 by 154 cm, of which the woven body is 123 cm, with cord work of about 70 cm at each side. A British Museum hammock in handspun cotton is likewise double-woven, off-white with tassels along both long sides and off-white and brown cotton ropes joined at each short end as the suspension.

**Baby slings and hammocks** — Women spin cotton and weave the thread into baby slings as well as hammocks; this, with clay pots, is the women's side of household manufacture.

**Beaded woman's apron** — A woman's apron worked entirely in beads, collected in British Guiana by Walter Roth, is the one garment in the collection.

**Basketry sifters and squeezers (*nirsh*)** — The manioc press named *nirsh* in Wapishana is a long plaited cylinder, open at one end and fitted with heavy loops at both; filled with grated cassava and hung from the roof of the dwelling, a lever threaded through the lower end is pressed down so the cylinder stretches and the poisonous juice is squeezed out. Plaiting is men's work. Sifter trays are woven on a square wooden frame in black and white fibre with red feathers at the corners; squeezers combine the same black-and-white fibre with red feather trim.

**Backpack basketry** — Carrying baskets are woven onto a wooden and cane framework, the rim edged in bark wrapping and bound with fibre rope; a child's version adds red, blue and black feathers, and a separate plaited cover (the "knapsack-cover") sheathes the back-basket. A child's basket in graded browns has wooden rim supports and red and blue feathers.

**Mats and trays** — A square plaited mat and a "freak-tray" made from half an *ite* leaf, both collected by Roth, round out the plaited forms.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used describe only one item of Wapishana dress: a woman's apron made of beads, collected in British Guiana. Introduced crafts include needlework and dressmaking, but the sources give no account of garment types, head coverings, belts, footwear or ceremonial dress distinct from daily wear.

### Architecture

Early Wapishana settlements were temporary clusters of homes; since the twentieth century villages have been permanent and usually arranged around a church, with schools, meeting houses and shops added by government. Villagers gather at the church or school to discuss local affairs, and men often play soccer in open ground nearby afterwards; the dwelling itself appears in the sources only through its roof, from which the manioc press is hung. In some places people have preferred to live in open country at a distance from their fields, putting up separate structures at the farms for food processing; a few families live on their farms, though others in the community look on this poorly. Land is not held as private property, and house and garden space is assigned flexibly, with newcomers required to obtain permission from villagers before settling. Brazilian villages average about 150 inhabitants and Guyanese ones about 500. The sources do not describe house form, materials, roof construction or architectural decoration.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Women make clay cooking pots. The storage jar in the Museum of Ethnography is built up from clay coils in a yellow-grey clay full of mica particles — most likely added — and is conical with the point downward, its narrow mouth slightly everted; it held cassava beer and belonged to a woman in Sand Creek who had received it in turn from the southern Wapishana. Men make wooden stools, and the basketry sieves, squeezers and presses used in preparing cassava and other foods. Cassava flour is toasted on iron griddles. Men also make arrows, fencing wire into points, but bows and arrows obtained from other Indigenous people have been almost entirely replaced by shotguns. Rustic furniture making is a recent introduction.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The collection holds one ornament: a child's bead necklace with a tapir hoof and toucan beaks hung from it, collected by Walter Roth in British Guiana. Feather decoration otherwise appears on objects rather than persons — red, blue and black feathers finish the corners and rims of sifters, squeezers, backpacks and children's baskets. The sources used do not describe tattooing, body painting, hair practices or other adornment.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not cover Wapishana instruments, song genres or performance occasions.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not cover Wapishana dance or dramatic traditions.

## Festivals & rituals

Healing and death furnish what the sources record of ritual life. Certain men once specialised in curing: they beat leaves and "blew" cures, and could use the same techniques to make people sick or to kill. No Wapishana now admits to these rituals and few follow them, but men and women perform a curing shaped by Catholicism, northeastern Brazilian folk medicine and other non-Indigenous practice. In most villages a Wapishana man serves as catechist, leading Sunday service when no priest is present. Deaths were attributed to evil spirits or to *kanaima* — healers who turned their powers to harm, acting out of envy to kill those wiser, better loved or more fortunate; the concept is tied to outsiders and enemies of the social group, in contrast to the kinship and cooperation binding its members. Contemporary Wapishana name hepatitis, malaria and pneumonia as causes of death while still often holding the true cause to be *kanaima* or another malevolent spirit. A person's prized possessions are buried with them for use in the afterlife. Polygyny, once practised by leaders, has nearly disappeared, possibly under missionary pressure, and most marriages are now consecrated by a Catholic priest; divorce is not uncommon and may be initiated by either spouse, with a village leader sometimes intervening to keep a couple together. Plants with magical properties form their own class in the language, *wapananinau*, with important functions for shamans of the traditional beliefs.

## Foodways

Cassava is the crop at the centre of Wapishana life, and has a bewildering variety of names in the language. Women grate it, express its juice, sieve it and toast it on iron griddles into flour and thick flat breads, locally called *beiju*; the poisonous juice is driven out beforehand in the plaited press, *nirsh*. Cassava beer was stored in coil-built clay jars. Other crops include sweet potatoes and further roots, squashes, tomatoes, greens, onions, dozens of kinds of hot pepper and many more. Men hunt deer, agouti, wild turkeys and birds; the whole family fishes. Cattle, swine, chickens, ducks and other animals introduced over the past two centuries are now part of the ordinary diet. Exchange of produce, animals and homemade food brings in the small sums of cash used to buy store food and household goods. Peddlers occasionally try to trade, but these transactions are exploitative and avoided by all but the most isolated. The sources do not describe ceremonial dishes, beverages beyond cassava beer, or dietary rules.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used do not record Wapishana folktales, epic or storytelling occasions, but they document the language work that carries oral knowledge. Many plants and animals endemic to the region are known only in Wapishana, and the language has its own taxonomy: three plant classes — *karam'makau* for plants gathered wild, *wapaurib bau* for domesticated plants, often named from the place or farmer they came from, and *wapananinau* for plants with magical properties — encode the cultivation criteria of their users. Wapishana was first used as a teaching language in Indigenous schools in 1987; it was recognised as an official language in the Brazilian municipalities of Cantá and Bonfim in the Serra da Lua region in 2014; Roraima Federal University opened an extension programme for learning it in 2009; and in Guyana organisations such as Wapichan Wadauniinao Ati'o work on preservation. A Wapishana dictionary is published in the Intercontinental Dictionary Series.

## Language & religion

Wapishana belongs to the Arawakan family and is spoken by over 13,000 people on both sides of the border — the only remaining Arawakan language of the circum-Roraima area. Kaufman (1994) treated Wapishana, Atorada and Mapidian as dialects; Aikhenvald (1999) separates Mawayana/Mapidian/Mawakwa from Wapishana and places them in a Rio Branco branch; Ramirez (2020) counts Atorai a dialect of Wapishana. Ethnologue puts Atorada's lexical similarity to Wapishana at 50% and Wapishana's to Mapidian at 10%. Wapishana and the Cariban language Pemon have borrowed heavily from one another through intensive contact. More than 80% of Wapishana speak the national language they are in contact with — Portuguese in Brazil, English in Guyana — and many speak both along with the mother tongue. Religious life today runs through Catholicism, village catechists and a curing practice blended with northeastern Brazilian folk medicine, alongside persisting belief in *kanaima*.

## Sources & further reading

---
title: "Macushi"
subtitle: "Brazil"
region: "Latin America"
tags: [ethnography, latin-america]
---

## Overview

The Macushi (*Makuusi*; Portuguese *Macuxi*, also written Macusi, Macussi, Makushi, Makusi, Teueia and Teweya) are an Indigenous people of the borderlands where northern Brazil, southern Guyana and eastern Venezuela meet. In Brazil they live in northeastern Roraima, along the Rio Branco and the Contingo, Quino, Pium and Mau rivers, and they are the largest Indigenous group in that state and a part of the population of Boa Vista; in Guyana they occupy the northern and southern Rupununi Savannah. Instituto Socioambiental puts the population at about 43,192 — 33,603 in Brazil, 9,500 in Guyana, 89 in Venezuela. Their language belongs to the Macushi-Kapon branch of the Cariban family, and they are counted, with the Arecuna, Kamarakoto and Taurepan, as a sub-group of the Pemon. For folk culture they matter above all as cassava cultivators and as makers of cotton hammocks, featherwork and curare — goods that circulated widely in the region.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Cotton hammock** — Woven cotton hammocks are the best-documented Macushi textile. In the nineteenth century the Macushi "specialized in producing hammocks, various crafts, and a potent form of curare," trading them to other Amerindian groups, often for cassava graters and blow-pipes. A hammock registered in 1947 is coloured blue, red and yellow with synthetic dyes and finished with a tasselled fringe; a second, registered in 1950, is plain cotton.

**Shoulder cloak (dance ornament)** — A man's dance ornament built from a band of woven cotton, from which hang five loose twisted cords, each ending in a ball of down. The woven band plus pendant cords distinguishes it from the solidly feathered capes below.

**Featherwork capes and tippets** — Capes of egret feathers on twine and of macaw feathers on twine are catalogued as medicine men's garments; a further cape or collar of feathers is fastened with cotton cord. A tippet of red macaw feathers and cotton is recorded as worn by a chief or by a dancer at a feast.

**Plaited palm matting and trays** — A serving tray plaited from *ite*-palm leaf was collected in 1912 at the village of Aynaymong, south of Roraima; fire-fans are plaited from palm leaves in the same technique.

**Cane and bamboo casing** — The *matape*, a cassava squeezer, is plaited from cane; a double-case quiver is made of split bamboo lined with reed and coated outside with a thick gum or resinous pitch, with a fibre cord twisted around the middle.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name no motif names, but they describe the ornament carried on specific objects: incised designs picked out in red and white pigment on the triangular blade of a chief's club; four bird-headed figures carved at the broad end of a war club; bands of black lines on the top and bottom of a manioc grater; zigzag lines on a dance rattle-stick; and glass beads strung in alternating red and white on a nose ornament.

### Clothing & dress

The sources describe Macushi dress almost entirely through ceremonial and dance pieces rather than everyday wear. Headgear is the most varied category: head-dresses of feathers mounted on wood with twine and cotton, a crown of feathers and reed, and a basketry frame made to carry a head-dress. Over the shoulders go feather capes — egret and macaw — attributed to medicine men, a feather cape or collar closed with cotton cord, and the cotton-and-down shoulder cloak worn by men in dance. The red macaw-feather tippet is explicitly a chief's or dancer's garment for a feast, so featherwork marks both office and performance. For the feet there is a pair of sandals cut from a split palm-branch, the foot held to the convex side by lengths of two-ply twisted fibre twine. A cotton anklet survives as one of a pair. Body paint belongs to dress as well: a small cane-and-cotton container is catalogued as a container for body paint. The sources do not describe ordinary daily clothing, belts or women's garments.

### Architecture

Macushi villages are linked to one another by tracks and paths, and within a village the houses are built around a central courtyard. Residence after marriage is uxorilocal — the couple lives in the wife's family's village — and the father-in-law holds great importance in Macushi kinship, so the built cluster reflects the kin group that assembled it. Before European colonization the Macushi were semi-nomadic; permanent settlements formed later, usually around Catholic or Anglican missions or government-built schools, and the Brazilian government has since added schools and hospitals. Named Macushi settlements in Guyana include Annai, Kwatamang, Surama, Rewa, Crash Water, Karasabai and Yupukari in the northern Rupununi, and St. Ignatius and Moco-Moco in the south. In Brazil the territory consists of three blocks: the Raposa Serra do Sol Indigenous Territory, the largest and most populated, the San Marcos Indigenous Territory, and small areas around isolated villages in the extreme northwest. The sources do not describe house materials, roof construction or architectural decoration.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The one documented pot is a cooking vessel of red-fired clay, built up from rolls of clay — coil-built, not wheel-thrown — collected in 1912 by Otto Thulin at Aynaymong on the Rio Wailang, a tributary of the Rio Mau (Rio Ireng) southeast of Mount Roraima, during an expedition to Guyana with Olof Liljewalch. Cassava processing accounts for most of the household kit: a wooden manioc grater set with small stones and striped with black lines, the cane *matape* squeezer, the plaited *ite*-palm tray, a palm-leaf fire-fan, and a calabash bowl with a blackened interior. Wooden clubs carry the clearest carving: a chief's club used as a badge of office, knobbed at one end and cut to a triangle at the other with red and white incised work, and a war club bound with cotton cord and carved with four bird-headed figures. Hunting gear includes reed-and-cane poisoned arrows, iron-tipped fish arrows, a bundle of about fifty darts poisoned with curare, and a cotton wrapping for blowpipe arrows.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Silver crescent-shaped nose ornaments are the signature piece: each has two pierced projections above for suspension and a row of teeth cut along the lower edge — one example with eight teeth, another with six. A third nose ornament strings fourteen glass beads, alternating red and white, above a semicircular silver plate, combining imported beads with worked silver. Necklaces use animal and plant materials: a man's necklace of seeds on a double cotton string, and a plaited fibre cord tied with numerous deliberate knots and threaded with about 150 acouri teeth. A cotton anklet completes the body ornament recorded here, along with the cane container for body paint. The sources do not describe tattooing, hairdressing or specific paint designs.

## Music & performance

Macushi instruments in the collections fall into three families. Flutes are made of bone — one with three finger holes and cotton-cord wrappings at both ends, another finished with cotton tassels on loosely twisted cord, a third of deer or possibly large-cat bone — and there is a double flute of reed in which the longer tube is stopped at the upper end with one large and one small hole above and two below, while the shorter tube is open with two oblong facing openings and four small holes along the side between them. Bamboo pan-pipes are also recorded. Membranophones include the *sampura'*, a drum hollowed from a section of palm trunk with skin stretched taut over each end and a cord strung across one head with a small piece of wood wedged beneath it to yield a different note, and a cylindrical wooden drum headed with deer skin, laced with cotton string and struck with a wooden beater. Rattles are tied to dancing: sticks of wood or cane, one ornamented with zigzag lines, carry plaited cotton bands hung with *Thevetia peruviana* seeds and are used to beat time in dancing. A longer conjuring wand, a stick about four feet long with cords of roughly 2 ft 8 in and 3 ft 6 in at each end strung with large halved *sibeni* seeds, was rattled by *piai*-men at their dances.

## Dance & theatre

The sources name no individual Macushi dances, but they document the apparatus and the personnel of dancing clearly. Rattle-sticks of wood and cane, hung with thevetia seeds on plaited cotton bands, were used to beat time in dancing; the *piaiman* — the medicine-man and spiritual leader, called *piai*-man or conjurer in the older catalogue language — rattled a long seed-hung wand at his dances; and the red macaw-feather tippet was worn by a chief or by a dancer at a feast, as was the cotton-and-down shoulder cloak listed as a man's dance ornament. Costume therefore distinguishes ritual performance by a specialist from festive dancing by chiefs and others. No dramatic or puppet tradition appears in the sources.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources give no annual festival calendar. What they do document is the ritual world that the objects serve. Feasts are attested indirectly, through the chief's or dancer's feather tippet worn at one. Ritual authority rests with the *piaiman*, the medicine-man and spiritual leader, whose feather capes, conjuring wand and dances the collections record; the role is shared with neighbouring peoples such as the Patamona and Akawaio. Against him stands belief in *keinaimi* (*kanaima*), an evil spirit personified as an "outsider" who brings death and misfortune, associated with shape-shifting into animals — jaguars, bats, armadillos — and with attacks on people caught alone, who are assaulted and die some days later; the same term also covers stealthy, assassin-like action used as protection, which can rebound on those it was meant to shield. Life-cycle practice is documented at marriage: the couple settles in the wife's family's village, and the father-in-law becomes a figure of great importance. Village standing is measured by success in cassava farming. Since the eighteenth century Catholic and Anglican missions have anchored many permanent settlements; the Jesuit Cuthbert Cary-Elwes settled among the Rupununi Macushi in 1909, learned the language, and stayed more than twenty-three years.

## Foodways

Macushi subsistence combines hunting, fishing and shifting cultivation, with fish-poisoning used to take fish. Hunting gear is well represented: reed and cane arrows poisoned at the tip, iron-headed fish arrows, and bundles of some fifty darts poisoned with curare — a potent form of which the Macushi themselves produced and traded in the nineteenth century, when they also acquired blow-pipes and cassava graters by exchange. The staple is bitter cassava, and traditional life relies on it heavily. Cultivation is divided by gender: men clear the land, women tend and harvest. Women are also the main processors, and the recorded products are cassava bread, *farine*, *parakari*, *wo* (a drink), starch tapioca and *casereep*. The processing chain survives in the objects: a wooden grater set with small stones, the cane *matape* squeezer for expressing the poisonous juice, the plaited *ite*-palm tray, a palm-leaf fire-fan for the hearth, the coil-built red clay cooking pot from Aynaymong, and a calabash bowl with blackened interior. In Macushi lore cassava was created to be cultivated and is overseen by a Cassava Mother, *kisera yan*. Village status is correlated with success in cassava farming.

## Oral tradition & literature

Macushi oral history makes the people descendants of the sun's children: the benevolent *Insikiran* (*Inshkirung*) and his malevolent brother *Makunaima*, also called *Negi*, who created fire and also diseases; the brothers are likewise credited with the discovery of *Washacá*, the Tree of Life. The Macushi hold to a life principle, *stkaton*, which comes from the sun. Narrative also carries history: the memories of villages abandoned and escape plans laid as Portuguese settlers, rubber extractivists, mineral developers and later *grileiros* — forgers of land titles — pressed into the territory are still preserved in Macushi oral histories, documented for Instituto Socioambiental by the anthropologist Paulo Santilli. Written literature in the language began with the New Testament, translated into Macushi in 1996 and printed in Latin script. Among contemporary Macushi authors and public figures are the Brazilian artist, activist and writer Jaider Esbell (1979–2021) and the activist and tribal leader Bernaldina José Pedro (1945–2020).

## Language & religion

Macushi is a Cariban language of the Macushi-Kapon group and the most populous language in the family, written in the Latin script. Abbott (1991) describes its basic word order as OVS, with SOV used to foreground the subject; vowels may be nasal, marked [ã], and the word carries a high or low (unmarked) pitch — *átí* 'you go' against *àtí* 'he goes' — the high pitch falling on the final, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable. Numerals precede the noun they modify; Carson notes the native numeral system cannot express large numbers, so quantifiers are used instead. Macushi communities live in contact with Portuguese in Brazil, English in Guyana, Spanish in Venezuela, and Wapixana. Crevels (2012) lists the language as "potentially endangered" and the UNESCO Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger as "vulnerable," status 6b, Threatened; in the 1950s Macushi were hesitant to teach it to outsiders, and it was disparaged as "slang" beside official Portuguese. Religious life combines the *piaiman* and *kanaima* complex described above with long-established Catholic and Anglican mission presence.

title: "Macushi"

region: "Latin America"

## At a glance
| | |
|---|---|
| Who | The Macushi, an Indigenous people of the borderlands where Brazil, Guyana and Venezuela meet |
| Where | Northeastern Roraima in Brazil and the Rupununi Savannah in Guyana |
| How many | About 43,192 people: 33,603 in Brazil, 9,500 in Guyana, 89 in Venezuela |
| Language | Macushi, a Cariban language of the Macushi-Kapon group, written in Latin script |
| Religion | A blend of indigenous beliefs centered on the piaiman (medicine man) and kanaima (evil spirit), with Catholic and Anglican mission influence |
| Known for | Cassava cultivation and processing · Woven cotton hammocks · Featherwork and capes · Curare poison production · Silver nose ornaments |

## Overview

The Macushi are the largest Indigenous group in northeastern Roraima, Brazil, and also live in Guyana and Venezuela. They speak a Cariban language and are part of the broader Pemon cultural group. Their material culture centers on cassava farming, cotton weaving, featherwork and metalwork that circulated widely in the region. They live in uxorilocal villages organized around family groups and have maintained oral traditions, ritual practices and a blend of indigenous and Christian beliefs.

## Material culture

Macushi material culture reflects their mastery of plant fibers, feathers and metalwork, with objects designed for both everyday use and ritual performance.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Woven cotton is the foundation of Macushi textile arts, from hammocks to dance ornaments.

- **Cotton hammock** — A woven cotton hammock dyed in bright colors with synthetic dyes or left plain, finished with tasselled fringe, traded widely in the region.
- **Shoulder cloak** — A man's dance ornament made from a woven cotton band with five hanging twisted cords, each ending in a ball of down.
- **Featherwork cape** — A cape made of egret or macaw feathers on twine, fastened with cotton cord, worn by medicine men or chiefs.
- **Plaited palm tray** (*ite-palm*) — A serving tray woven from ite-palm leaf, used in food preparation and serving.
- **Cassava squeezer** (*matape*) — A plaited cane device used to squeeze poisonous juice from grated cassava.

### Clothing & dress

Macushi dress emphasizes featherwork and ornament for ceremony and dance rather than everyday wear.

- **Feathered headdress** — Head-dresses of feathers mounted on wood with twine and cotton, or a crown of feathers and reed.
- **Feather tippet** — A red macaw-feather collar worn by a chief or dancer at feasts, marking office and performance.
- **Palm sandals** — Sandals cut from split palm-branch with the foot held to the convex side by lengths of twisted fibre twine.
- **Cotton anklet** — A woven cotton band worn around the ankle as body ornament.
- **Body paint container** — A small cane-and-cotton container used to hold body paint for adornment.

### Architecture

Macushi villages are organized around a central courtyard with houses linked by paths, built by family groups in uxorilocal settlements.

- **Village courtyard layout** — Houses are built around a central courtyard, reflecting the kin group that assembled them.
- **Raposa Serra do Sol Indigenous Territory** — The largest and most populated Macushi territory in Brazil.
- **San Marcos Indigenous Territory** — A second major Macushi territory block in Brazil.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Macushi households are organized around cassava processing, with objects of clay, wood and plant fibers designed for food production.

- **Red clay cooking pot** — A coil-built vessel collected in 1912 at Aynaymong, used for cooking.
- **Wooden manioc grater** — A wooden grater set with small stones and striped with black lines, used to grate cassava root.
- **Chief's club** — A carved wooden club used as a badge of office, knobbed at one end and triangular at the other with red and white incised work.
- **War club** — A wooden club bound with cotton cord and carved with four bird-headed figures.
- **Calabash bowl** — A gourd bowl with a blackened interior used for food storage and preparation.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Silver nose ornaments are the signature Macushi jewelry, often paired with necklaces of teeth, seeds and beads.

- **Silver nose ornament** — A crescent-shaped silver piece with pierced projections above for suspension and teeth cut along the lower edge.
- **Beaded nose ornament** — A semicircular silver plate strung above with fourteen glass beads alternating red and white.
- **Acouri-tooth necklace** — A plaited fibre cord tied with numerous knots and threaded with about 150 acouri teeth, worn by men.
- **Seed necklace** — A man's necklace of seeds strung on a double cotton cord.

## Music & performance

Macushi musicians play bone flutes, reed pipes, drums and rattles, with rattles tied to dancing and ritual.

- **Bone flute** — A flute made of bone with three finger holes and cotton-cord wrappings, or finished with cotton tassels.
- **Double reed flute** — A flute in which a longer tube is stopped at the upper end while a shorter tube is open, used to create multiple notes.
- **Sampura drum** (*sampura'*) — A drum hollowed from a section of palm trunk with skin stretched over each end and a cord strung across one head with a wood piece beneath it for tone variation.
- **Dance rattle stick** — A stick of wood or cane ornamented with zigzag lines, carrying plaited cotton bands hung with thevetia seeds and used to beat time in dancing.
- **Conjuring wand** — A stick about four feet long with cords strung with large halved sibeni seeds, rattled by piaiman at their dances.

## Dance & theatre

Macushi dancing involves rattle-sticks and specialized costumes that distinguish ritual performance by specialists from festive dancing.

- **Piaiman dancer** (*piaiman*) — A medicine-man and spiritual leader who rattles a long seed-hung wand at his dances, marked as a ritual specialist.
- **Rattle-stick dance** — Dancing accompanied by wood or cane rattle-sticks hung with thevetia seeds on plaited cotton bands to beat time.
- **Feast dancing** — Chief or community members dance in feather tippets and cotton-and-down shoulder cloaks at feasts.

## Festivals & rituals

Macushi ritual life centers on the piaiman's authority and the dangerous kanaima spirit, with feasts and life-cycle practices marking community standing.

- **Piaiman** — A medicine-man and spiritual leader who wears feather capes, dances with a conjuring wand and holds ritual authority.
- **Kanaima spirit** (*kanaima, keinaimi*) — An evil outsider spirit that brings death and misfortune through shape-shifting into animals and attacking people caught alone.
- **Feast** — A ceremonial gathering where chiefs and dancers wear feathered ornaments and tippets marking their status.
- **Uxorilocal marriage** — After marriage the couple settles in the wife's family's village, making the father-in-law a figure of great importance.
- **Cassava farming success** — Village standing is measured by success in cassava cultivation.

## Foodways

Macushi subsistence rests on bitter cassava cultivation and processing, with hunting and fishing providing protein and trade goods.

- **Bitter cassava** — The staple crop, cleared by men and tended and harvested by women, supporting traditional Macushi life.
- **Cassava bread** (*cassava bread, farine*) — Processed cassava products made by women during the preparation chain.
- **Curare poison** (*curare*) — A potent arrow and dart poison produced and traded by the Macushi in the nineteenth century.
- **Fish-poisoning** — A hunting technique using poison to take fish from rivers and streams.
- **Cassava Mother** (*kisera yan*) — A supernatural being who oversees cassava cultivation in Macushi lore, where cassava was created to be farmed.

## Oral tradition & literature

Macushi oral history traces descent from the sun's children and records territorial struggles against colonial settlers and land forgers.

- **Insikiran** (*Insikiran, Inshkirung*) — The benevolent sun-child who, with his malevolent brother Makunaima, created the world and discovered the Tree of Life.
- **Makunaima** (*Makunaima, Negi*) — The malevolent brother of Insikiran who created fire and diseases.
- **Washacá** — The Tree of Life, discovered by the sun-children in Macushi creation narrative.
- **Life principle** (*stkaton*) — A spiritual essence that comes from the sun in Macushi belief.
- **New Testament translation** — The New Testament translated into Macushi in 1996 and printed in Latin script, marking the start of written literature.

## Language & religion

Macushi is a Cariban language with OVS word order, marked as vulnerable to language loss, and the community blends indigenous piaiman beliefs with Catholic and Anglican mission Christianity.

- **Macushi language** (*Macushi*) — A Cariban language of the Macushi-Kapon group, the most populous in its family, written in Latin script with high and low pitch marking distinctions.
- **OVS word order** — The basic word order of Macushi places the object before the verb and subject, with SOV used to foreground the subject.
- **Language endangerment** — Macushi is listed as vulnerable and potentially endangered, having been disparaged as slang beside official Portuguese.
- **Piaiman complex** (*piaiman*) — A ritual system centered on the medicine-man and the kanaima spirit, blended with long-established Catholic and Anglican mission presence.

## Glossary

- *Macushi* — An Indigenous people of the Brazil-Guyana-Venezuela borderlands
- *matape* — A plaited cane squeezer for expressing cassava juice
- *ite-palm* — A palm species whose leaves are plaited into trays and fans
- *piaiman* — A medicine-man and spiritual leader who conducts rituals and dances
- *kisera yan* — The Cassava Mother, a supernatural being overseeing cassava cultivation
- *stkaton* — A life principle or spiritual essence that comes from the sun
- *Washacá* — The Tree of Life discovered by the sun-children
- *sampura'* — A drum made from a palm trunk section with skin heads and a tone-modifying cord
- *thevetia seeds* — Seeds used as rattles on dance sticks and conjuring wands
- *sibeni seeds* — Large seeds halved and strung on a conjuring wand
- *curare* — A potent poison used on arrows and darts for hunting
- *farine* — A processed cassava product made by women
- *wo* — A cassava drink made by women

## Sources & further reading

- Cary-Elwes, Cuthbert; Bridges, John (ed.). Rupununi Mission: the story of Cuthbert Cary-Elwes. London: Jesuit Missions, 1985.
- Paulo Santilli, anthropologist, on Macushi history and territory for Instituto Socioambiental (Povos Indígenas no Brasil).
- Crevels, Mily (2012) on the vitality of Brazilian Indigenous languages, listing Macushi as potentially endangered; UNESCO Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger (Macushi: "vulnerable").
- Abbott (1991) on Macushi OVS word order; Carson on Macushi numerals and quantifiers.
- The New Testament in the Macushi Language of Brazil (1996).
- Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macushi and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macushi_language

- Museum of World Culture / Världskulturmuseet, Gothenburg (Otto Thulin and Olof Liljewalch collection, 1912): https://www.varldskulturmuseerna.se

title: "Bora"
subtitle: "Brazil"
region: "Latin America"
tags: [ethnography, latin-america]

## Overview

The Bora are an Indigenous people of the Amazon in Peru, Colombia and Brazil, living in the country between the Napo, Putumayo and Caquetá rivers. The Wikipedia account of the group gives their number as approximately 2,000; counts of speakers of the Bora language are higher, with about 2,328 in Peru along the northeastern Yaguasyacu, Putumayo and Ampiyacu rivers and about 500 in the Putumayo Department of Colombia. Bora belongs to the proposed Bora–Witoto language family and is tonal — a trait it shares in the region only with Ticuna. Over roughly the last forty years the Bora have become a largely settled people in permanent forest settlements. In folk-culture terms they are known for a detailed working knowledge of rainforest plant life, for feather and fibre ornament made from hand-twisted cotton, and for large wooden signal drums recorded in the field in the 1940s.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources document one fibre tradition in any detail, and it is an ornament rather than a woven cloth.

**Twisted-cotton feather headdress** — A headdress in the Museum of Ethnography (accession 1865.01.0231) is built on a base of coarse, twisted cotton threads, with yellow and red feathers set so that a crescent of feathering stands around the head and a bunch of cotton threads hangs at the nape; the cotton cord is secured with a knot of plant-fibre thread. The museum's note records Thomas Whiffen's observation that twisted cotton was used in this region only by the Bora, who made a few head ornaments from it — which is what distinguishes the piece from the fibre work of neighbouring peoples.

The sources used here name no further textile traditions and no motif vocabulary.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not describe Bora everyday or ceremonial clothing. What they record of dress is ornament worn on the body: necklaces, wrist bands of snakeskin and ear ornaments, all collected in northwestern Amazonas (Brazil) on the Swedish Amazon expedition of 1923–1925, together with the feather headdress described above. Nothing in these records separates men's from women's dress, or ceremonial from daily wear.

### Architecture

The only statement the sources make about Bora building is that the Bora have, over roughly the last forty years, come to live mostly in permanent forest settlements; no house form, material or roof type is described.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

No ceramics or metalwork appear in the sources. Two classes of wooden object are documented. Bows and arrows are named as the main weapons used in person-to-person conflict. Large **wooden drums** were photographed in 1941 on the Yaguasyacu river, in the triangle between the Amazon and the Putumayo in northeastern Peru, during A. L. Wenner-Gren's expedition of 1940–1941; the catalogue distinguishes one of them as the "male" drum of a pair, and the accompanying original label records that the collection was sent on to the Museum of the American Indian in New York. The photographs are attributed on the catalogue card to Dr. Paul Fejos, though the museum notes that Norman Mathews was the expedition's photographer and has been assumed to be the maker.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Four of the objects shown are personal ornaments collected by Douglas Melin in northwestern Amazonas on the Swedish Amazon expedition of 1923–1925: two necklaces (1926.07.0024 and 1926.07.0025), a pair of wrist bands made of snakeskin (1926.07.0026a–b), and a pair of ear sticks of cane (1926.07.0027a–b) whose surfaces are decorated with designs burned into the material. With the feather headdress on its twisted-cotton base, these make up the whole of the body adornment the sources attest. No tattooing, body paint or hair practice is described in them.

## Music & performance

The sources document a single instrument, and they document it as an object rather than as a repertoire. The wooden drums photographed on the Yaguasyacu river in 1941 were made in at least two sizes or genders, the catalogue identifying one as the "male" drum by comparison with the companion image of the pair. The photographs come from the Wenner-Gren expedition of 1940–1941 and reached the Gothenburg museum in 1965 through Mrs. M. Wenner-Gren, Carl-E. Grenninger and Henry Wassén; the catalogue record cites Julian Steward's chapter "The Witotoan Tribes" in volume 3 of the *Handbook of South American Indians* (1946) as its ethnographic reference. The same record places the photographs with a Bora sub-group it names Bua, glossing the name as "crocodile." No song genre, singer, vocal style or performance occasion is named in any of the sources used here, and nothing in them describes how the drums were played or what they communicated.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not cover Bora dance or dramatic performance.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not describe a festival calendar or named life-cycle rites. They do record two features of social and religious life. Bora families practise exogamy, marrying outside the group. The Bora worldview is animist and makes no distinction between the physical and the spiritual world, spirits being understood as present throughout it. The elaborate Bora knowledge of the plants of the surrounding rainforest, and in particular the complex importance of trees — a concern they share with other Indigenous peoples of the Peruvian Amazon such as the Urarina — is the one domain the sources treat as both practical and more than practical.

## Foodways

The sources used do not cover Bora food, cooking or drink.

## Oral tradition & literature

No Bora narrative cycle or epic is named in the sources, but they record substantial documentation of Bora speech. A written form of the language was developed by the Wycliffe Bible Translators Wesley and Eva Thiesen with speakers in the village of Brillo Nuevo on the Yaguasyacu river: first school books from Bora into Spanish, then a translation of the New Testament, and finally a full dictionary and grammar, which in turn made further textbooks possible so that speakers could be taught to read and write their own language against the pressure of Spanish and Portuguese. Their daughter Ruth is the first non-native recorded to have learned the language. A published collection of Bora folkloric texts exists, and the Bora DoReCo corpus compiled by Frank Seifart holds audio recordings of narrative texts with phone-level transcription, translations and morphological annotation. Separately, the Universidad Nacional de Colombia, funded by the Modern Endangered Archives Program at the UCLA library, digitized a large body of recordings from three Indigenous groups of the Colombian Amazon, among them the Miraña.

## Language & religion

Bora is spoken in the western Amazon and belongs to the proposed Bora–Witoto family; early investigators took it to be related to Witoto, but there is very little similarity between the two, and a nineteenth-century museum note still describes Bora as a divergent dialect of Witoto. It is tonal, contrasts vowel length, and has 350 classifiers — more than any other language so far described. Miraña, spoken along the Caquetá-Japurá river from Colombia into Brazil, is 94 per cent mutually comprehensible with Bora proper; Muinane, on tributaries of the Caquetá in central Colombia, about 50 per cent. Loukotka (1968) also lists Bora (Boro) on the Cahuinari river and in a colony at Méria on the Igara Paraná, Imihitä (Emejeite) on the Jacaré river, and the poorly attested Fa:ai of the Sierra Futahy. Literacy in Bora among Peruvian speakers runs at 10 to 30 per cent, and in Spanish as a second language at 25 to 50 per cent. Religion, as the sources give it, is animist.

Two historical facts belong here because they shaped the rest. During the rubber boom and the Putumayo genocide around the turn of the twentieth century the Bora suffered enslavement and physical abuse, with hundreds held at rubber stations of Julio César Arana's company — Entre Rios, La Sabana, Santa Catalina and Abisinia — and an unknown number fleeing across the Caquetá river. The ancestral lands are now threatened by illegal logging, and the Bora hold no indigenous reserves.

---
title: "Munduruku"
subtitle: "Brazil"
region: "Latin America"
tags: [ethnography, latin-america]
---

## Overview

The Munduruku — also recorded as Mundurucu, Maytapu and Cara Preta, and known by their own name *Wuy Jugu* — are an Indigenous people of the Brazilian Amazon, historically centred on the Tapajós river valley, a territory called Mundurukânia in the nineteenth century. Today they live in southwestern Pará along the Tapajós and its tributaries (municipalities of Santarém, Itaituba and Jacareacanga), in eastern Amazonas along the Canumã River (Nova Olinda and Borba), and in northern Mato Grosso in the Peixe River region (Juara); some communities belong to the Coatá-Laranjal Indigenous Land. They settle forest margins of navigable rivers, with traditional villages in the "Tapajós fields", patches of savannah inside the rainforest. The largest concentration is in the Munduruku Indigenous Territory, most villages strung along the Cururu River. An estimated 13,755 people in 2014 speak a language of the Tupi family. In folk-culture terms they are known above all for featherwork regalia and spiral-coiled basketry, both well represented in European collections.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources available here document two bodies of work in detail: feather assemblage bound with hand-spun cotton, and coiled vine basketry.

**Featherwork regalia** — The largest documented body of Munduruku material culture is a family of feather objects built on cotton string: head-dresses, crowns, caps or hoods (one worked entirely in black feathers on cotton cord), belts and girdles, a feather petticoat or skirt, and armlets, leglets and paired pendants. The structural principle is consistent — feathers mounted and lashed onto cotton string or cord, occasionally onto cotton cloth — so that a single technique yields ornaments for head, waist and limbs.

**Feathered sceptres and staffs** — Plumed rods combining feather with cane or reed, cotton string and resin. Catalogued examples pair a reed handle with mounted blue, red and yellow feathers, or with red, yellow and black, making deliberate colour triads a feature of the form rather than an accident of available plumage.

**Cipó spiral basketry** — Baskets coiled from *cipó* (vine) in spiral technique, collected on the Rio Paracuny in 1926 by Curt Nimuendajú. The documented repertoire includes tall and low conical baskets and a shallow plaited basketry dish, so the same coiling tradition covers both carrying and serving vessels.

The sources used do not name motifs for any of these traditions, nor do they describe loom weaving.

### Clothing & dress

What the sources record of Munduruku dress is almost entirely the feather assemblage described above, and the catalogue entries do not distinguish men's from women's wear. Head coverings appear in two forms: open head-dresses of feathers and string, and closed caps or hoods, including one made up in black feathers on cotton cord. A feather crown is catalogued separately from the head-dresses. For the body there are belts and girdles of feathers on cotton string, and a feather petticoat or skirt; for the limbs, armlets, leg-bands, leglets and pendants that survive in pairs. A further ornament is mounted on cotton cloth rather than string. Two early images give some sense of how such pieces were worn: a portrait drawing of a Munduruku man made by H. Florence at Salto Augusto in 1828, and an engraving after J. Barbosa Rodrigues's *Tribu dos Mundurucus* (Rio de Janeiro, 1882) showing a man with a head trophy. The sources do not describe footwear or everyday, non-ornamental clothing.

### Architecture

The sources used do not describe Munduruku house form, materials or roof construction. They do record the residence pattern, which is the most distinctive feature of the Munduruku village: households are organised not by conjugal or affinal bonds but by sex and age, with all males over the age of thirteen living in one house and all the females, together with the boys under thirteen, in another. Villages themselves sit on the margins of navigable rivers and, in the traditional pattern, in the savannah clearings of the "Tapajós fields".

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The everyday objects documented for this atlas are basketry rather than pottery or metal. Three *cipó* baskets worked in spiral technique and one basket-plaited dish, all collected by Curt Nimuendajú at the Rio Paracuny in 1926, cover storage, carrying and serving; one of the baskets is explicitly recorded as low and conical. Beyond basketry, the catalogue records reed and cane as structural materials in the feathered sceptres and staffs, and resin as an adhesive. The sources used do not describe Munduruku ceramics or metalwork.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Munduruku body adornment as documented here is feather-based and worn on the limbs: armlets, leg-bands, leglets and pendants, all made of feathers mounted on cotton string, with pendants surviving as pairs. One further ornament is built on cotton cloth. The feather crown, caps and hoods extend the same technique to the head. The sources used do not document beadwork, seed necklaces, tattooing or hair practices. They do, however, record one body practice in detail: before the European arrival in America the Munduruku removed the skin from a man's head and dried it, producing a reduced head used for religious purposes — the practice behind their historical reputation as "head cutters". It is no longer carried out, though many of these trophy heads remain in museum collections worldwide, and a nineteenth-century drawing after Barbosa Rodrigues shows a Munduruku man holding one.

## Music & performance

One Munduruku instrument is documented in the material gathered for this atlas, and it is documented unusually precisely. A side-blown trumpet 95 cm long, from the Spix & Martius collection, is held by the British Museum as catalogue number 8731; the Museum of World Culture in Gothenburg holds a British Museum photograph of it, taken before 1935 and acquired from K. G. Izikowitz in June 1948. Izikowitz published the instrument as a drawing, figure 116 in his *Musical and Other Sound Instruments of the South American Indians* (Göteborg, 1935) — the standard early survey of South American Indigenous instruments, and the reason this trumpet is comparatively well recorded. The side-blown construction places it in a distinct class from the end-blown trumpets more often collected in the region. The feathered sceptres and plumed rods in the British Museum would plausibly have been carried in performance, but the catalogue entries assign them no performance context, and the sources used name no song genres, no ensemble types and no performance occasions.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not cover Munduruku dance or dramatic traditions.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used name no annual festivals and no life-cycle rites of birth, marriage or death. They do describe the ritual framework governing hunting, which structures Munduruku dealings with the forest. The Munduruku hold beliefs in multiple Supernatural Gamekeepers: every creature they hunt has a spirit mother deity who watches over her children and ensures that the animals return to the world after death. Observing the proper rules of respect toward the game keeps that rebirth cycle turning. These beliefs shape how Munduruku hunters treat their environment and carry consequences, positive and negative, for the survival of particular species. The one other ritual the sources record is the pre-Columbian preparation of dried, reduced heads for religious use, a practice now abandoned.

## Foodways

The sources used do not cover Munduruku staples, dishes, cooking methods or ceremonial food. They establish only that hunting is central enough to be governed by an elaborate set of ritual obligations to the spirit mothers of game animals, and that the coiled *cipó* baskets and the basket-plaited dish in Gothenburg served household food handling.

## Oral tradition & literature

Munduruku oral history explains the exonym by which the people are generally known: *Munduruku* is said to come from their enemies the Parintintin and to mean 'red ants', a reference to the Munduruku tactic of attacking en masse. The people's own name for themselves is *Wuy Jugu*, rendered elsewhere as *wuyjuyu* or *wuujuyû*, meaning 'people' or 'our people'; everyone outside the group is *pariwat*, and is spoken of with the term that also means 'prey'. That lexical division of the world into people and prey is the most-discussed feature of Munduruku speech. The sources name no epic cycle, folktale corpus or proverb collection. On the contemporary side, elementary schools operate in almost all villages and Brazilian government courses have handed education over to the Munduruku themselves, who are beginning to run their own formal schooling; Daniel Munduruku, an educator, author and museum director, is the group's best-known literary figure. Gomes (2006) frames present-day Munduruku politics as an attempt to "cut off the head" of adversaries through dialogue, across territorial, health, educational and linguistic disputes.

## Language & religion

Munduruku belongs to the Tupi family and forms, with Kuruaya, the Munduruku branch; roughly 10,000 people speak it in the Tapajós basin of north-central Brazil. It is an OV language with sixteen consonant phonemes, no consonant clusters, syllables of the shapes CV, CVC, V and VC, and four phonemic accents per syllable — three of pitch and one of laryngealization. Speakers in the Tapajós valley villages use Munduruku exclusively, even with non-Indigenous visitors; most women and children are monolingual, and bilingualism in Portuguese generally begins at school around age ten. Some language loss is occurring near the Madeira River and on town outskirts. The language lacks number words above five, a feature studied by Pierre Pica with Stanislas Dehaene and Elizabeth Spelke, who also showed that Munduruku speakers map numbers onto scales logarithmically; the lexical limit does not prevent calculation with larger quantities. On religion, the sources record the Supernatural Gamekeepers and the former preparation of reduced heads, and nothing further.

## Sources & further reading

- K. G. Izikowitz, *Musical and Other Sound Instruments of the South American Indians*, Göteborg, 1935 (the Munduruku side-blown trumpet is figure 116)
- J. Barbosa Rodrigues, "Tribu dos Mundurucus", pp. 27–28 in *Revista da Exposição Anthropologica Brazileira*, Rio de Janeiro, 1882
- P. Pica, C. Lemer, V. Izard and S. Dehaene, "Exact and approximate arithmetic in an Amazonian Indigene Group", *Science* 306 (5695), 2004, 499–503
- S. Dehaene, V. Izard, E. Spelke and P. Pica, "Log or linear? Distinct Intuitions of the number scale in Western and Amazonian Indigene Culture", *Science* 320 (5880), 2008, 1217–1220
- P. Pica and A. Lecomte, "Theoretical implications of the study of Numbers and Numerals in Mundurucu", *Philosophical Psychology* 21 (4), 2008
- Curt Nimuendajú's 1926 Rio Paracuny collection of *cipó* basketry, Museum of World Culture, Gothenburg; the Spix & Martius collection and the Munduruku featherwork in the British Museum
- "Wuy Jugu (Mundurucu) works", National Museum of the American Indian
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munduruku
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munduruku_language

## Overview

The Munduruku are an Indigenous Amazonian people centered historically on the Tapajós River valley and today spread across three Brazilian states. They live on forest margins of navigable rivers and traditional savannah clearings. They are known worldwide for their featherwork and basketry in European collections, and speak a Tupi language with distinctive features like the absence of number words above five.

## Material culture

Munduruku material culture centers on two major traditions: featherwork assemblies built on cotton string and coiled vine basketry, with lesser documentation of everyday objects and architecture.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Two main textile traditions are documented: feather assemblage on cotton string and coiled vine basketry.

- **Featherwork regalia** — Feathers mounted on cotton string or cloth forming head-dresses, crowns, caps, belts, skirts, and limb ornaments.
- **Feathered sceptres and staffs** — Plumed rods combining feathers with cane or reed, using deliberate colour triads of blue, red, yellow or red, yellow and black.
- **Cipó spiral basketry** (*cipó*) — Baskets coiled from vine in spiral technique, including tall and low conical shapes and shallow plaited dishes for carrying and serving.

### Clothing & dress

Munduruku dress as documented consists almost entirely of feather ornaments worn on the head, body, and limbs.

- **Head-dresses and caps** — Open head-dresses of feathers and string, and closed caps or hoods including one made entirely in black feathers.
- **Feather crown** — A separate head ornament of feathers on cotton string.
- **Feather belts and skirts** — Belts and girdles of feathers on cotton string, and a feather petticoat or skirt for the body.
- **Limb ornaments** — Armlets, leg-bands, leglets and paired pendants all made of feathers mounted on cotton string.

### Architecture

Munduruku villages organize households by sex and age rather than family bonds, situated on river margins and savannah clearings.

- **Male house** — A single communal house where all males over thirteen years old live together.
- **Female house** — A communal house housing all females and boys under thirteen.
- **Tapajós fields** — Savannah clearings inside the rainforest where traditional Munduruku villages are situated.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Munduruku everyday objects are documented primarily as basketry rather than pottery or metalwork.

- **Cipó baskets** (*cipó*) — Spiral-coiled vine baskets in tall and low conical forms for storage and carrying.
- **Basket-plaited dish** — A shallow plaited vessel for serving food.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Body adornment is feather-based, worn on limbs and head, with one documented practice of preparing reduced heads for ritual use.

- **Limb ornaments** — Armlets, leg-bands, leglets and paired pendants of feathers on cotton string.
- **Feather crowns and caps** — Head ornaments of feathers mounted on cotton string.
- **Reduced head** — The skin of a deceased man's head dried and prepared for religious purposes, a pre-Columbian practice now abandoned.

## Music & performance

One Munduruku instrument is well documented: a side-blown trumpet that represents a distinct construction type in the region.

- **Side-blown trumpet** — A 95 cm long trumpet held by the British Museum, distinguished from the more common end-blown trumpets of the region.

## Dance & theatre

No sources cover Munduruku dance or dramatic traditions.

## Festivals & rituals

Munduruku ritual life centers on hunting and respect for the Supernatural Gamekeepers who protect game animals.

- **Supernatural Gamekeepers** — Spirit mother deities who watch over each hunted creature and ensure the animals return to the world after death.
- **Hunting ritual obligations** — Rules of respect toward game that maintain the rebirth cycle and ensure the survival of species.

## Foodways

Hunting is central to Munduruku life and governed by elaborate ritual obligations to the spirit mothers of game.

- **Game hunting** — Central to Munduruku subsistence and governed by ritual beliefs in Supernatural Gamekeepers.

## Oral tradition & literature

Munduruku oral history explains their name and their own self-designation reflects a division of the world into people and prey.

- **Munduruku etymology** (*Munduruku*) — The exonym means 'red ants' from enemies the Parintintin, referring to the Munduruku tactic of attacking in masses.
- **Wuy Jugu** — The Munduruku's own name for themselves, meaning 'people' or 'our people'.
- **Daniel Munduruku** — An educator, author and museum director, the group's best-known literary figure.

## Language & religion

Munduruku is a Tupi language with distinctive phonetic features and an unusual absence of number words above five, while religion centers on Supernatural Gamekeepers.

- **Munduruku language** (*Munduruku*) — A Tupi family language with sixteen consonant phonemes, no consonant clusters, and four phonemic accents per syllable.
- **Number limit** — Munduruku lacks number words above five, but speakers map numbers logarithmically and can still calculate larger quantities.
- **Pariwat** — The Munduruku term for anyone outside the group, using the same word that also means 'prey'.

## Glossary

- *Munduruku* — The people's exonym, meaning 'red ants' in reference to their mass-attack tactics
- *Wuy Jugu* — The Munduruku's own name for themselves, meaning 'people' or 'our people'
- *pariwat* — Munduruku word for anyone outside the group, also meaning 'prey'
- *Tapajós fields* — Savannah clearings inside the rainforest where traditional villages are situated
- *cipó* — Vine used in spiral-coiled basketry for carrying and serving vessels
- *Supernatural Gamekeepers* — Spirit mother deities who protect hunted animals and ensure their rebirth
- *Parintintin* — A people historically hostile to the Munduruku
- *reduced head* — A dried human head prepared for pre-Columbian religious ritual purposes
- *side-blown trumpet* — A wind instrument played by blowing across the side, distinct from end-blown types
- *featherwork regalia* — Ornaments of feathers mounted on cotton string or cloth for head, body and limbs
- *logarithmically* — Mapping numbers on a logarithmic scale rather than a linear one

title: "Kali'na"
subtitle: "Venezuela"
region: "Latin America"
tags: [ethnography, latin-america]
---

## Overview

The Kali'na — also written Kalina, Caliña, Karìna, Kariña, Kalihna and Kalinya, and long known in European languages as the Caribs or mainland Caribs — are an Indigenous people of the northern coastal zone of South America, today living mostly in villages along the rivers and coasts of Venezuela, Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana and Brazil. Venezuela holds the largest share of the population, concentrated in two separate zones: the Llanos of the Orinoco river valley and the valley of the Cuyuni River, part of which lies in Guyana. Their language, *Karìna auran*, belongs to the Cariban family; the self-designation *Kalina* literally means "person." Before 1492 Kali'na settlement ran along the coast from the mouth of the Amazon to that of the Orinoco. For a folk-culture atlas they matter as a people whose history was carried orally rather than in writing, and whose material record survives largely in early twentieth-century collections of pottery, bows, basketry and instruments.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used here — the Wikipedia articles on the Kalina people and the Kali'na language, and the catalogue records of the objects shown — say nothing about Kali'na weaving, loom work or textile patterning, so no textile tradition can be described from them.

### Clothing & dress

The sources describe no garment types, head coverings, belts or footwear, for either everyday or ceremonial use; the only dress-related practice they record is body-painting, which forms part of the *Epekotono* mourning-conclusion celebration among the Kali'na of the Guianas.

### Architecture

House form, building materials and roof construction are not covered by these sources. What they do record is the settlement geography: in French Guiana the communities between the Maroni and the Mana rivers — Awala-Yalimapo (the only one where Kali'na are a majority), Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni, Mana and Iracoubo — plus the Amerindian village of Kourou and, in smaller numbers, the island of Cayenne. In Suriname the main settlements are Bernharddorp, Wit-Santi, Galibi, Powakka and Bigi Ston, with a large part of the population in the Para District, often in villages shared with the Lokono; Konomerume, near the Wajambo River, has about 349 residents, a majority of whom identify as Kari'nja. In Brazil, São José dos Galibi was founded in 1950 on the right bank of the Oyapock River by families from the Mana River region, while the Galibi Marworno live further inland along the Uaçá River, with Kumarumã as the main settlement. Archaeology on 310 km² of land recovered from the Sinnamary River by the Petit-Saut Dam has yielded 273 Amerindian sites, some about two thousand years old.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Pottery is the best-documented Kali'na craft in these collections. British Museum records list flat-bottomed globular vessels tapering to a neck and flaring at the rim, some in red slip with pale geometric designs, some varnished; a double-bodied bridge vessel; a jug with a looped handle from shoulder to rim; a lidded earthenware pot with slip-painted lines and spots; basins and bowls with waved rims and glazed, decorated interiors; a rounded vessel with a looped handle across the top, a spout to one side and bird wings and tail modelled around the others; and a group of polychrome-slipped figurines in the form of a frog balanced on four feet, an armadillo, a dog in a loose collar, an unidentified quadruped and a standing human figure with raised arms. Kali'na women prized pebbles of red porphyry, *takuwa*, collected around the Essequibo River for polishing their pottery; the same term also denotes jade. Stone axes and axe-heads are in the British Museum collection, and before contact the Kali'na worked with stone axes and hardwood machetes, iron tools arriving with Europeans. Hunting gear and containers reached the Museum of World Culture in Gothenburg: a strung bow 191 cm long, barbed iron-tipped arrows with feather fletching, and a lidded basket collected by Walter Roth on the Barama River in 1927.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Two armlets collected by Walter Roth on the Barima River in north-western Guyana in 1927 are the only ornaments the sources record; materials and construction are not described. Body-painting is attested as part of *Epekotono*. Nothing in these sources covers tattooing, hairdressing or other body modification.

## Music & performance

Kali'na music is built mainly on percussion. The *sanpula* (also *sambula*) is a large drum with a skin stretched over each end of the shell, the two heads held by hoops drawn together with cord and struck with a mallet. Two kinds of rattle are used, the *kalawasi* (or *kalawashi*) and the *malaka*. The flute, *kuwama*, is still made, though increasingly displaced by the European flute, and there is also a terra-cotta horn, the *kuti*. A bone flute with three finger-holes and incised ornament, collected by Walter Roth on the Barima River in 1927, is among the objects shown here. Music, along with dancing and body-painting, is one of the elements of *Epekotono*, which these sources identify as nowadays the only occasion for gatherings of this kind among the Kali'na. Song genres, instrumental repertoires and professional or specialist performers are not described in the sources used.

## Dance & theatre

Dancing is recorded only as a component of the *Epekotono* celebration, where it accompanies body-painting, music and the symbolic burning of the deceased's belongings; the sources name no individual dances and no dramatic or masked traditions.

## Festivals & rituals

The one ceremony these sources treat in detail is *Epekotono*, the event that closes mourning among the Kali'na of the Guianas. The death of a family member opens a mourning period that can last a year or more, and *Epekotono* ends it. Preparations are organised by a respected member of the village and can take several months to assemble; collecting money for the event is a more recent addition to that role. The celebration is public and draws people from neighbouring villages. It includes body-painting, music, dancing and the symbolic burning of the dead person's belongings, marking the departure of the spirit. When it concludes, mourning is over, ordinary social behaviour resumes, and widows may remarry. Non-Kali'na may attend as guests, but the occasion works to reinforce Kali'na identity, signalled above all by the explicit use of the Kali'na language. *Kasiri*, a cassava-derived beer, is an important part of traditional Kali'na celebrations. Beyond this, the sources record no annual or seasonal festival calendar and no birth, coming-of-age or marriage rites. One modern date is documented: Sylvia Kajoeramari, a Kali'na member of Suriname's National Assembly, successfully led the effort to make the International Day of the World's Indigenous Peoples a public holiday in Suriname.

## Foodways

The sources name a single Kali'na foodstuff: *kasiri*, a beer made from cassava, central to traditional celebrations. No staple dishes, cooking methods, ceremonial foods or dietary rules are described in the material used here.

## Oral tradition & literature

Having no written form of their language before the arrival of Europeans, the Kali'na transmitted their history orally from one generation to the next through tales of myth and legend, and Kali'na remains primarily an oral language today. European observers long failed to distinguish between the various Caribbean peoples, and interest faded after the age of exploration until the late twentieth century, when the French researcher Gérard Collomb, a CNRS specialist in Kali'na culture, took up the subject and the Kali'na themselves began to set down their own history — in particular Félix Tiouka, president of the Association of Amerindians of French Guiana (AAGF), and his son Alexis. Collomb and Tiouka's *Na'na Kali'na — Une histoire des Kali'na en Guyane* (2000) came out of that work. Episodes of contact are preserved in Kali'na vocabulary: Europeans were first understood as *Palanakiłi*, spirits of the sea, a word still used for white people, and France was *Pau:wa*, "The Land of the Whites," the destination of the fifteen Kali'na from Sinnamary and Iracoubo sent in July 1882 to be exhibited at the Jardin d'Acclimatation in Paris, and of a second group in 1892. Edmundo Magaña and Fabiola Jara's study "The Carib sky" (1982) treats Carib celestial knowledge, and *Adaheli* is named as the Sun in the mythology of the Orinoco region.

## Language & religion

Kali'na — also called Kari'nja, Carib and Galibi — is a Cariban language of the Guianan Carib branch, treated as "Carib proper" for its complex pronominal prefix system and ergative-absolutive alignment. The Kalina people article gives above 10,000 speakers (Venezuela 5,000, French Guiana 3,000, Suriname 2,500, Guyana 475, Brazil 100); the language article gives around 7,400 and classifies the language as highly endangered, spoken by elders. Dialects are Venezuelan Carib (1,000), Guyanese Carib (2,000), Western Surinamese Carib (500) and Eastern Surinamese and French Guianese Carib (3,000); Suriname's two varieties are Aretyry in the west and centre and Tyrewuju, used by the majority there. The alphabet has 18 letters, but standardisation is hampered by orthographies shaped by Spanish, Portuguese, Dutch, French and English — the ethnonym alone is written in nine different systems. These sources describe no religious affiliation or ritual specialists.

## Sources & further reading

- Gérard Collomb and Félix Tiouka, *Na'na Kali'na — Une histoire des Kali'na en Guyane*, Ibis Rouge Éditions, 2000 (ISBN 978-2-84450-068-7)
- Gérard Collomb, *Kaliña. Des Amérindiens à Paris. Photographies du prince Roland Bonaparte*, Éditions Créaphis, Paris, 1992; and, with Félix Tiouka and M.P. Jean-Louis, *Pau:wa Itiosan:bola : Des Galibi à Paris en 1892*, Awala-Yalimapo, 1991
- Jil Silberstein, *Kali'na : Une famille indienne de Guyane française*, Albin Michel, 2002 (ISBN 2-226-13300-3)
- Jean Hurault, *Français et indiens en Guyane. 1604–1972*, Paris, 1972; Guyane Presse Diffusion, Cayenne, 1989. Serge Mam Lam Fouck, *Histoire générale de la Guyane française*, Ibis Rouge Éditions, Cayenne, 1996 (ISBN 978-2-84450-163-9)
- Gérard Collomb (CNRS) on Kali'na culture and history; Edmundo Magaña and Fabiola Jara, "The Carib sky," *Journal de la Société des Américanistes* 68 (1982), 105–132, https://doi.org/10.3406/jsa.1982.2212
- Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalina_people and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kali%27na_language
- Smithsonian Folkways search: https://folkways.si.edu/search?query=Carib+Venezuela
- Museum collections holding the objects shown: British Museum, https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection ; Museum of World Culture (Världskulturmuseet), Gothenburg, https://www.varldskulturmuseerna.se/en/

| Where | Northern coastal South America: Venezuela, Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana, and Brazil |
| How many | Over 10,000 speakers (Venezuela 5,000, French Guiana 3,000, Suriname 2,500, Guyana 475, Brazil 100) |
| Language | Kali'na, a Cariban language, highly endangered |
| Religion | Not documented in available sources |
| Known for | Oral history and storytelling · Epekotono mourning ceremony · Cassava beer (kasiri) · Pottery and basketry · Percussion music and drums |

## Overview

The Kali'na are an Indigenous people of northern South America who once lived along the coasts from the Amazon to the Orinoco. Today they live mostly in river and coastal villages across Venezuela, Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana, and Brazil. They have no written tradition and passed their history through oral tales. Their material culture—pottery, basketry, and instruments—survives mainly in early twentieth-century museum collections.

## Material culture

Kali'na material culture is known mainly through pottery, basketry, hunting gear, and musical instruments preserved in museum collections from the early 1900s.

### Textile & pattern traditions

No weaving or textile traditions are documented for the Kali'na.

### Clothing & dress

No garments or everyday dress are recorded, only body-painting as part of ceremonies.

- **Body-painting** — Applied during the Epekotono mourning-conclusion celebration among Kali'na of the Guianas.

### Architecture

House forms and building methods are not documented, but Kali'na settlements cluster in specific river and coastal regions.

- **Awala-Yalimapo** — The only Kali'na-majority settlement in French Guiana, between the Maroni and Mana rivers.
- **Galibi** — A main settlement in Suriname along the coast and rivers.
- **São José dos Galibi** — Founded in 1950 on the Oyapock River in Brazil by families from the Mana River region.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Pottery is the best-documented Kali'na craft, showing skill in form, decoration, and figurative sculpture.

- **Slip-painted vessels** — Flat-bottomed globular pots with red slip and pale geometric designs, or glazed decorated bowls with waved rims.
- **Polychrome figurines** — Clay figures including frogs, armadillos, dogs, and human forms with raised arms.
- **Red porphyry polishing stone** (*takuwa*) — Pebbles collected from the Essequibo River and prized by Kali'na women for polishing pottery.
- **Stone axes** — Pre-contact tools later replaced by European iron tools.
- **Hunting basket** — Lidded containers woven for carrying hunting gear and supplies.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Little is documented about Kali'na ornaments beyond armlets and body-painting.

- **Armlets** — Ornaments collected from the Barima River region; materials and construction not described.

## Music & performance

Kali'na music centers on percussion drums, rattles, and flutes, performed mainly at the Epekotono ceremony.

- **Sanpula drum** (*sanpula or sambula*) — A large two-headed drum with skin stretched over each end and held by hoops, struck with a mallet.
- **Rattles** (*kalawasi or kalawashi; malaka*) — Two kinds of percussion rattles used in Kali'na music.
- **Kuwama flute** (*kuwama*) — A wooden flute still made but increasingly displaced by European instruments.
- **Terra-cotta horn** (*kuti*) — A clay horn used in traditional Kali'na music.
- **Bone flute** — A three-hole flute with incised ornament, collected from the Barima River in 1927.

## Dance & theatre

Dancing is recorded only as part of the Epekotono ceremony; no named dances or dramatic traditions are documented.

- **Epekotono dancing** (*Epekotono*) — Dancing that accompanies body-painting, music, and the symbolic burning of the deceased's possessions.

## Festivals & rituals

The Epekotono ceremony is the primary documented occasion for Kali'na gathering, marking the end of mourning and use of the Kali'na language.

- **Epekotono** — A public mourning-conclusion celebration lasting a year or more, featuring body-painting, music, dancing, and the burning of the deceased's belongings to release the spirit.
- **Kasiri** — A cassava-derived beer central to traditional Kali'na celebrations.

## Foodways

Only one Kali'na foodstuff is documented: kasiri, a cassava beer.

- **Kasiri** — A beer made from cassava, central to traditional Kali'na celebrations and gatherings.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Kali'na transmitted history orally through myth and legend, with modern documentation beginning in the late twentieth century.

- **Na'na Kali'na — Une histoire des Kali'na en Guyane** — A 2000 history by Gérard Collomb and Félix Tiouka, drawing on Kali'na oral tradition and research.
- **Palanakiłi** — The Kali'na word for Europeans, originally meaning 'spirits of the sea,' still used for white people.
- **Pau:wa** — The Kali'na name for France, meaning 'The Land of the Whites,' destination of Kali'na sent for exhibition in Paris in 1882 and 1892.

## Language & religion

Kali'na is a highly endangered Cariban language with complex grammar; no religious practices are documented.

- **Kali'na language** (*Kali'na (Kari'nja, Carib, Galibi)*) — A Cariban language with 7,400 speakers, mainly elders, spread across five countries in four regional dialects.
- **Aretyry dialect** (*Aretyry*) — The Western and central Surinamese variety of Kali'na.
- **Tyrewuju dialect** (*Tyrewuju*) — The Eastern Surinamese and French Guianese variety, spoken by the majority in Suriname.

## Glossary

- *Epekotono* — A mourning-conclusion celebration marking the end of a mourning period, featuring body-painting, music, dancing, and symbolic burning of the deceased's belongings.
- *kasiri* — A cassava-derived beer central to traditional Kali'na celebrations.
- *takuwa* — Red porphyry pebbles from the Essequibo River, prized for polishing pottery; also denotes jade.
- *malaka* — A second type of rattle used in Kali'na music.
- *kuwama* — A wooden flute still made by the Kali'na but increasingly displaced by European instruments.
- *kuti* — A terra-cotta horn used in traditional Kali'na music.
- *Palanakiłi* — The Kali'na word for Europeans, originally meaning 'spirits of the sea.'
- *Pau:wa* — The Kali'na name for France, meaning 'The Land of the Whites.'
- *Kalina* — Self-designation of the Kali'na people, literally meaning 'person.'
- *Aretyry* — The Western and central Surinamese dialect of Kali'na.
- *Tyrewuju* — The Eastern Surinamese and French Guianese dialect of Kali'na, spoken by the majority in Suriname.

title: "Warao"
subtitle: "Venezuela"
region: "Latin America"
tags: [ethnography, latin-america]
