## Overview

The Chamacoco are an Indigenous people of Paraguay divided into two groups: the Ebytoso, long established along the Paraguay River, and the Tomáraho, who lived inland until displacement in the 1970s. Their language, Yshyr ahwoso, belongs to the Zamucoan family and is now endangered. While the Ebytoso abandoned their rituals under missionary pressure, the Tomáraho retained initiation ritual, shamanic knowledge, and myth. They are known above all for their feather-work ceremonial art and the mythic tradition of the ahnapzöro, the gods who taught them to hunt and use tools.

## Material culture

Chamacoco material culture is documented chiefly through feather ornaments, cordage bags and pouches, and dancing regalia collected in the early twentieth century.

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources document a plaited and corded craft economy built from string, twine and fibre cordage.

- **Bags and pouches** (*väska, bolsa, påse*) — The most repeated object type in museum collections, with four bags and one sack catalogued from the Chaco in 1917.
- **Men's belt** (*mansgördel*) — A single man's girdle collected in the Paraguayan Chaco.
- **Fly-whisk** (*flugfläkt*) — A hand-held whisk from the same Boggiani collection series.
- **Feather mantle** — A man's dancing cloak of feathers and string held by the British Museum, the clearest surviving link between ceremonial dress and feather work.

### Clothing & dress

Everyday clothing is not described in the sources; ceremonial dress is documented only through men's dance regalia in feather and cordage.

- **Feather head-dress** (*fjäderprydnad, huvudprydnad*) — A feather ornament stuck into the hair rather than a fitted cap, making it a hair fixture rather than headgear.
- **Dancing tassels and pendants** — Men's ornaments of feathers and string catalogued as dancing regalia.
- **Shoulder ornament** — Worked from egret feathers, quills and twine.
- **Feather band** — An ornament of uncertain use worked from feathers.

### Architecture

The sources do not describe house forms or building materials, only the history of settlement and displacement.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

No ceramic or metalworking tradition is named in the sources, but basketry and wood carving are documented as living object trades.

- **Stone axe** — Catalogued tentatively as a woman's axe made of stone, wood, feather and string, a composite in which hafting cordage and feather elements sit alongside the working stone head.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Personal ornament as it survives in collections is feather work covering wrist, upper arm, shoulder, ear and hair.

- **Feather earring** (*örhänge*) — Of brown feathers, catalogued as a piece from the Chaco.
- **Arm ornaments** (*armprydnad*) — Two matching pieces of brown feathers catalogued as a pair.
- **Wristlets or bracelets** — Two feather-and-fibre pieces held by the British Museum.

## Music & performance

No instruments, song genres, or musical performance contexts are described; evidence of performance is indirect and material.

- **Dancing regalia** — A man's dancing cloak and two men's dancing tassels or pendants place feather ornament at the centre of documented dance practice.

## Dance & theatre

Dance survives in the sources as costume rather than choreography, documented through the boys' initiation ceremony.

- **Boys' initiation ceremony** — The ritual context for feather dancing regalia, retained by the Tomáraho after the Ebytoso abandoned their rituals under missionary pressure.
- **Ahnapzöro** (*anapsoro*) — Powerful, terrible gods with no features in their faces, covered in feathers, hair or strange colours, who initiated the yshyr into their ritual ceremonies.

## Festivals & rituals

The central ritual is the boys' initiation ceremony, whose mythic charter is the arrival and destruction of the ahnapzöro.

- **Eshönewörta** (*Ashnuwerta*) — A leading ahnapzoro who showed the yshyr that the gods could be killed by a blow to the ankle.
- **Karcha Balut** — The place where Nemur took up a snail and loosed the raging river that became the Paraguay River.
- **Balut** — The master or spokesperson of each animal who makes the hunt possible and punishes excess severely.

## Foodways

The Chamacoco were traditionally hunter-gatherers and now farm and raise livestock, working as ranch hands and day labourers.

- **Yacareceros** — Dissident yshyr groups who survive by alligator poaching, a prohibited activity conducted upriver in the marshlands of the Río Negro.

## Oral tradition & literature

The central narrative is the Big Myth of the ahnapzöro, whose closing episode is simultaneously an origin account of the Paraguay River and a binding obligation on the people.

- **The Big Myth** (*ahnapzöro*) — The central Chamacoco narrative of gods who taught the yshyr to hunt and use tools, then were destroyed, surviving in versions that differ between Ebytoso and Tomáraho tellers.
- **Nemur** — One of two ahnapzöro who escaped destruction and created the Paraguay River from a snail shell.
- **Syr** — A figure in the myth who received Nemur's final words binding the yshyr people to follow the words or face sickness, hunger and enemies.
- **Kytymaraha** — Syr's clan, the last of which will be decimated if the yshyr fail to follow the words.

## Language & religion

Yshyr ahwoso is a Zamucoan language with four dialects, now endangered under pressure from Spanish and Guaraní; the Ebytoso converted to Christianity while the Tomáraho preserved shamanism.

title: "Otavalo"
subtitle: "Ecuador"
region: "Latin America"
tags: [ethnography, latin-america]

## Overview

The Otavalo are an indigenous people of the Andean highlands of Imbabura Province in northern Ecuador, centred on the city of *Otavalo*, which lies at an elevation of 2,532 metres (8,307 ft) in high, cool country north of Quito. In 1990 their number was estimated at 45,000 to 50,000 in the Otavalo area, with a further 5,000 to 8,000 living elsewhere in Ecuador or abroad. They speak *Kichwa*, the Quechua dialect of Ecuador, and Spanish, having lost their earlier language — probably a Barbacoan one — sometime after the sixteenth century. Commerce and handcrafts are their principal economic activities, and they enjoy a higher standard of living than most indigenous groups in Ecuador and many mestizos of their area. In folk-culture terms they matter as weavers and as traders: Otavalo-styled textiles woven with alpaca or llama wool are exported to North America, and tourism draws outsiders to the area for the culture and local dress.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources for this atlas record no vernacular Otavalo names for the weaves below; each is described here as the catalogue describes it.

**Woman's woven waist-band** — A cotton band worked so that the two faces differ, one pink and the other red, with added decoration in pink, red and green wool. A second example is bright pink with yellow and white bands on the outer face and tassels at one end, likewise decorated with wool. The reversible two-colour construction is the distinguishing feature of the type as catalogued.

**Warp-patterned band** — A long, narrow band in warp-rips technique, the pattern carried entirely by a densely set warp in undyed white and blue against a sparser weft. The warp begins and ends in loops; the weaving runs to the very end on one side while the other side is left as fringe.

**Embroidered woollen shawl** — A white wool shawl worked in embroidery, catalogued as belonging to the Otavalo costume and to an Otavalo family.

**Embroidered girl's dress** — A white dress with floral decoration in pale blue, thinly worked at the neck and across the shoulders, and lace around the neck opening and the sleeve openings.

**Export weaving** — Textiles in Otavalo style woven with alpaca or llama wool, made for the textile industry and sent to North America; some Otavalo businessmen and women run these operations.

**Motif vocabulary.** Twist-stripes picked up into lozenges (diamond figures set in banded grounds); lengthwise striping concentrated along the selvedges; flower sprays in pale blue on white embroidered dress linen.

### Clothing & dress

The local dress of the Otavalo is itself an attraction for visitors to the area, and the museum records treat garments as parts of a named ensemble, "the Otavalo costume," rather than as isolated pieces. Documented women's wear comprises a white embroidered wool shawl, fastened at the breast with a long pin made for that purpose; a white felt hat, specified in the catalogue as a woman's hat; woven waist-bands of cotton, one face pink and the other red, or bright pink banded with yellow and white and finished with tassels at one end; multiple strands of glass-bead necklaces; and a pair of slippers made of cloth with a stiffening inside. For girls there is a white dress with pale blue floral embroidery at the neck and shoulders and lace at the neck and sleeve openings. The sources used here do not describe men's dress, and they do not distinguish ceremonial from everyday clothing.

### Architecture

The sources used for this profile say nothing about Otavalo house forms, building materials or built decoration.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The household objects documented here are modest and mostly items of costume and carriage. A metal pin serves specifically to fasten the shawl of the Otavalo costume. Cloth slippers, catalogued as a pair, are stiffened internally. A photograph in the Finnish Heritage Agency collection shows an Otavalo woman carrying a large pot on her back, with Lake San Pablo behind her — the only vessel form the sources attest. Several of the objects shown, including beadwork and a bamboo flute, were bought in the market at Otavalo, which the catalogue entries name repeatedly as the point of purchase; market exchange is thus visible in the collection record itself, consistent with commerce being a principal Otavalo activity.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Beadwork is the best-documented adornment. One necklace consists of small gold-coloured glass beads threaded on fourteen separate cords; another is built of four cords strung with large gold-coloured glass beads; a third is a single cord of red glass beads, long enough to be wound. All three were bought in the market at Otavalo. The shawl pin, though functional, is worn at the front of the costume. The sources used here do not mention tattooing, body painting or hair practices.

## Music & performance

One instrument is documented: a panpipe made of bamboo, bought in the Otavalo market. The sources used here name no song genres, ensembles or performance occasions.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used for this profile do not cover Otavalo dance or dramatic traditions.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used for this profile do not cover the Otavalo festival calendar or life-cycle rites. Ecuador has no inscriptions on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage lists that bear on this group.

## Foodways

What the sources give is subsistence rather than cuisine, and it is mostly historical. The Otavalo area was densely populated and farmed under irrigation; fields called *camelones*, or *Waru Waru* raised fields, were built to regulate the water supply to crops. Maize and potatoes were the important highland products, with coca and other tropical and sub-tropical crops grown at lower, warmer altitudes. Domesticated guinea pigs were an important source of animal protein, alongside wild game such as deer. Unlike Andean peoples further south in Peru and Bolivia, the Otavalo apparently kept no domesticated llamas or alpacas before the Incas. Long-distance traders called *mindaláes* brought cotton, coca, salt and dried fish from the Pacific coast up into the highlands, trading especially with people on the western slopes of the Andes in the Mira River valley, about 75 kilometres (47 mi) north of the city of Otavalo. Today most Otavalo are subsistence farmers who cultivate crops such as potatoes and also raise livestock. The sources used here name no prepared dishes, ceremonial foods or drink traditions.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used for this profile do not cover Otavalo folktales, epic or storytelling. They do record that the Otavalo and other Andean peoples of northern Ecuador are often identified with the pre-Columbian Cara people and Cara culture, and treated as descendants of the semi-mythical Quitu culture, from which the name of Quito comes.

## Language & religion

Before Quechua, the language of the area was *Caranqui* or *Cara* (Kara), an extinct language of Ecuador generally classed as Barbacoan on the strength of similarities to Pasto and Tsafiki, though the evidence is not conclusive because the documentation is poor; it was replaced by Quechua, perhaps surviving as late as the eighteenth century, and appears in turn to have influenced Imbabura Quechua. The Otavalo, the Caranqui, the Cayambe and the Cochasquí were small-scale chiefdoms north of Quito, similar in artistic technique, subsistence, settlement pattern and language, with a combined pre-Inca population estimated at 100,000 to 180,000. The Otavalo today speak Kichwa and Spanish. On religion the sources record only the colonial context: vineyards owned by the Dominican Order were called "fields of blood" for the Otavalo labourers who died working them.

## Sources & further reading

- Collier, John, Jr., and Aníbal Buitrón. *The Awakening Valley*. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1949.
- Meisch, Lynn. *Otavalo: Weaving, Costume and the Market*. Quito: Ediciones Libri Mundi, 1987.
- Newson, Linda A. *Life and Death in Early Colonial Ecuador*. Norman: University of Oklahoma Press, 1995.
- Salomon, Frank. *Native Lords of Quito in the Age of the Incas*. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1986.
- Lynn Meisch is the standing documentarian of Otavalo weaving, costume and market trade; Frank Salomon's work on the pre-Hispanic northern Ecuadorian chiefdoms is the source for the *mindaláes* traders.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otavalo_people
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otavalo_language
- https://folkways.si.edu/search?query=Ecuador
- British Museum online collection: https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection (woman's woven waist-bands)
- Museum of World Culture / Världskulturmuseerna online collection (Gothenburg ethnographic collections: Otavalo costume, beadwork, bamboo panpipe, warp-patterned band)

The Otavalo replaced their earlier Barbacoan language with Kichwa, probably after the sixteenth century, and later adopted Spanish.

- **Kichwa** — The Quechua dialect of Ecuador spoken by the Otavalo today alongside Spanish.
- **Caranqui or Cara** (*Kara*) — Extinct Barbacoan language formerly spoken in the Otavalo area, replaced by Quechua perhaps surviving until the eighteenth century.

## Glossary

- *Kichwa* — The Quechua dialect spoken in Ecuador
- *camelones* — Raised agricultural fields built for irrigation
- *Waru Waru* — Raised fields that regulate water supply to crops
- *mindaláes* — Long-distance traders who brought goods from coast to highlands
- *Caranqui* — Extinct Barbacoan language formerly spoken in the Otavalo area
- *Cara* — Another name for Caranqui, the extinct language
- *Barbacoan* — Language family of northern Ecuador and southern Colombia
- *warp-rips* — Weaving technique where pattern is carried by the warp threads
- *Otavalo costume* — Named ensemble of traditional local dress including shawl, hat, waist-band and necklaces
- *alpaca* — South American camelid animal whose wool is used in textiles
- *llama* — South American camelid animal whose wool is used in textiles

---
title: "Saraguros"
subtitle: "Ecuador"
region: "Latin America"
tags: [ethnography, latin-america]
---

## Overview

The Saraguros are a people of the Kichwa nation, most of whom live in Saraguro Canton in the Loja Province of southern Ecuador, at intermediate Andean elevations between about 1,800 and 2,800 metres. Ecuador's INEC census of 2010 counted 30,183 people in the canton, a figure that covers both the Indigenous and the non-Indigenous residents. Most Saraguros now speak Spanish, while *Runashimi* or Kichwa, a Quechua dialect, is also spoken and is the object of revitalization work. Oral tradition holds that their ancestors were resettled into the area by the Inca state, and the people are known for having kept much of their land, their customs and their distinctive dress — a black-and-white wool costume whose colours they read as signs of ceremony and nobility rather than of mourning.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

Saraguro textiles documented in the sources are wool garments, several of them built from plain rectangles joined by seams, with colour and embroidery carrying the design rather than figurative weaving.

**Anaco** — the *anaco* is a women's garment made, most of the time, of wool; a skirt is worn beneath it, its edge embroidered in designs chosen to match the sash and the blouse.

**Rebozo** — the *rebozo* or cloth is made from sheep's wool and dyed black (blue versions are also now found) and is worn against the cold.

**Poncho** — the black wool *poncho* is men's dress reserved mostly for gala occasions. British Museum examples are built from two rectangles of black wool sewn along their long sides with a head-hole left at the centre; some carry fuchsia stripes, others are joined with contrasting red or green thread, and one is blue cloth with a red stripe running down each long side and the neck opening woven in rather than cut.

**Tunic** — catalogued tunics are a single rectangle of black cloth folded in half and sewn partway down the sides, with a hole cut for the neck; one is stitched with fuchsia wool.

**Zamarro** — the *zamarro* is made of white wool and covers only the front of the body, from the ankles to the waist.

**Wool trousers** — the museum's Saraguro trousers show three treatments: a two-piece white wool garment whose rectangles are sewn to a multicoloured waistband and fastened around the leg with metal snaps at the bottom corners; blue wool trousers with a multicoloured waistband; and black wool trousers lined inside the waistband with white cotton striped in blue. Everyday men's trousers described in the sources are black and reach the knee.

**White wool hat** — the woman's hat is woollen and white with black designs, and can weigh as much as a pound and a half.

**Motif vocabulary.** Black and white — the paired colours of ceremony and nobility, attributed by the Saraguros, following the chronicler Cieza de León, to Inca usage; the black-and-white plumage of the *Curiquingue* (carunculated caracara), a bird symbolic of Inca royalty whose signs still appear on Kapak Raymi costumes; crescent forms, used for earrings and tendrils; the black figures worked on the white hat; and the fuchsia, red and green stripes and seam threads of the ponchos and tunics.

### Clothing & dress

Women wear the *anaco* over an embroidered skirt, with a blouse or shirt whose embroidery now appears in many designs, a girdle that holds both anaco and skirt and is understood to represent women's fertility and the protection of the womb (its designs matching the shirt), the black *rebozo* for warmth, and the heavy white-and-black wool hat. Men wear black knee-length trousers, the white *zamarro* over the front of the legs, a leather belt whose gold knobs and other decoration display the wearer's wealth, and the black wool *poncho* for gala events. Saraguros did not wear shoes until the 1950s; their footwear is now black. Long braided hair is kept by men as a marker that the sources trace to Inca nobility. Black dress read as mourning for Atahualpa is a debunked theory, though black-as-mourning has been adopted, especially by younger generations.

### Architecture

The sources describe no vernacular house form. What they do record is that Saraguros were required by the Spanish to keep a *tambo* — an inn or way-station — on a major communication route, and that their successful argument that running it obliged them to retain their land and its resources helped them hold their territory; they managed the tambo until a motor road reached the area in the 1940s. The settlements lie along the Inca road, the *Kapak Ñan*, which ran from Cuzco to Tumebamba and on to Quito, and Inca ruins stand nearby, although the town of Saraguro itself appears to have been founded by the Spanish. In the twentieth-century celebration of Inca heritage, Inca architecture has been copied.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources name no Saraguro ceramic tradition. Metalwork appears in dress: the *tupu*, a silver jewel with a coloured pearl at its centre, and the gold knobs of the men's leather belt. The British Museum trousers are fastened with metal snaps.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Three forms are documented. The *tupu* is a silver pin set with a coloured pearl, used to fasten the woman's cloth and hung from a chain worn around the neck; within families the tupu (also called the mole) passes from mother to daughter as inheritance down the generations. The *wallka* is a multi-coloured fabric made with beads. Earrings and tendrils take crescent shapes. For hair, the sources record men's long braids, understood as a nobility marker retained from the Inca army's elite soldiers.

## Music & performance

The sources name no Saraguro instrument or song genre; what they document is a contemporary scene. Young, cosmopolitan Saraguro musicians in Ecuador's southern highlands are working to reconstitute a Saraguro Kichwa identity through a creative and selective process in which they discard, amplify and reinvent what they take to be authentic Saraguro musical culture — a break from tradition that signals both their aspiration to lives other than those tradition and stereotype assign them, and their actual opportunity to lead such lives. Greater participation in formal education, occupational diversity and mobility underpin this. The sources also record ways of self-expression that are compatible with Indigenous self-identification without depending on ties to an Inkaic past: a large number of Saraguro youth, primarily male, affiliate with a heavy metal subculture, listening to national and international metal bands, playing in local bands and organising local concerts. Musicians are among the occupations contemporary Saraguros hold.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not cover Saraguro dance or theatrical traditions, beyond noting that Curiquingue symbolism is carried on costumes at the Kapak Raymi celebrations.

## Festivals & rituals

The one festival named in the sources is **Kapak Raymi**, the Great Celebration, held in Saraguro, at which costumes continue to carry the symbols of the *Curiquingue*, the black-and-white carunculated caracara that inhabits the Saraguro parish and páramos and was a bird of Inca royalty. Twentieth-century Saraguros celebrate their Inca heritage more broadly: schools have been named after Inca emperors and Inca customs recreated. Floral offerings are treated as a living form of Saraguro spiritual culture and resistance, and are the subject of Sisa Pacari Bacacela Gualan's *Cultura espiritual: Una resistencia de los Saraguros en la actualidad: Las Ofrendas Florales*. Indigenous justice is exercised, in Carmen Lozano's account of her own work, to harmonize the balance of life within the community. The sources record no life-cycle rites, except that the *tupu* passes from mother to daughter as an inheritance.

## Foodways

The sources used do not describe Saraguro dishes, staples or cooking. They record that Saraguros are traditionally farmers and livestock herders, that sheep's wool supplies their cloth, that many continue agro-pastoralist activities alongside professional careers, and that Saraguro activists and intellectuals campaign for food sovereignty.

## Oral tradition & literature

Oral tradition is the principal source for Saraguro origins: it holds that the ancestors of the present-day people were moved to Saraguro by the Incas from other areas, possibly from the Colla or other peoples of the Lake Titicaca and Cuzco regions, under the forced-resettlement policy called *mitma*, and it transmits — alongside historical records — the attribution of the black and white of Saraguro clothing to ceremony and nobility. Written and documentary work by Saraguro intellectuals is substantial. Sisa Pacari Bacacela Gualan is the author of *Ecuador Chinchasuyupi Quichuacunapac Ñaupa Rimai = Literatura Indígena En Los Andes Del Sur Del Ecuador*, of the study of floral offerings, and of *El Quinto Gobernador de los Saraguros: Historia Social y Organizativa*. Luis Fernando Sarango Macas wrote *The Education Paradigm of Abya Yala*. Inti Cartuche Vacacela has published academic articles on interculturality and plurinationality. The 2010 film *Saraguro: Historia Escrita con Sangre Inka* traces the people's origins, combining anthropological data with Inkan cosmovision in consultation with the Saraguros themselves.

## Language & religion

The Saraguros belong to the Kichwa nation. Most now speak Spanish; *Runashimi* or Kichwa, a Quechua dialect, is also spoken, and language revitalization efforts are being implemented, with the preservation of Kichwa named among the ways the people assert their Inca heritage. Institutional support for the language and for Indigenous education includes the Pluriversity "Amawtay Wasi" and the Coordination of Organizations of the Kichwa Saraguro People (CORPUKIS, within ECUARUNARI and CONAIE), and Bacacela Gualan has served as Secretary for Bilingual Education in the Unión Nacional de Educadores del Ecuador. On religion the sources are nearly silent: they document spiritual culture only through floral offerings, described as a contemporary Saraguro resistance.

## Sources & further reading

- Sisa Pacari Bacacela Gualan, *Ecuador Chinchasuyupi Quichuacunapac Ñaupa Rimai = Literatura Indígena En Los Andes Del Sur Del Ecuador*
- Sisa Pacari Bacacela Gualan, *Cultura espiritual: Una resistencia de los Saraguros en la actualidad: Las Ofrendas Florales*; and *El Quinto Gobernador de los Saraguros: Historia Social y Organizativa*
- Luis Fernando Sarango Macas, *The Education Paradigm of Abya Yala*
- *Saraguro: Historia Escrita con Sangre Inka* (film, 2010)
- Amawtay Wasi Pluriversity; I.C.C.I. (Instituto Científico de Culturas Indígenas); Saraguro.org
- Wikipedia, "Saraguro people": https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saraguro_people

## At a glance

## Overview

The Saraguros live in the Andean highlands of southern Ecuador and speak Spanish and Kichwa. Oral tradition says their ancestors were resettled here by the Inca state. They are known for keeping their land, customs, and black-and-white wool clothing that they read as signs of ceremony and nobility, not mourning.

## Material culture

Saraguro material culture centers on wool textiles in black and white, built from simple rectangles with meaning carried through color and embroidery rather than woven designs.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Saraguros weave black and white wool textiles in simple rectangular forms, with design carried by color, embroidery, and symbolic motifs.

- **Anaco** — A women's garment made of wool, worn as a skirt with embroidered edges matching the sash and blouse.
- **Poncho** — A black wool men's garment worn for gala occasions, sometimes with fuchsia, red, or green stripes or contrasting thread.
- **Rebozo** — A black or blue sheep's wool cloth worn for warmth against the cold.
- **Zamarro** — A white wool garment covering the front of the body from ankle to waist, worn by men.
- **White wool hat** — A woman's heavy white wool hat with black designs, weighing up to a pound and a half.

### Clothing & dress

Men and women dress distinctly in wool garments that display wealth, fertility, and status through color, embroidery, and decoration.

- **Long braided hair** — Men wear long braids as a marker of nobility, a tradition traced to Inca elite soldiers.
- **Leather belt** — Men's belts are decorated with gold knobs and metalwork to display the wearer's wealth.
- **Girdle** — A woman's girdle holds the anaco and skirt and represents fertility and the protection of the womb.

### Architecture

The Saraguros maintained a Spanish-required inn (tambo) on the Inca road, which became key to their keeping their land and resources.

- **Tambo** — An inn or way-station that Saraguros were required by Spain to maintain on a major route, helping them retain their territory.
- **Kapak Ñan** — The Inca road running from Cuzco through Saraguro to Tumebamba and Quito, along which settlements were built.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Saraguro metalwork appears mainly in dress ornaments and fasteners made of silver and gold.

- **Tupu** — A silver pin with a colored pearl at its center, used to fasten cloth and hung from a chain around the neck.
- **Metal snaps** — Metal fasteners used at the bottom corners of wool trousers.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Saraguro jewelry centers on inherited silver ornaments and beadwork passed through families, especially from mother to daughter.

- **Mole** (*tupu*) — A silver pin with a colored pearl, fastening cloth and inherited by women down the generations.
- **Wallka** — A multi-colored fabric made with beads.
- **Crescent earrings and tendrils** — Earrings and decorative tendrils shaped like crescents, a recurring motif in Saraguro adornment.

## Music & performance

Young Saraguro musicians are reconstituting Kichwa identity through creative reinvention of musical traditions, while others participate in national heavy metal subcultures.

- **Contemporary Saraguro music scene** — Young musicians selectively discard, amplify, and reinvent what they see as authentic Saraguro music, reflecting new opportunities beyond tradition.
- **Heavy metal subculture** — Many Saraguro youth, primarily male, listen to metal bands, play in local bands, and organize concerts as an alternative form of self-expression.

## Dance & theatre

Little is documented about Saraguro dance or theater, except that Curiquingue symbolism appears on costumes at Kapak Raymi.

## Festivals & rituals

Kapak Raymi, the Great Celebration, centers on black-and-white symbolism of the sacred Curiquingue bird, while floral offerings represent contemporary spiritual resistance.

- **Kapak Raymi** — The Great Celebration held in Saraguro, where costumes carry the black-and-white symbols of the Curiquingue, a royal Inca bird.
- **Floral offerings** — Treated as a living form of Saraguro spiritual culture and resistance.
- **Indigenous justice** — Exercised within the community to harmonize the balance of life.

## Foodways

The Saraguros are traditionally farmers and livestock herders; many continue agro-pastoral activities alongside modern careers and advocate for food sovereignty.

- **Agro-pastoralism** — Raising sheep for wool and farming remain central practices, often combined with professional work.
- **Food sovereignty** — Saraguro activists campaign for food sovereignty and control over their agricultural resources.

## Oral tradition & literature

Oral tradition traces Saraguro origins to Inca forced resettlement (mitma), while contemporary Saraguro intellectuals produce substantial written work on history, education, and culture.

- **Mitma** — The Inca forced-resettlement policy under which Saraguros' ancestors were moved to Saraguro from other regions, possibly Lake Titicaca areas.
- **Sisa Pacari Bacacela Gualan** — A leading Saraguro intellectual who has authored works on Indigenous literature, floral offerings, and Saraguro history and organization.

## Language & religion

Most Saraguros speak Spanish; Kichwa/Runashimi is also spoken and is undergoing revitalization as part of asserting Inca heritage and Indigenous identity.

- **Kichwa** (*Runashimi*) — A Quechua dialect spoken by Saraguros and the subject of language revitalization efforts.
- **Amawtay Wasi** — A Pluriversity supporting Indigenous education and Kichwa language preservation.
- **CORPUKIS** — The Coordination of Organizations of the Kichwa Saraguro People, supporting language and Indigenous education within larger Indigenous networks.

## Glossary

- *poncho* — A black wool men's garment for gala occasions
- *rebozo* — A black or blue wool cloth worn for warmth
- *zamarro* — A white wool garment covering the front of the legs

title: "Palestinians"
subtitle: "Palestine"
region: "Middle East North Africa"
tags: [ethnography, middle-east-north-africa]
---

## Overview

Palestinians (Arabic: الفلسطينيون, *al-Filasṭīniyyūn*) are an Arab national group native to the region of Palestine, sharing close linguistic and cultural ties with other Levantine Arabs. Roughly half of the world's Palestinian population lives in the territory of former Mandatory Palestine — the land between the Mediterranean Sea and the Jordan River, now encompassing Israel and the occupied Palestinian territories — including over 1.4 million refugees or internally displaced people in the Gaza Strip, over 870,000 in the West Bank and around 250,000 in Israel proper, where Palestinians make up almost 21 percent of the population. Of the diaspora, 2.3 million are registered refugees in Jordan, over a million live between Syria and Lebanon, about 750,000 in Saudi Arabia, and around half a million in Chile. In folk-culture terms the material documented here is overwhelmingly that of the villages — the *fellahin* — and above all their embroidered dress.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Thob** — The village woman's dress, cut either with long narrow sleeves and a square neck opening or with large pointed sleeves, in white or indigo-dyed cotton. Its surface is organised by named panels rather than by continuous field pattern: the chest panel (*qabbeh*), yoke, upper sleeves (*sawa'id*), cuffs, the front and back furrows (*mawaris*), the side panels (*banayeq*) and the lower back of the skirt, each worked in cross-stitch — deep magenta and pink on white grounds — with the densest and most vividly coloured cotton thread reserved for the chest panel.

**Machine-worked thob** — Later examples are both seamed and embroidered on a sewing machine, which carries a wave- or snail-like motif in red cotton thread alongside the *mawaris* and along the hem: the same panel scheme executed by a new tool.

**Jellaya** — The festive dress of Beit Dajan, made of indigo-blue or black linen embroidered over its entire surface, worn at weddings and other celebrations together with black linen trousers (*sirwal*) embroidered down the legs. It was the most costly of the many dresses making up a bride's trousseau in Beit Dajan and its surroundings, and was the dress a bride wore when she first appeared in public.

**Linen underdress** — Worn beneath the *thob*, of cream handwoven linen with red and blue selvedge stripes, its chest panel lightly worked in cross-stitch and satin stitch in burgundy, red and green floss silk. The collar is of red-and-white Syrian silk *ikat*, and the neck opening is trimmed with braided yellow silk cord looped to take braided green buttons — an assembly that puts imported Syrian silk against locally woven linen.

**Decorative seam and repair stitching** — Construction itself is ornamental: side and sleeve seams joined with knotted zigzag joining stitch in floss silk and then re-embroidered in feather stitch, chest panels bordered with zigzag appliqué, and patched neck openings re-worked in feather and buttonhole stitch in contrasting cotton, so that mending extends the pattern rather than interrupting it.

**Embroidered cushion covers** — Household furnishing in the same technique: cotton embroidered with silk thread, and finer examples in navy silk cross-stitched in yellow, brown, green, pink and white, with a central panel of ordered motifs.

**Motif vocabulary.** *mafatih nujum* (stars-and-keys), appearing four to a central panel; flowers with stems; a wave or snail-like running motif worked by machine along hems and furrows.

### Clothing & dress

Women's dress is layered: the handwoven linen underdress with its *ikat* collar beneath the embroidered *thob*, and for weddings the fully embroidered *jellaya* with embroidered *sirwal* trousers. Colour and ground fabric vary by garment — white cotton, indigo-dyed cotton, black or indigo linen — while the embroidered zones stay in the same named positions (*qabbeh*, *sawa'id*, *mawaris*, *banayeq*). Men's documented outerwear is the square cape *abayeh* (also *abay*), here in green-and-white striped silk twill with the seams trimmed in braided cotton wrapped in metal foil. The sources used do not describe Palestinian head coverings, belts or footwear, nor regional dress styles beyond the village examples above and the Beit Dajan bridal trousseau.

### Architecture

The sources used do not describe Palestinian vernacular house forms, materials or ornament. The single architectural subject documented is monumental and religious: Al-Aqsa Mosque (*al-Masjid al-ʾAqṣā*, "the Farthest Mosque") in the Old City of Jerusalem, built on the Temple Mount, known in Islam as the al-Aqsa Compound or *Haram esh-Sharif*. Muslims hold that Muhammad was transported there from the Great Mosque of Mecca during the Night Journey, and Islamic tradition holds that he led prayers towards the site until the sixteenth or seventeenth month after his migration from Mecca to Medina, when he was directed to turn towards the Kaaba. The wider built record of Palestine named in the sources is a sequence of periods rather than described forms — Biblical, Roman, Byzantine, Umayyad, Abbasid, Fatimid, Crusader, Ayyubid, Mamluk and Ottoman — strata that Palestinians have come to understand as part of their own identity over the last century.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources used do not cover Palestinian ceramics, metalwork or wooden household objects. The only metal in the documented objects is decorative trim: the braided cotton wrapped in metal foil edging the seams of the man's *abayeh*. Of everyday furnishing, only the embroidered cushion covers are represented.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used do not cover Palestinian jewellery, tattooing, henna or hair practices.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not cover Palestinian instruments, song genres or musical performance contexts. No UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage elements are listed for the country in the material consulted.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not cover Palestinian dance or dramatic traditions.

## Festivals & rituals

The annual festival calendar is not covered by the sources used. Of life-cycle rites, only marriage is documented, and only through dress. In Beit Dajan and its surrounding villages a bride's trousseau comprised many dresses, of which the embroidered *jellaya* was the most costly; it was worn with embroidered *sirwal* trousers at weddings and other celebrations, and specifically at the moment the bride first appeared in public. The sources say nothing of birth, coming-of-age or funerary observance, and nothing of the ritual calendars of the religious communities they name. Two secular commemorations are recorded: the United Nations has observed an annual International Day of Solidarity with the Palestinian People since 1978, and the sources note the 1948 establishment of Israel, the 1948 Palestinian expulsion and the 1967 Palestinian exodus as the events around which a shared Palestinian future came to be articulated.

## Foodways

The sources used do not cover Palestinian staples, dishes, ceremonial food or coffee and tea customs.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used document print rather than oral literature. Palestinian self-description in writing begins with Khalil Beidas, who introduced the term *Filasṭīnī* in a 1898 Arabic translation of a Russian work on the Holy Land, followed by Salim Quba'in and Najib Nassar in 1902. After the 1908 Young Turk Revolution eased Ottoman press censorship, dozens of newspapers and periodicals were founded in Palestine — among them *Al-Quds*, *Al-Munadi*, *Falastin*, *Al-Karmil* and *Al-Nafir* — which used the word "Filastini" more than 170 times across 110 articles between 1908 and 1914, and wrote of a "Palestinian society" (*al-mujtama' al-filasṭīnī*), a "Palestinian nation", the "people of Palestine" (*ahl*/*ahālī Filasṭīn*) and the "sons of Palestine" (*abnā' Filasṭīn*). Contributors included Christian and Muslim Palestinians, emigrants and non-Palestinian Arabs; the Christian-owned *Falastin*, founded in 1911, addressed its readers as Palestinians from the outset. The sources name no epic, folktale cycle or proverb collection.

## Language & religion

Palestinians are Arabic-speaking, writing in the Arabic script, and share close linguistic ties with other Levantine Arabs; the sources used do not describe Palestinian dialects. Religiously the population is mixed: in 1919 Palestinian Muslims and Christians together constituted 90 percent of the population of Palestine, and the Palestinian National Charter's definition of "Palestinians" as Arab nationals resident until 1947 takes in Arabic-speaking Muslims, Arab Christians, and the Samaritan and Druze communities. Some Palestinian families, notably in the Hebron and Nablus regions, claim Jewish and Samaritan ancestry respectively and preserve customs and traditions associated with it. Islam's place in local devotion is documented through Jerusalem: Al-Aqsa Mosque and the *Haram esh-Sharif* compound, tied to the Night Journey. Folk religious practice beyond this is not covered.

## Sources & further reading

- Rashid Khalidi, *Palestinian Identity: The Construction of Modern National Consciousness* (1997) — considered a foundational text on the emergence of Palestinian identity.
- James L. Gelvin, *The Israel-Palestine Conflict: One Hundred Years of War* — argues Palestinian nationalism emerged in the interwar period.
- Widad Kawar, cited as Kawar 2011 (p. 238) in the National Museum of World Cultures Foundation record for the Beit Dajan *jellaya*, on Palestinian dress and the bridal trousseau.
- Scholarly positions summarised in the Wikipedia article above, for the dating debate: Assaf Likhovski, Baruch Kimmerling and Joel S. Migdal, Walid Khalidi, Benny Morris, Bernard Lewis, Efraim Karsh, Tamir Sorek, David Seddon, and Nazmi Al-Ju'beh on Arab identity as linguistic and cultural affiliation.
- Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestinians
- UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: no inscriptions for this country in the material consulted.

subtitle: "Palestine"
region: "Middle East North Africa"

## At a glance
| | |
|---|---|
| Who | Palestinians, an Arab national group |
| Where | Palestine — the land between the Mediterranean Sea and the Jordan River, now Israel and the Palestinian territories; also in diaspora across Jordan, Syria, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, and Chile |
| How many | About half the world's 10+ million Palestinians live in former Mandatory Palestine; 2.3 million registered refugees in Jordan alone |
| Language | Arabic, Levantine dialect |
| Religion | Predominantly Muslim; also Arab Christian, Samaritan, and Druze communities |
| Known for | Elaborately embroidered village dresses (thob) with named panel sections · Machine-worked embroidery adapting traditional patterns to modern tools · The bridal jellaya dress and trousseau traditions of Beit Dajan · Written articulation of Palestinian national identity from 1898 onward |

## Overview

Palestinians are an Arab national group native to the region of Palestine, sharing close linguistic and cultural ties with other Levantine Arabs. Half the world's Palestinian population lives in former Mandatory Palestine, with major diaspora communities in Jordan, Syria, Lebanon, and Saudi Arabia. The documented material culture focuses overwhelmingly on village women's embroidered dress and household furnishings. Palestinian identity as a self-conscious national category emerged in writing from 1898 and crystallized through newspapers and print after 1908.

## Material culture

Palestinian village material culture is dominated by embroidered textiles, particularly women's layered dress with named embroidered panels and machine-worked variations.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Embroidered cotton and linen textiles organize pattern into named panels rather than continuous fields, with cross-stitch in magenta and pink on white.

- **Thob** — The village woman's dress in white or indigo cotton, organized by named panels (chest, yoke, sleeves, cuffs, furrows, side panels) each worked in cross-stitch with deep magenta and pink thread.
- **Machine-worked thob** — Later examples seamed and embroidered on a sewing machine with wave or snail-like motifs in red thread along the same traditional panels.
- **Jellaya** — The festive dress of Beit Dajan in indigo-blue or black linen embroidered over its entire surface, worn at weddings with embroidered black linen trousers and the most costly item in a bride's trousseau.
- **Linen underdress** — Cream handwoven linen worn beneath the thob with red and blue selvedge stripes, a lightly embroidered chest panel, and a collar of red-and-white Syrian silk ikat.
- **Embroidered cushion covers** — Household furnishings in cotton embroidered with silk thread, finer examples in navy silk cross-stitched in multiple colours with ordered central panel motifs.

### Clothing & dress

Women's dress is layered and colour-coded by garment, with embroidery fixed in named positions; men's documented outerwear is a striped silk cape.

- **Sirwal** — Black linen trousers embroidered down the legs, worn with the jellaya at weddings and celebrations.
- **Abayeh** (*abayeh (also abay)*) — A square cape in green-and-white striped silk twill with seams trimmed in braided cotton wrapped in metal foil.
- **Qabbeh chest panel** (*qabbeh*) — The embroidered chest panel of the thob, worked with the densest and most vividly coloured cotton thread.

### Architecture

The documented architecture is monumental and religious, centred on a single structure and its theological significance.

- **Al-Aqsa Mosque** (*al-Masjid al-ʾAqṣā*) — The Farthest Mosque on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem's Old City, where Islamic tradition holds Muhammad was transported during the Night Journey and led prayers before being directed towards the Kaaba.
- **Haram esh-Sharif** (*Haram esh-Sharif (al-Aqsa Compound)*) — The sacred compound on the Temple Mount, known to Muslims as the site of Muhammad's Night Journey.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources do not document Palestinian ceramics, metalwork or wooden household objects; only decorative metal trim appears in the record.

- **Metal-foil-wrapped braid** — Braided cotton wrapped in metal foil used to trim the seams of the man's abayeh.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources do not cover Palestinian jewellery, tattooing, henna or hair practices.

## Music & performance

The sources do not cover Palestinian instruments, song genres or musical performance contexts.

## Dance & theatre

The sources do not cover Palestinian dance or dramatic traditions.

## Festivals & rituals

Marriage is the only life-cycle rite documented, known through bridal dress; secular commemorations mark the 1948 establishment of Israel and Palestinian displacements.

- **Bridal trousseau** — In Beit Dajan, a bride's trousseau comprised many dresses, with the embroidered jellaya being the most costly and worn at the moment the bride first appeared in public.
- **International Day of Solidarity with the Palestinian People** — Observed annually by the United Nations since 1978.

## Foodways

The sources do not cover Palestinian staples, dishes, ceremonial food or coffee and tea customs.

## Oral tradition & literature

Palestinian identity emerged through print literature from 1898, articulated by intellectuals and newspapers that defined a shared Palestinian nation and society.

- **Khalil Beidas** — Introduced the term Filasṭīnī in an 1898 Arabic translation of a Russian work on the Holy Land.
- **Palestinian newspapers (1908–1914)** — After the Young Turk Revolution eased Ottoman press censorship, dozens of newspapers including Al-Quds, Al-Munadi, Falastin, Al-Karmil and Al-Nafir used the word Filastini more than 170 times and wrote of Palestinian society, nation, and people.
- **Falastin newspaper** (*Falastin*) — A Christian-owned newspaper founded in 1911 that addressed its readers as Palestinians from the outset.

## Language & religion

Palestinians are Arabic-speaking and religiously mixed — Muslim, Christian, Samaritan, and Druze — unified by Arab national identity defined by language and culture.

- **Levantine Arabic** — Palestinians speak Arabic and share close linguistic ties with other Levantine Arabs; dialects are not described in the sources.
- **Palestinian National Charter definition** — Defines Palestinians as Arab nationals resident in Palestine until 1947, taking in Arabic-speaking Muslims, Christians, Samaritans, and Druze.

## Glossary

- *thob* — Village woman's dress, cut with long narrow or large pointed sleeves, embroidered in cross-stitch
- *jellaya* — Festive dress of Beit Dajan in indigo or black linen, fully embroidered, worn at weddings
- *sirwal* — Black linen trousers embroidered down the legs, worn with the jellaya
- *qabbeh* — The chest panel of the thob, worked with the densest and most vividly coloured embroidery
- *ikat* — Resist-dyed fabric, used for Syrian silk collars on Palestinian underdresses
- *al-Masjid al-ʾAqṣā* — Al-Aqsa Mosque, the Farthest Mosque on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem
- *Haram esh-Sharif* — The sacred compound on the Temple Mount, also called the al-Aqsa Compound
- *Filasṭīnī* — Palestinian; the term introduced in written Arabic in 1898

## Sources & further reading

- Rashid Khalidi, Palestinian Identity: The Construction of Modern National Consciousness (1997) — considered a foundational text on the emergence of Palestinian identity.
- James L. Gelvin, The Israel-Palestine Conflict: One Hundred Years of War — argues Palestinian nationalism emerged in the interwar period.
- Widad Kawar, cited as Kawar 2011 (p. 238) in the National Museum of World Cultures Foundation record for the Beit Dajan jellaya, on Palestinian dress and the bridal trousseau.
- Scholarly positions summarised in the Wikipedia article above, for the dating debate: Assaf Likhovski, Baruch Kimmerling and Joel S. Migdal, Walid Khalidi, Benny Morris, Bernard Lewis, Efraim Karsh, Tamir Sorek, David Seddon, and Nazmi Al-Ju'beh on Arab identity as linguistic and cultural affiliation.

---
title: "Ojibwe"
subtitle: "Canada"
region: "North America"
tags: [ethnography, north-america]
---

## Overview

The Ojibwe (also Ojibway, Ojibwa or Chippewa; plural *Ojibweg*) are an Anishinaabe people whose homeland, *Ojibwewaki*, covers much of the Great Lakes region and the northern plains and reaches into the subarctic and the northeastern woodlands. In Canada they live from western Quebec through Ontario, Manitoba and Saskatchewan to eastern British Columbia; in the United States from Michigan through Wisconsin and Minnesota, with communities in North Dakota and Montana. Their total population is roughly 320,000, about 160,000 of them in Canada registered with one of some 200 bands, making them Canada's second-largest First Nations population after the Cree. Their language, *Anishinaabemowin* or *Ojibwemowin*, belongs to the Algonquian family. In folk-culture terms they are known for birchbark canoes, birchbark scrolls, copper mining and trade, and the harvesting of wild rice and maple syrup, and for the Midewiwin society that keeps the scrolls of events, oral history, songs, maps, stories, geometry and mathematics.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Glass beadwork (*manidoominensikaan*)** — The dominant pattern-bearing craft in the museum collections shown here: woven and sewn glass seed beads worked onto cloth, velvet and tanned skin. Museum documentation records beadwork as traditionally women's work and glosses the Ojibwe term as compounded from the words for "spirit" and for "seed" or "bead."

**Beaded bands (*band*, woven strips)** — Long narrow strips of woven glass beads, several of them about half a metre long and one a full metre, collected in the Great Lakes region and northern Midwest. One strip appears to carry animal figures — otter or turtle, or both — worked into the beading as part of the pattern.

**Bandolier bags** — The flashiest and most important item of Woodlands formal attire in the 1800s, according to the Cleveland catalogue: a shoulder bag of plain-weave cotton and twill-weave wool with velvet, plaited wool binding, wool tassels and glass beads. The form evolved from smaller native bags, perhaps under the influence of British ammunition pouches.

**Beaded pouches and pipe bags** — Buckskin pouches worked with beads, cloth and stroud, including bags made to hold a smoking pipe, and beaded knife cases of native-tanned skin with glass, silk and wool.

**Medicine bags** — A composite bag of red velvet bound in black, elaborately beaded, with a long wide shoulder sling rising from the bottom of the bag and tassels ending in red wool.

**Beaded panels and horse trappings** — Flat panels of beads, cloth and wool, catalogued as possible horse trappings.

**Birchbark work (*wiigwaas*)** — Not textile, but the other great patterned surface: cylindrical bark boxes and oval bark dishes sewn to bent withe hoops with strips of bark, their rims reinforced and decorated with wavy cut bark strips laid inside-out for contrast, and bark trays recorded under Ojibwe names.

**Motif vocabulary.** Floral motifs, introduced by Europeans into Woodlands imagery but taken up enthusiastically because plants are held to be animate and powerful — one bandolier bag carries blueberries, described in the catalogue as "soul food" that refreshes the spirit; otter and turtle figures, both meaningful in Anishinaabe kinship and cosmology, on a beaded band; Thunderers, a sun and cattle painted on a drum; zoomorphic drawings on birchbark scrolls; *doodem* (clan) signs, carved on grave markers and shown beside portrait heads in a printed group portrait of nine men; and a flower carved into the head of a wooden club.

### Clothing & dress

Footwear is *makizinan* (moccasins); one of the explanations offered for the name Ojibwe is "those who cook/roast until it puckers," referring to the fire-curing of moccasin seams to make them waterproof, and another derivation points to the puckered seam itself. A pair of child's moccasins of skin, cloth and beads survives from northern Minnesota. Photographs of the later nineteenth century show the mix of Ojibwe and imported dress then worn: a woman in a cloth dress at the door of a birchbark wigwam; a studio portrait of a woman named Josephine in earrings, several necklaces, a dress and moccasins; a woman in a beaded vest, armbands and skirt beside a man in a brimmed felt hat, beaded shirt and beaded belt; men photographed in feathered headgear, in blankets wrapped over western suits, and in one case a necklace that appears to be made of human hair. Blankets draped or wrapped over the head recur in several photographs. For ceremonial and social dance, the jingle dress worn by women at powwows originated with the Ojibwe — dark cloth dresses hung with rows of tin cones, often cut from tobacco-can lids, that jingle as the dancer moves; both Plains and Woodlands Ojibwe claim the earliest form, and the style has since spread to all tribes as a distinctly Ojibwe contribution to Pan-Indianism.

### Architecture

The characteristic dwelling is the *wiigiwaam* (wigwam), built either as a *waginogaan*, a domed lodge, or as a *nasawa'ogaan*, a pointed lodge, framed on willow saplings and covered with birch bark and juniper bark. A stereoscope photograph in the British Museum shows a birchbark wigwam standing in a clearing with a woman seated at its entrance; another shows a campsite with a wigwam, a tipi behind it and an upturned canoe in front. A postcard photograph records a bark-built house with snowshoes leaning against it and birchbark baskets and model canoes hung on cords across its front. Most Ojibwe today live in modern housing, but the older structures are still raised for particular sites and events. Over burials, many families erect a *jiibegamig* or "spirit house" on the mound; historically such a mound carried a wooden marker inscribed with the dead person's *doodem*.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Bark, wood and stone dominate the household objects here; the sources record no pottery. Birchbark is worked into cylindrical boxes (*ask*), oval dishes, trays and baskets, and into canoes — the collections include a miniature bark canoe with the bark sewn to its ribs. A cradle (*a'dikina'gun*) of mixed materials came from Nipigon, Ontario. Tools and implements include a stone-bladed adze or axe lashed to a wooden handle with twisted fibre cord; a wooden club with a squared-off handle, a circle carved with a flower for its head and a metal ring with a cotton strap at the butt; and two lacrosse sticks of wood and buckskin. Smoking pipes are carved in hard wood, inlaid with lead and crested, or cut in black stone inlaid with white metal and stars of catlinite. Copper, mined and traded across the continent as far back as the Hopewell tradition, is held to come from the body of the underwater serpent *Mishebeshu*; maple sugar was once granulated by boiling syrup down and working it in a trough with wooden paddles.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Adornment in the collections is made of beads and shell. A necklace of plaited glass beads and several beaded bands came from the Great Lakes region; a beaded choker in red and white fields divided by strips of leather has at its centre a concave pink disc carrying two yellow-metal balls, with two short cords hanging from its back, each strung with a cylindrical bead and knotted around a shell at the end — the collector recorded such chokers as status symbols among the Ojibwe. Studio portraits show women wearing earrings and multiple necklaces, and one man a necklace apparently of human hair. The *miigis* (cowrie) shell, which occurs naturally only on distant coasts, is used in certain ceremonies and figures throughout the migration story; its presence inland is evidence of a trade network spanning the continent. Some Ojibwe have had the image of their guardian *manitou* tattooed on the body.

## Music & performance

The collections hold three instruments. A flute of two pieces of wood, about two feet long and coloured red, was made by the Serpent River on Lake Huron. A second wood-and-skin flute is catalogued under the names *Pib-be-gwun* and *Siyontanka*. And there is a drum: a military drum of European shape in wood, skin and cord, repainted with Thunderers across its upper half, what may be a sun at the middle, and cattle below — creatures the cataloguer connects with the underworld. Two birchbark scrolls bear zoomorphic drawings said to represent musical notes, which places song inside the same pictorial writing system used in the Midewiwin rites. Beyond that, the sources distinguish two summer gathering types: *jiingotamog*, spiritual, and *niimi'idimaa*, the social gathering or powwow, held at reservations across *Anishinaabe-Aki*, Anishinaabe Country. The Red Lake, White Earth and Leech Lake reservations are known for singing hymns in the Ojibwe language. The sources used do not otherwise describe Ojibwe song genres or performance occasions.

## Dance & theatre

The sources name only one dance tradition in any detail: the women's jingle-dress dancing of the powwow, for which the Ojibwe-origin tin-cone dress was made, and the social *niimi'idimaa* gatherings at which such dancing takes place. One further dance-like practice is domestic rather than ceremonial — "jigging" wild rice, dancing or walking on the parched grain to loosen its hulls. The sources used do not cover Ojibwe dramatic or masking traditions.

## Festivals & rituals

The year turns on harvests. Wild rice, *manoomin*, is gathered in late summer and early autumn, two people to a canoe, one poling while the other knocks the ripe grain in with knocking sticks, on rice beds called *Manito Gitigaan*, the Great Spirit's Garden; tobacco and prayers are offered to secure a good harvest. Spring is the maple sugar harvest, taught in some schools by having elders and older students narrate the work in Ojibwemowin while the youngest gather wood, help drill the trees and haul sap. Summer brings the *jiingotamog* and the *niimi'idimaa*, and the season for picking berries, hunting and making medicines. The central life-cycle rite before the twentieth century was the vision quest, undertaken by almost every Ojibwe male at puberty to establish a lifelong relationship with a guardian *manitou*; the practice declined sharply under the reservation system and missionary pressure. Ritual specialists hold powers from the *manitouk*: the commonest is the *Jiisakiiwinini*, whose *Jiisakiiwin* or shaking-tent rite calls on spirits for healing. The Midewiwin, a healing society formed among southern Ojibwe by at least the eighteenth century, keeps its own birchbark scrolls and pictorial script. Hunting carries its own observances — a conciliatory mourning for the slain animal, an apology, an offering of tobacco, kin terms spoken over it, and the decorating of a killed bear's skull. The dead are buried in mounds under spirit houses; wild rice is often among the first and last foods an Ojibwe person eats.

## Foodways

*Manoomin*, wild rice, is the defining food: nutty in flavour, uneven in colour and size when grown wild, eaten by Ojibwe people as early as two thousand years before contact with white settlers, and named in the prophecy that sent the Anishinaabeg west to "the place where there is food upon the waters." After knocking, the grain is parched in an iron kettle over an open fire, jigged to strip the hulls, then winnowed by tossing it up so the wind carries the chaff off. Treaties of 1837 and 1854 guaranteed the right to harvest it, though the right was not always honoured, and in the 1930s Minnesota declared a state of emergency over the collapse of the rice beds and leaned on Native elders to write and enforce statutes protecting them. The other staples are fish, maple sugar, venison and corn, with beans, squash and potatoes grown alongside, and blueberries, blackberries, choke cherries, raspberries, gooseberries and huckleberries foraged; deer, beaver, moose, goose, duck, rabbit and bear were hunted in summer. Frybread and "Indian tacos" have displaced some older dishes, and communities have answered with gardens in food deserts and a mobile kitchen teaching food preparation.

## Oral tradition & literature

Storytelling is central to Anishinaabe life: stories are held to create worlds, to bind the generations through teaching and listening, and to connect people with the non-human world. Ojibwe tradition separates ordinary stories about living people from sacred stories about the *manitouk* — *tipacimowinak* and *kanatipacimowinak* in the Severn River area, *dbaajmowin* and *aadsookaan* among the southeast Ojibwe. Stories of the *manitouk* were told only in winter, when the water was frozen and *Mishebeshu* could not be drawn out by the telling. The recurring figures are *Nanabush*, the culture hero and trickster who taught people to hunt and fish, found wild rice and invented snowshoes but could also be greedy or cruel; *Amik*, the beaver, whose stories are about making shared worlds; and *Nokomis*, the grandmother. The Seven Grandfather Teachings — wisdom, respect, love, honesty, humility, bravery and truth, each with its animal — are still in use. Elders are the "knowledge keepers"; the historian Anton Treuer has recorded stories from about fifty elders and writes them out with his mentor, the Ponemah elder Eugene Stillday, in Ojibwe and in English translation. Narratives were also recorded in pictographs serving as mnemonics, and the *wiigwaasabak* birchbark writing is still used by traditional people and by young people on social media.

## Language & religion

*Anishinaabemowin* is an Algonquian language descended from Proto-Algonquian, with dialects running west to east: Western Ojibwe (Saulteaux), Southwestern Ojibwe (Chippewa), Northwestern Ojibwe, Severn Ojibwe (Oji-Cree), Ottawa (Odawa), Eastern Ojibwe and Algonquin. It is the second most spoken First Nations language in Canada after Cree and fourth in North America, and it served for centuries as a trade language around the Great Lakes. Boarding schools drove heavy loss; immersion schools such as Waadookodaading on the Lac Courte Oreilles Reservation, the Ojibwe People's Dictionary, and a Mille Lacs partnership with Rosetta Stone now work the other way, and Ojibwe has been the official language of Red Lake since 2011. Ojibwe religion is polytheistic, centred on the *manitouk*: the *animikeek* (thunderbirds), the underwater serpents *Mishebeshu*, the four winds, the owners of animal species, the *windigo*, and *Nanabush*, with the creator *Kitche Manitou* above them. Many Ojibwe practise it alongside Christianity, usually Catholicism, identifying *Kitche Manitou* with the Christian God.

## Sources & further reading

- Frances Densmore, *Chippewa Customs* — the source cited in the Museum of World Culture records for the Ojibwe term for beadwork and for its place as women's work
- Anton Treuer — Ojibwe historian; recordings and bilingual transcriptions of elders' stories, made with the Ponemah elder Eugene Stillday
- Theresa S. Smith — scholar of religion, on the *manitouk* as "the power beings of the Ojibwe cosmos"
- Alfred Irving Hallowell — anthropologist of the northern Ojibwe, author of the concept of "other-than-human persons"
- Leanne B. Simpson, *A Short History of the Blockade* — on *Amik* and the Seven Grandfather Teachings
- Christopher Vecsey — historian of Ojibwe religion, on *Kitche Manitou* and *Mishebeshu*
- The Ojibwe People's Dictionary, in collaboration with the University of Minnesota — searchable in English and Ojibwe, with voice recordings
- *Ojibwe Waasa-Inaabidaa* — PBS documentary on the history and culture of the Anishinaabe-Ojibwe of the Great Lakes
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe_mythology
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe_language
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe_cuisine
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe_religion
- https://folkways.si.edu/search?query=Ojibwe
- https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection — Met bandolier bag, charm bag, knife case and the flute catalogued as *Pib-be-gwun*
- https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection — British Museum birchbark scrolls, painted drum, pipes, lacrosse sticks and nineteenth-century photographs
- https://www.clevelandart.org/art/collection/search — Cleveland Museum of Art bandolier bag

title: "Ojibwe"

## At a glance
| | |
|---|---|
| Who | Ojibwe (Ojibway, Ojibwa, Chippewa), an Anishinaabe people |
| Where | Great Lakes region and northern plains, from western Quebec to British Columbia in Canada; Michigan to Montana in the US |
| How many | About 320,000 total; 160,000 in Canada registered with about 200 bands |
| Language | Anishinaabemowin (Ojibwemowin), an Algonquian language |
| Religion | Polytheistic, centered on the manitouk (spirit beings); many also practice Christianity |
| Known for | Birchbark canoes and scrolls · Wild rice and maple syrup harvesting · Glass beadwork · Midewiwin healing society · Jingle dress dancing |

## Overview

The Ojibwe are Canada's second-largest First Nations population, spread across the Great Lakes and northern regions. They speak Anishinaabemowin, an Algonquian language that served as a trade language for centuries. Their culture centers on harvests, storytelling, and relationships with spirit beings. They are known for distinctive crafts, traditional foods, and the Midewiwin society that preserves knowledge through birchbark scrolls.

## Material culture

Ojibwe material culture emphasizes patterned surfaces through beadwork and birchbark work, with practical objects made from bark, wood, and stone.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Glass beadwork is the dominant craft, sewn onto cloth and skin in geometric and animal designs.

- **Glass beadwork** (*manidoominensikaan*) — Woven and sewn seed beads on cloth, velvet and tanned skin, traditionally women's work.
- **Bandolier bags** — Shoulder bags of cotton and wool with velvet, beads and tassels, the flashiest formal attire in the 1800s.
- **Birchbark boxes and dishes** (*wiigwaas*) — Cylindrical boxes and oval dishes sewn to bent hoops with decorative cut bark strips for contrast.
- **Beaded bands** (*band*) — Long narrow strips of woven glass beads, sometimes featuring animal figures like otter or turtle.
- **Medicine bags** — Red velvet bags elaborately beaded with long shoulder slings and wool tassels.

### Clothing & dress

Ojibwe dress mixed traditional moccasins and beaded garments with imported cloth and blankets.

- **Moccasins** (*makizinan*) — Skin and cloth footwear with beads, waterproofed by fire-curing the seams.
- **Jingle dress** — Dark cloth dress hung with rows of tin cones cut from tobacco-can lids, originating with Ojibwe women and spreading to all tribes.
- **Beaded shirts and belts** — Cloth garments decorated with glass beads worn for formal occasions.

### Architecture

The characteristic dwelling is the wigwam, framed on saplings and covered with birch and juniper bark.

- **Wigwam** (*wiigiwaam*) — Domed or pointed lodge covered in birch bark and juniper, still built for particular sites and events.
- **Domed wigwam** (*waginogaan*) — Rounded lodge structure framed on willow saplings.
- **Pointed wigwam** (*nasawa'ogaan*) — Cone-shaped lodge structure framed on willow saplings.
- **Spirit house** (*jiibegamig*) — Small structure erected over burials to house the spirit of the deceased.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Everyday objects are made from bark, wood and stone, with no pottery recorded in the collections.

- **Birchbark canoe** — Bark sewn to wooden ribs, used for traveling waterways and still made as miniatures.
- **Cylindrical bark box** (*ask*) — Storage container made from bent birchbark.
- **Wooden club** — Squared-off handle with a circle head carved with a flower and metal ring.
- **Lacrosse stick** — Wood and buckskin implement used in the traditional game.
- **Carved pipe** — Hard wood or black stone inlaid with lead or white metal, used for smoking.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Adornment is made of beads and shell, with chokers serving as status symbols.

- **Beaded necklace** — Plaited glass beads strung together, worn with multiple necklaces in formal dress.
- **Beaded choker** — Red and white beaded band with concave disc center and shell-tipped cords, a status symbol.
- **Cowrie shell** (*miigis*) — Rare shell from distant coasts used in ceremonies and traded across the continent as evidence of wide networks.
- **Guardian spirit tattoo** (*manitou*) — Image of a person's spiritual guardian marked on the body.

## Music & performance

Musical instruments include flutes and drums; songs are recorded in birchbark scrolls using pictographic notation.

- **Wooden flute** — Two-piece red wooden flute about two feet long, made at Serpent River on Lake Huron.
- **Painted drum** — Military-style wooden drum repainted with Thunderers, sun and cattle representing the underworld.
- **Summer spiritual gathering** (*jiingotamog*) — Spiritual gathering held at reservations.
- **Powwow** (*niimi'idimaa*) — Social gathering held at reservations across Anishinaabe Country for singing, dancing and celebration.

## Dance & theatre

The main documented dance tradition is jingle-dress dancing performed at powwows.

- **Jingle-dress dancing** — Women's dance performed at powwows wearing the distinctive tin-cone dress.
- **Wild rice jigging** — Domestic practice of dancing or walking on parched grain to loosen its hulls.

## Festivals & rituals

The year revolves around harvests, with vision quests formerly central to male life and healing societies still active.

- **Wild rice harvest** (*manoomin*) — Late summer and early autumn gathering by canoe, with tobacco and prayers offered to the Great Spirit's Garden.
- **Maple sugar harvest** — Spring activity, taught in schools with elders narrating in Ojibwemowin while students gather wood and haul sap.
- **Vision quest** — Puberty rite undertaken by males to establish a lifelong relationship with a guardian spirit, now declined.
- **Shaking-tent rite** (*Jiisakiiwin*) — Healing ceremony performed by a ritual specialist calling on spirits for healing.
- **Midewiwin** — Ancient healing society that keeps birchbark scrolls and pictorial scripts recording sacred knowledge.

## Foodways

Wild rice is the defining food, with fish, maple sugar, venison and corn forming the staple diet.

- **Wild rice** (*manoomin*) — Nutty-flavored grain eaten for two thousand years, knocked from beds called the Great Spirit's Garden and parched, jigged and winnowed.
- **Maple sugar** — Spring harvest syrup granulated by boiling and working in a trough with wooden paddles.
- **Fish and venison** — Staple proteins hunted and caught throughout the year.
- **Foraged berries** — Blueberries, blackberries, choke cherries, raspberries, gooseberries and huckleberries gathered in summer.

## Oral tradition & literature

Storytelling is central to Ojibwe life, with sacred and ordinary stories kept separate and recorded in birchbark pictographs.

- **Nanabush** — Culture hero and trickster who taught people to hunt and fish, found wild rice and invented snowshoes.
- **Seven Grandfather Teachings** — Seven teachings of wisdom, respect, love, honesty, humility, bravery and truth, each paired with an animal.
- **Birchbark writing** (*wiigwaasabak*) — Pictographs serving as mnemonics for stories and knowledge, still used by traditional people and young people on social media.
- **Sacred stories** (*aadsookaan*) — Stories about spirit beings told only in winter when water was frozen to prevent drawing out the underwater serpent.

## Language & religion

Anishinaabemowin is an Algonquian language with seven dialects; religion centers on the manitouk, often practiced alongside Christianity.

- **Anishinaabemowin** — Algonquian language, the second most spoken First Nations language in Canada and fourth in North America.
- **Manitouk** — Spirit beings in Ojibwe religion, including thunderbirds, underwater serpents and animal owners.
- **Creator spirit** (*Kitche Manitou*) — Supreme creator spirit, often identified with the Christian God by Ojibwe practicing both religions.
- **Underwater serpent** (*Mishebeshu*) — Powerful spirit being from which copper is believed to come, whose presence must not be invoked in warm months.
- **Windigo** — Spirit being in Ojibwe cosmology representing a dangerous cannibal entity.

title: "Cree"
subtitle: "Canada"
region: "North America"
tags: [ethnography, north-america]
