## Overview

The Cree are a North American Indigenous people numbering more than 350,000 in Canada, where they form one of the country's largest First Nations macro-communities. Their homelands cover most of eastern and central Canada — from *Eeyou Istchee* on the east coast of James Bay in northern Quebec, across northern Ontario and the Canadian Prairies, into British Columbia and the Northwest Territories — with smaller communities in Montana, chiefly on Rocky Boy's Indian Reservation. Eight dialect-and-region groupings are usually distinguished (Plains, Woodland, Rocky, Swampy, Moose and East Cree, with the closely related Atikamekw, Innu and Naskapi), and settlements such as Moose Factory Island at the mouth of the Moose River, Mistissini on Lake Mistassini, and Whapmagoostui at the mouth of the Great Whale River anchor them. The language belongs to the Algonquian family. In folk-culture terms the Cree are known internationally for floral beadwork and silk embroidery on smoked mooseskin, and for pictures made by biting folded birchbark.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Floral beadwork** — Glass seed beads worked in flowering sprays on dark blue velvet bags (the drawstrings of surviving examples have been replaced by non-Native hands) and on smoked mooseskin panels cut from coats; one such beaded hide ornament from Island Lake, Manitoba, entered a Swedish collection as a gift in 1931. A hood of wool and cotton dated 1840–50 and legging panels of about 1870 combine wool cloth with glass beads and wood.

**Silk floral embroidery on smoked mooseskin** — Mittens and skin boots embroidered with floral work in silk floss, with skin fringing and multicoloured plaited wool cord ending in pompoms; the boots are worked in cotton thread instead, with pompoms of blue and burgundy wool on a braided cord tied around the upper leg.

**Quillwork** — A panel bag of about 1820–40 is sewn of native-tanned skin and worked with quill alongside glass beads and metal; the catalogue record does not describe the technique further.

**Embroidery on felted wool** — Trade cloth itself becomes the ground: a shot pouch of grey felted wool embroidered with multicoloured flowers and fitted with a metal zipper, and a rifle-case of the same grey wool carrying three sets of embroidered flowers, closed with a moose-skin end-piece and plastic buttons.

**Birchbark biting** — A rectangle of birchbark bearing four birds with outstretched wings and heads turned inwards, the image produced by biting the folded bark.

**Plaited and finger-woven cordwork** — Multicoloured plaited wool cords with pompoms join mittens and tie boots; a shot pouch hangs from a red and blue wool strap that appears to be finger-woven.

**Cloth appliqué and rickrack borders** — A baby-carrier of red checked cotton lined in off-white, bordered in brown cotton printed with white flowers, trimmed with orange rickrack and edged with pierced moose skin threaded with red nylon string; a rifle-case of denim is likewise banded with rickrack and embroidery.

**Motif vocabulary.** Multicoloured flower sprays (the dominant device, on hide, velvet and felted wool alike); blue flowers on red cloth; white flowers on brown cotton ground; birds with outstretched wings, in bitten birchbark.

### Clothing & dress

The documented working garment is the smoked mooseskin jacket: pull-over type with a straight hem, two chest pockets, short fringing along the seams and hem, two buttons at the neck opening, a separate hood sewn on, and a partial cotton lining. With it go paired mittens joined by a strip so they hang from the neck, skin boots with embroidered uppers and leg fringe, and moccasins, which photographs show worn with decorated leggings. Accessories carried on the body include firebags (wool, silk, glass beads and metal, about 1820), shot pouches, purses and small oval skin pouches with beaded ornament beneath the opening, of the kind used to hang a watch. Infants were dressed in caps of red cloth printed with blue flowers, lined in white cotton, with a ruffled border framing the face and ties at each front corner. Ceremonial and formal dress recorded in late nineteenth-century photographs differs sharply: the Plains Cree chief Kah-mi-yo-ki-suck-way (Fine Day) was photographed in two-horned head-gear with fur; He Shows His Blood, at Maple Creek, wore an arm band of deer hoof and skin, a bead and shell gorget choker and two eagle feathers in his hair; another man appears in a warbonnet on horseback. Women are shown wrapped in blankets, men at The Pas in hats, coats, trousers and boots.

### Architecture

The sources describe mobile dwellings rather than permanent houses. The basic residential unit was the lodge — eight to a dozen people, usually two related married couples and their families, sharing either a *wigwam*, a domed tent, or a *tipi*, a conical one. Several lodges moving and hunting together formed a band, and because lodges could leave bands and bands could form and dissolve easily, the built environment was designed to be struck and reassembled; banishment from any band was regarded as a severe punishment. Photographs from Battleford, Saskatchewan, show tipis standing in encampments behind assembled riders, and a Sun Dance lodge whose long supporting beams and covering material are visible behind a screen of cut shrubs, with men seated on the ground inside and standing behind the shrubs. The other structures the records name are colonial: the Hudson's Bay Company posts around which many communities grew, including Charles Fort of 1668 at the mouth of the Rupert River (later Fort Rupert or Rupert House, now Waskaganish), Moose Factory founded in 1672–73, and Fort Albany, established between 1675 and 1679.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources record no Cree ceramics or metalworking. What they do document is birchbark and skin work: the birchbark canoe, photographed upside down beside a tipi at a lakeshore, and bitten birchbark pictures. Household and hunting gear in the collections is overwhelmingly sewn — rifle-cases tailored from felted wool or denim and closed with moose skin and buttons, shot pouches, purses, and a cloth baby-carrier. Imported components are worked in without apology: metal zippers across a pouch and a purse, plastic buttons, canvas tape, orange rickrack and red nylon string. Pipes, flintlock muskets and rifles appear in the photographs as possessions rather than as products.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Adornment documented in the photographic record is made from animal and trade materials: a bead and shell gorget choker, an arm band of deer hoof and skin, and eagle feathers worn in the hair, two at a time. Headdresses, feathers and two-horned head-gear with fur distinguish chiefs and Sun Dance participants, who also carry feather fans. Beadwork otherwise ornaments carried objects — the glass and iron beads below the opening of a small skin watch-pouch — rather than the body itself. The sources describe no tattooing, no cosmetic practice and no hair traditions.

## Music & performance

The sources name no Cree instruments, song genres or singers. The only performance context they document is the Sun Dance: a photograph taken at Battleford in June 1895 shows six men, five standing and one mounted, as participants following a two-day Sun Dance ceremony, three of them holding sticks and a feather fan, and a second photograph shows the men assembled inside the dance lodge, some in headdresses and feathers, several with feather fans, in a mixture of Cree and settler clothing.

## Dance & theatre

The Sun Dance is the one dance tradition the sources attest, and they attribute it to the Cree as its source: Ojibwe communities living near the Plains region also performed it, a practice likely adopted from the Cree. The 1895 Battleford photographs record it as a two-day ceremony held in a purpose-built lodge screened with cut shrubs. No theatrical or masked traditions are described.

## Festivals & rituals

There was no calendar of festivals in the sources' account; the rhythm was the hunting year. Bands maintained strong ties with their neighbours through intermarriage and assembled at different points in the year to hunt and socialize together, and apart from these regional gatherings there was no higher-level formal structure — questions of war and peace were settled by consensus in councils of allied bands, each clan sending a representative with a vote. War brought a temporary commander, the *okimahkan*, an office distinct from that of the peace chief, whose role was closer to a diplomat's; Big Bear led his band into the run-up to the 1885 North-West Rebellion, but once fighting began Wandering Spirit became war leader. The deepest ritual logic the sources record is that of the hunt. The Cree traditionally drew no cultural separation between the religious and the secular, and the anthropologist Colin Scott characterised their worldview as animistic, conceiving the world as a community of living entities and relationships. Success in a hunt requires the cooperation of the prey animal, and the kill is therefore understood as a gift: the animal should be killed respectfully, without waste, and with consideration for the well-being of the wider population of its species. The Sun Dance is the named ceremonial gathering. Birth, marriage and funeral rites are not covered by the sources used here.

## Foodways

The sources do not name a single Cree dish, cooking method or beverage tradition. They describe subsistence rather than cuisine: the Cree were hunter-gatherers whose bands moved and hunted together, those who moved onto the Great Plains adopting bison hunting and becoming known as the Plains Cree, while some of the Naskapi remain caribou hunters and more nomadic than many of the Innu. The hunt was governed by the ethic described above — the prey's cooperation, no waste, regard for the species' wider population. Animal pelts dominate the economic record: four Cree men were photographed at The Pas holding large assemblages of pelts, and after acquiring firearms from the Hudson's Bay Company the Cree moved as traders onto the plains, acting as middlemen for the company; with the Assiniboine they were important intermediaries in the First Nations trading networks of the northern plains, and the Iron Confederacy they formed with the Assiniboine, the Métis Nation and the Saulteaux was a major force in the fur trade from the 1730s to the 1870s.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources name no epic cycle, but they document a living narrative and oratorical tradition and its modern documentation. Among the Cree and the northern Ojibwe, the thunderbirds are sometimes called *pinesiwak*. Oratory survives in published form in *The Counselling Speeches of Jim Kâ-Nîpitêhtêw* (1998), a text collection notable also for using full punctuation in Cree. Preston's *Cree Narrative: Expressing the Personal Meaning of Events* (National Museum of Man, 1976) treats storytelling as a means of conveying the personal significance of events. Revitalization work is extensive: speakers of various dialects are compiling dictionaries for their communities, including the Cree Language Resource Project's online bilingual dictionary; free Cree-language electronic books for beginners became available to Alberta teachers in 2013; the Cree School Board publishes its annual report in Cree as well as English; and a movie has been dubbed into Cree in the Northwest Territories, where a Medicinal Plant Guide was produced in Cree and English with elders' input. Joshua Whitehead is among the writers using the Cree language in poetry.

## Language & religion

Cree — also called Cree–Montagnais–Naskapi — is a dialect continuum of Algonquian languages spoken by approximately 86,475 people across Canada in 2021, making it the Indigenous language with the most speakers in the country; the Northwest Territories is the only jurisdiction granting it official status, alongside eight other Aboriginal languages. Endonyms vary by dialect: *nêhiyawêwin* (Plains), *nīhithawīwin* (Woods), *ininîmowin* (Eastern Swampy), *ililîmowin* (Moose), *iyiyiu-Ayamiwin* (Northern East Cree), *nehirâmowin* (Atikamekw). Speakers of the western and central dialects write in Cree syllabics, a variant of Canadian Aboriginal syllabics with Western and Eastern forms, while the easternmost dialects use the Latin script exclusively; Standard Roman Orthography serves Plains and Swampy Cree. Cree also underlies the contact languages Michif, Northern Michif, Bungi, Oji-Cree and Nehipwat. Cree religion has no formal leadership or organizational structure and displays much internal variation, shares many elements with Ojibwe practice, and centres on an animistic understanding of the world and on the ethics of the hunt.

- Adrian Tanner, *Bringing Home Animals: Religious Ideology and Mode of Production of the Mistassini Cree Hunters*. New York: St. Martin's Press, 1979

## Overview

The Cree are an Indigenous people of Canada with settlements across vast territories from the east coast to the northwest. They traditionally lived as hunter-gatherers in mobile bands, with those on the Great Plains hunting bison. The Cree maintain a living oral tradition and animistic worldview centered on respectful hunting practices and the cooperation of prey animals.

## Material culture

Cree material culture emphasizes sewn and woven work—beadwork, embroidery, and plaited cord—combining native materials like mooseskin and birchbark with imported glass beads, silk, and trade cloth.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Flowering designs in glass beads and silk embroidery on smoked mooseskin are the Cree's most distinctive textile work.

- **Floral beadwork** — Glass seed beads worked in flowering sprays on dark blue velvet bags and smoked mooseskin panels cut from coats.

- **Birchbark biting** — Pictures made by biting folded birchbark to create designs of birds with outstretched wings.
- **Quillwork** — Panels sewn of native-tanned skin and worked with quill alongside glass beads and metal.
- **Plaited and finger-woven cordwork** — Multicoloured wool cords with pompoms join mittens and tie boots, often in red and blue.

### Clothing & dress

Everyday wear centered on the smoked mooseskin jacket with hood and paired mittens, while ceremonial dress featured feathers, horns, and trade cloth.

- **Smoked mooseskin jacket** — Pull-over garment with chest pockets, fringing, buttons at the neck, and a separate sewn hood with cotton lining.
- **Skin boots** — Embroidered uppers and leg fringe, worn with moccasins and decorated leggings.
- **Paired mittens** — Joined by a wool strip so they hang from the neck, often embroidered with floral designs.
- **Shot pouches** — Sewn from felted wool or trade cloth, embroidered with flowers and closed with metal zippers or buttons.
- **Infant caps** — Red cloth printed with blue flowers, lined in white cotton, with ruffled borders framing the face.

### Architecture

The Cree built mobile dwellings designed to be struck and moved with hunting bands rather than permanent houses.

- **Wigwam** — A domed tent housing eight to a dozen people, usually two related married couples and their families.
- **Tipi** — A conical tent used as a residential unit in mobile bands, visible in photographs from Battleford and Saskatchewan encampments.
- **Sun Dance lodge** — A purpose-built structure with long supporting beams and a shrub screen, used for the two-day Sun Dance ceremony.
- **Moose Factory** — A Hudson's Bay Company post founded in 1672–73 around which many Cree communities grew.
- **Fort Rupert** — Colonial post established at the mouth of the Rupert River in 1668, also known as Charles Fort or Waskaganish.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The Cree produced no documented ceramics or metalwork, instead focusing on sewn and woven objects incorporating imported materials.

- **Birchbark canoe** — A watercraft photographed upside down beside tipis at lakeshore camps.
- **Rifle-cases** — Tailored from felted wool or denim, closed with moose skin and buttons or plastic fasteners.
- **Bitten birchbark pictures** — Rectangles of folded birchbark bearing bird or other designs created by biting.
- **Shot pouches** — Sewn pouches with embroidered decoration and hanging straps, often using metal zippers.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Adornment used animal materials and trade goods, with feathers and horned headdresses distinguishing chiefs and ritual leaders.

- **Gorget choker** — A bead and shell necklace worn as a sign of status.
- **Arm band** — Made of deer hoof and skin, worn as a mark of distinction.
- **Eagle feathers** — Two feathers worn in the hair by chiefs and Sun Dance participants.
- **Two-horned headdress** — A chief's headdress with fur, worn in formal and ceremonial contexts.

## Music & performance

The Sun Dance is the only documented performance tradition, with no Cree instruments or song genres recorded in the sources.

- **Sun Dance** — A two-day ceremony held in a purpose-built lodge, with participants in headdresses and feathers holding sticks and feather fans, photographed at Battleford in 1895.

## Dance & theatre

The Sun Dance is the sole documented dance tradition, with no theatrical or masked traditions described.

- **Sun Dance** — A two-day ceremony believed to originate with the Cree and later adopted by neighbouring Ojibwe communities.

## Festivals & rituals

There was no annual festival calendar; instead, the hunting year structured community rhythms, with the Sun Dance as the named ceremonial gathering.

- **Sun Dance** — A two-day ceremonial gathering held at different times, with a purpose-built lodge and specific ritual roles.
- **Hunt** — The central ritual practice governed by ethics of respect: the animal should be killed without waste and with regard for the species' wider population.
- **War leader** (*okimahkan*) — A temporary commander appointed during conflict, distinct from the peace chief or diplomat.
- **Council of allied bands** — Questions of war and peace settled by consensus, with each clan sending a representative with a vote.

## Foodways

The sources record subsistence practices rather than cuisine: the Cree were hunter-gatherers who hunted bison on the plains or caribou in the north.

- **Bison hunting** — Plains Cree bands adopted bison hunting and became known as the Plains Cree.
- **Caribou hunting** — Naskapi communities remained caribou hunters and more nomadic than many of the Innu.
- **Fur trading** — After acquiring firearms, Cree men moved as traders onto the plains and became important intermediaries for the Hudson's Bay Company and First Nations networks.
- **Iron Confederacy** — Alliance formed with the Assiniboine, Métis Nation and Saulteaux that became a major force in the fur trade from the 1730s to the 1870s.

## Oral tradition & literature

A living narrative and oratorical tradition is documented in published texts and modern revitalization efforts.

- **Thunderbirds** (*pinesiwak*) — Beings sometimes called pinesiwak among the Cree and northern Ojibwe.
- **The Counselling Speeches of Jim Kâ-Nîpitêhtêw** — A 1998 text collection of oratory using full punctuation in Cree.

Cree is an Algonquian language spoken by about 86,475 people, making it Canada's most-spoken Indigenous language; religion is animistic with no formal structure.

## Overview

The Tsimshian (*Tsʼmsyen*, "Inside the Skeena River") are an Indigenous people of the Pacific Northwest Coast, living mainly in coastal British Columbia around Terrace and Prince Rupert on the lower Skeena River, and at Metlakatla, Alaska, on Annette Island — the only reservation in that state. The Tsimshian estimate 45,000 Tsimshian people, with roughly 10,000 federally registered members in eight First Nations communities; about 1,450 Alaska Tsimshian are enrolled in the Metlakatla Indian Community. They speak *Sm'algyax*, "real or true tongue," of the Tsimshianic family. Society is matrilineal: identity, clans and property pass through the mother's line, and a stratified ranking system is reflected in some 27 distinct Tsimshian terms for "chief." Archaeology shows 5,000 years of continuous habitation around Prince Rupert Harbour. In folk-culture terms the Tsimshian are credited with inventing Chilkat weaving, and their carvers, weavers and feast-hosts sustain object traditions held in museums worldwide.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Chilkat weaving** — A weaving tradition the Tsimshian are credited with inventing, worked with western red cedar alongside other materials; cedar bark was the coast's universal fibre, made into clothing as well as tools, roofing, armour, building materials and canoe skins.

**Cedar-bark twining** — Twined cedar-bark work produced wide-brimmed hats, including one with a single weft of black-dyed bark run near the edge, and cylindrical lidded baskets. A surviving wooden weaving frame with its woven strap still attached documents the loom technology itself.

**Basketry with false embroidery** — A twined cylindrical cedar-bark basket made to sheathe a glass jar carries designs in "false embroidery" worked in grass and maidenhair fern on both body and lid — overlay patterning in contrasting plant fibres rather than dyed wool. Other baskets combine grass, straw and red cedar bark.

**Button blankets** — The dance cape known as a button blanket is cut from wool trade cloth and outlined in shell buttons; a mid-19th-century Tsimshian example dates to 1850–60. A 1903 photograph of chiefly regalia was attributed to Coast Tsimshian partly on the strength of the symbols worked on the blankets.

**Motif vocabulary.** Formline design (black and red formline painting on wood; dorsal fins and facial features carved in formline), salmon heads, killer whale and whale blowhole, raven, frog, wolf, eagle, Thunderbird, sea lion and seal, sturgeon-like fish, beaver, bird heads, and crest clan emblems — *Gispwudwada* (Killer Whale or Fireweed), *Ganhada* (Raven or Frog), *Laxgibuu* (Wolf), *Laxsgiik* (Eagle).

### Clothing & dress

Everyday dress drew on western red cedar bark, which was fashioned into clothing as well as armour; twined cedar-bark hats with wide brims shed the coastal rain. Ceremonial dress is sharply distinguished and is what the museum record preserves best. Chiefs wore a *frontlet* — a carved forehead ornament mounted on a headband — of wood set with abalone shell and pigment, one dated 1820–40. Over the shoulders went the button blanket dance cape of wool trade cloth and shell buttons. A shaman's headdress survives made of goat horns with leather and wire; another, described as made for a dog feast, combines vegetable fibre, wood and horn. Ritual officiants also wore head-rings, including a fire-eater's crown of vegetable fibre. Masks include one carved in the shape of a bird's head. A 1903 photograph of a ruling chief and family in regalia shows a frontlet, a mask worn on top of the head, patterned blankets, and three children wearing wolf skins. Sources name no distinct footwear or belt traditions.

### Architecture

Because salmon gave a dependable food base, the Tsimshian built permanent towns rather than moving camps, and lived in large longhouses framed and clad with cedar house posts and panels chosen to withstand a wet climate; a single house was very large and usually sheltered an entire extended family. The settlement year was double: winter villages stood in and around the islands of Prince Rupert Harbour and Venn Pass (Metlakatla), and families returned to summer villages along the lower Skeena when the salmon ran. House form left its mark on tribal names — *Gitasts'uu* (Kitasoo) means "(People of) a large, tiered house-depression." Monumental carving accompanied the houses: a 19th-century Tsimshian totem pole is held by the Smithsonian, and a historic photograph records the original setting of the Kapshkoltsh pole. When the Hudson's Bay Company moved its fort to present-day Lax Kwʼalaams in 1834, nine Tsimshian tribal chiefs relocated their houses to the surrounding area for trading advantage.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources describe no pottery; stone and cedar carry the household repertoire. Stone mauls and clubs are the best-documented form: heads of granite, light grey igneous rock and whitish quartzite, grooved for hafting and crowned with crests — a salmon head, an animal face with eyes, lips and teeth, a carved head read as a whale's blowhole. Hafts of hard wood were lashed on with sinew, leather thongs, or windings of spruce or cedar root; one example from Fort Simpson, in Coast Tsimshian territory, is labelled simply "Stone hammer." Two types of stone hammer were in use along the coast historically, and some are still used today. Cedar vessels include an oblong feast trough rimmed with inlaid shell opercula, darkened almost black by the eulachon oil it served. Bentwood and plank boxes were carved and painted, including burial-box walls and a box bearing a sea-lion design. Halibut were taken with a two-part V-shaped hook whose upper arm was carved as a spiritual helper — otters, seals, halibut, wolves and sea monsters being the usual subjects.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Engraved silver bracelets are the signature ornament in the collection, and they are signed work by named makers: one bearing a Thunderbird is inscribed "Thunderbird Bill Hellin 83," another with a frog "D M Dennis. 83 Frog." Inlay with haliotis (abalone) shell runs through high-status objects — the 1820–40 frontlet, an elkhorn club surmounted by a bird's head, and a carved wood-and-horn ornament set with abalone and copper that was probably once the upper element of a headdress or mask. Shell opercula were inlaid along the rims of feast bowls. The sources do not describe tattooing, body painting or hair practices.

## Music & performance

The wooden trumpet is the instrument most specifically tied to the Tsimshian: a large carved *trätrumpet* in the Stockholm collection is documented as used above all by the Tsimshian in "Nakmnok" performances and at the initiation of members into the secret societies, and similar trumpets were used by the northern and southern Kwakiutl groups and the Haida. These trumpets were often sounded in secret by concealed performers, to mark an arrival. Rattles are the other major class: a 19th-century Raven rattle of cedar with pebbles inside and polychrome painting, and a mid-19th-century face rattle of wood, fibre and leather. Percussion and sound-making also include a whale-shaped wooden clapper with carved lips, nose and eyes, painted in black and red formline, and a two-piece tapering hollowed wooden instrument catalogued ambiguously as a wind instrument or clapper, with a mouthpiece at the narrow end and vegetal-fibre bindings. A 1903 photograph of chiefly regalia includes a box drum whose design contributed to the Coast Tsimshian attribution. Music belongs to the feast: the Tsimshian feast system, or potlatch — called *yaawk* for one specific event — is the setting in which law is declared, knowledge transmitted, and chiefly stewardship demonstrated.

## Dance & theatre

The sources document the regalia and the occasions rather than named dance repertoires. Dance capes (button blankets), frontlets worn on the forehead, masks on the crown of the head, bird's-head masks and a fire-eater's crown all point to masked performance within the feast and within the secret societies, whose initiations the hidden wooden trumpets announced. David A. Boxley, *Laxsgiik*, was the first to host a potlatch and raise a totem pole in modern times in Metlakatla, Alaska. Beyond this, the sources used do not describe specific dances or dramatic forms.

## Festivals & rituals

The ceremonial year centres on the feast system rather than a calendar of seasonal festivals; the Tsimshian recognise four different types of feast. Today the potlatch is held to honour deaths and burials and to mark succession to name-titles, and it functions as the agency of social reproduction, the expression of law, the transmission of knowledge, and the demonstration of a chief's obligation to steward resources and attend to community needs. Planning and delivery follow very specific protocols that bind guests as well as hosts: it is untoward to hold out one's hand while payments — what outside observers call gifts — are being distributed. Life-cycle rites are equally formal. Marriage was an extremely formal affair of several prolonged and sequential ceremonies, and arranged marriages and births were common as a way of protecting rights of access to territories and resources. Taboos prohibited women and men from eating improper foods during and after childbirth; several such taboos are still actively practised. Hereditary chieftainship passes through the maternal line via the mother's brother, but the inheritor must be trained in proper behaviour and groomed for specific obligations, since no lineage should be sullied by the misconduct of a high-ranking member. Burial boxes, carved and painted, belong to this ritual complex.

## Foodways

Salmon is the centre of Tsimshian nutrition, as it has been since the abundance of sea life allowed permanent towns to be built; it remains central despite large-scale commercial fishing in the area, and families historically moved to summer villages on the lower Skeena when the salmon returned. Halibut was fished with the carved two-part hook, set about a metre above the bottom and usually worked singly rather than in gangs. Eulachon oil was a staple: an oblong cedar trough in the collection is so impregnated with it that oil still seeps from the wood. Berries of *Vaccinium vitis-idaea* ssp. *minus* were eaten. At Annette Islands Reserve the community held the only right in Alaska to keep using fish traps after statehood in 1959, taking fish as food for reserve residents; required to use them at least once every three years, they stopped early in the 2000s and lost the right. Feast foods are distributed under the protocols described above, and food taboos attach to childbirth. The sources name no individual dishes, and do not describe tea or other beverage traditions.

## Oral tradition & literature

Tsimshian narrative is transmitted orally and divided by genre. An *adaawx* — "true tellings" — concerns animal spirits in human guise and is generally tied to the origin of the earth and of the peoples on it; a *malesk*, by contrast, is an adventure or history tale meant to entertain rather than explain. The Raven, called *Txamsem*, *We-gyet* or Giant, is the central figure, part of the Raven Tales shared across the Pacific Northwest Coast, and is understood as creator of the universe and intermediary between its physical and spiritual forms. In the creation narrative a pampered chief's son sickens and dies, a youth "bright as fire" appears in his bed in a dark and still universe, is tricked by slave spirits into eating scabs, develops an insatiable appetite, and is sent away with a raven blanket to become Raven; as he learns generosity he hosts a potlatch and wishes his guests to stone, giving form to a previously immaterial world. *Txamsem* has a brother, *Logobola*, held responsible for the scarcity of fresh clear water and for the fog in which Txamsem became lost. Henry W. Tate and Walter Wright worked as oral historians, and William Beynon of the Gitlaan as an ethnographer; artists today continue storytelling in their own media.

## Language & religion

*Sm'algyax* — "real or true tongue" — is one of four Tsimshianic lects: Coast Tsimshian on the lower Skeena and at New Metlakatla, Southern Tsimshian at Klemtu (extinct in 2013 with its last speaker), Nisg̱a'a on the Nass, and Gitksan on the upper Skeena. Most linguists treat Tsimshianic as an independent family; its inclusion in Edward Sapir's Penutian hypothesis remains genuinely contested, with Marie-Lucie Tarpent finding the connection probable and others holding the family unrelated to any other North American language. In 2016 only 160 people in Canada were recorded as Tsimshian speakers, and about 50 of the 1,300 Tsimshian in Alaska still speak Coast Tsimshian; courses have been offered at the University of Alaska Southeast since 2023. Tsimshian religion centred on the "Lord of Heaven," who sent supernatural servants to earth to aid people in need, and held that charity and purification of the body — by cleanliness or fasting — was the route to the afterlife. Anglican, Methodist and Presbyterian missionaries, William Duncan foremost among them, worked among the Tsimshian from the 19th century.

## Sources & further reading

- Boas, Franz. *Tsimshian Texts*. Washington: Bureau of American Ethnology, Bulletin 27, 1902; and "Tsimshian," in *Handbook of American Indian Languages*, Bulletin 40, part I, 1911, pp. 287–422.
- McNair, Peter L., Alan L. Hoover and Kevin Neary. *The Legacy: Continuing Traditions of Canadian Northwest Coast Indian Art*. Victoria: British Columbia Provincial Museum, 1980.
- Holm, Bill. "Will the Real Charles Edensaw Please Stand Up?: The Problem of Attribution in Northwest Coast Indian Art," in *The World Is as Sharp as a Knife*. Victoria: British Columbia Provincial Museum, 1981, pp. 175–200.
- Mithun, Marianne. *The Languages of Native North America*. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1999.
- Tarpent, Marie-Lucie. "Tsimshianic and Penutian: Problems, Methods, Results, and Implications," *International Journal of American Linguistics* 63 (1997), 52–244.

## At a glance
| | |
|---|---|
| Who | The Tsimshian, an Indigenous people of the Pacific Northwest Coast |
| Where | Coastal British Columbia around Terrace and Prince Rupert on the lower Skeena River, and Metlakatla, Alaska |

## Overview

The Tsimshian are an Indigenous people of coastal British Columbia and Alaska with 5,000 years of continuous habitation. Society is matrilineal, with identity and property passing through the mother's line, and a complex ranking system expressed in chiefly titles. The Tsimshian are celebrated for their mastery of cedar work, weaving, carving and the potlatch feast system, which governs law, knowledge transmission and social order.

## Material culture

Tsimshian material culture centres on the red cedar, worked into textiles, clothing, architecture and decorated objects that merge practical function with spiritual meaning.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Cedar bark and wool trade cloth are woven and twined into blankets, hats and baskets with distinctive formline designs and shell inlay.

- **Chilkat weaving** — A weaving tradition the Tsimshian are credited with inventing, worked with western red cedar and other materials.
- **Cedar-bark twining** — Twined cedar-bark work produces wide-brimmed hats and cylindrical lidded baskets.
- **Button blankets** — Dance capes cut from wool trade cloth and outlined in shell buttons, used in ceremonial performance.
- **Formline design** — Black and red painted designs on wood featuring dorsal fins, facial features, salmon heads, killer whales, ravens and clan emblems.
- **False embroidery basketry** — Twined cedar-bark baskets with overlay patterning in grass and maidenhair fern rather than dyed wool.

### Clothing & dress

Everyday dress uses cedar bark; ceremonial dress is sharply distinguished and includes carved frontlets, button blankets and animal skins.

- **Frontlet** — A carved wooden forehead ornament mounted on a headband, set with abalone shell and pigment, worn by chiefs.
- **Button blanket cape** — A dance cape of wool trade cloth outlined in shell buttons worn over the shoulders in ceremony.
- **Shaman's headdress** — Ritual headdress made of goat horns with leather and wire, or vegetable fibre, wood and horn.
- **Head-ring** — Worn by ritual officiants including a fire-eater's crown of vegetable fibre.
- **Carved bird's-head mask** — Masks carved in the shape of a bird's head worn on top of the head during ceremonial performance.

### Architecture

The Tsimshian built permanent cedar longhouses framed with house posts and panels, settling year-round in winter villages and moving to summer villages when salmon ran.

- **Cedar longhouse** — A large house framed and clad with cedar house posts and panels, sheltering an entire extended family.
- **Winter villages** — Permanent settlements in and around the islands of Prince Rupert Harbour and Venn Pass.
- **Summer villages** — Seasonal settlements along the lower Skeena where families returned when the salmon ran.
- **Totem pole** — Monumental carved cedar poles that accompanied houses, including the Kapshkoltsh pole.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The Tsimshian produced no pottery; stone tools and cedar vessels carry the household repertoire.

- **Stone mauls and clubs** — Heads of granite or quartzite crowned with carved crests like salmon heads or whale blowholes, hafted with wood and sinew.
- **Feast trough** — An oblong cedar vessel rimmed with inlaid shell opercula, darkened by eulachon oil.
- **Bentwood box** — Carved and painted plank boxes used for burial and storage, bearing designs like sea-lion motifs.
- **Halibut hook** — A two-part V-shaped hook whose upper arm is carved as a spiritual helper like an otter or seal.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Engraved silver bracelets signed by named makers are the signature ornament, often inlaid with abalone shell.

- **Engraved silver bracelet** — Signed work by named makers bearing designs like Thunderbirds or frogs, such as those by Thunderbird Bill Hellin and D M Dennis.
- **Abalone inlay** (*haliotis*) — Shell inlay that runs through high-status objects including frontlets, clubs and feast bowls.
- **Shell opercula inlay** — Shell opercula inlaid along the rims of feast bowls.

## Music & performance

The wooden trumpet and rattles are the main instruments, sounded during secret society initiations and feasts.

- **Trätrumpet** — A large carved wooden trumpet used by the Tsimshian in Nakmnok performances and secret society initiations, often sounded by concealed performers.
- **Raven rattle** — A 19th-century cedar rattle with pebbles inside and polychrome painting.
- **Face rattle** — A mid-19th-century rattle of wood, fibre and leather shaped like a face.
- **Whale-shaped clapper** — A wooden percussion instrument painted in black and red formline with carved lips, nose and eyes.
- **Box drum** — A drum whose design contributed to identifying Tsimshian regalia in historical photographs.

## Dance & theatre

Masked performance within feasts and secret societies is documented through regalia, though named dance repertoires are not recorded.

- **Button blanket dance cape** — A wool cape outlined in shell buttons worn in masked performance.
- **Forehead frontlet** — A carved forehead ornament worn during dance and masked performance.
- **Crown mask** — A mask worn on the crown of the head during ceremonial dance.
- **Bird's-head mask** — A carved mask shaped like a bird's head worn during performance.
- **Fire-eater's crown** — A vegetable-fibre crown worn by a ritual performer in the feast and secret societies.

## Festivals & rituals

The potlatch feast system is the centre of ceremonial life, serving as the means of declaring law, transmitting knowledge and demonstrating chiefly stewardship.

- **Potlatch** (*yaawk*) — A feast held to honour deaths, mark succession to name-titles and express law and social obligation through formal payment distribution.
- **Four feast types** — The Tsimshian recognise four different types of feast, each with specific protocols binding guests and hosts.
- **Marriage ceremony** — An extremely formal affair of several prolonged and sequential ceremonies, often arranged to protect territorial rights.
- **Childbirth taboos** — Taboos prohibited women and men from eating improper foods during and after childbirth, many still actively practised.
- **Burial box ritual** — Carved and painted burial boxes are central to the ritual complex of death and succession.

## Foodways

Salmon is the centre of Tsimshian nutrition, with halibut and eulachon oil as staples; families moved seasonally to summer villages on the Skeena when salmon ran.

- **Salmon** — The centre of Tsimshian nutrition for 5,000 years, enabling permanent towns and remaining central despite commercial fishing.
- **Halibut** — Fished with a carved two-part hook set about a metre above the bottom, usually worked singly.
- **Eulachon oil** — A staple so pervasive that cedar troughs still seep oil from their wood centuries later.
- **Vaccinium berries** (*Vaccinium vitis-idaea ssp. minus*) — Wild berries eaten as part of the seasonal diet.
- **Fish traps** — At Annette Islands Reserve, the community held the only right in Alaska to use fish traps after statehood in 1959.

## Oral tradition & literature

Tsimshian narrative is divided into two genres: adaawx (true tellings about animal spirits and origins) and malesk (adventure and history tales).

- **Adaawx** — True tellings concerning animal spirits in human guise, generally tied to the origin of the earth and peoples.
- **Malesk** — Adventure or history tales meant to entertain rather than explain.
- **Raven Tales** (*Txamsem, We-gyet, or Giant*) — Stories of the central figure Raven, understood as creator of the universe and intermediary between physical and spiritual forms.
- **Raven creation narrative** — A story in which a pampered chief's son dies and is replaced by a youth who becomes Raven after learning generosity through hosting a potlatch.
- **Logobola** — Raven's brother, held responsible for the scarcity of fresh clear water and the fog.

## Language & religion

Sm'algyax is one of four Tsimshianic lects; traditional religion centred on the Lord of Heaven and supernatural servants, later influenced by Anglican, Methodist and Presbyterian missionaries.

- **Sm'algyax** — Real or true tongue, the main Tsimshian language spoken on the lower Skeena and at New Metlakatla.
- **Tsimshianic lects** — Four related languages: Coast Tsimshian, Southern Tsimshian (extinct 2013), Nisg̱a'a and Gitksan.
- **Lord of Heaven** — The central figure of traditional Tsimshian religion who sent supernatural servants to aid people in need.
- **Spiritual purification** — Charity and purification of the body through cleanliness or fasting was the route to the afterlife.
- **Language revitalization** — In 2016 only 160 people in Canada spoke Tsimshian; university courses have been offered at the University of Alaska Southeast since 2023.

## Glossary

- *Sm'algyax* — Real or true tongue; the Tsimshian language
- *adaawx* — True tellings; sacred narratives about animal spirits and origins
- *malesk* — Adventure or history tale meant to entertain
- *yaawk* — A specific type of potlatch feast
- *potlatch* — A ceremonial feast for honouring deaths, succession and demonstrating chiefly stewardship
- *trätrumpet* — A large carved wooden trumpet used in secret society initiations
- *frontlet* — A carved forehead ornament worn by chiefs
- *formline* — A style of black and red painted design on wood with carved facial features and fins
- *Txamsem* — Raven, the central creator figure in Tsimshian mythology
- *We-gyet* — Another name for Raven in Tsimshian tradition
- *Logobola* — Raven's brother, responsible for water scarcity and fog
- *haliotis* — Abalone shell, used for inlay in high-status objects
- *eulachon oil* — A staple food oil extracted from eulachon fish
- *Nakmnok* — A performance in which wooden trumpets were used

## Overview

The Coast Salish are a large, loose grouping of ethnically and linguistically related Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast, living in British Columbia and the U.S. states of Washington and Oregon. Their territories run from the northern limit of the Salish Sea along the inside of Vancouver Island, cover most of southern Vancouver Island, all of the Lower Mainland, and most of Puget Sound and the Olympic Peninsula; the Tillamook or Nehalem around Tillamook, Oregon are the southernmost. These homelands coincide with the modern metropolitan areas of Victoria, Vancouver and Seattle. The term covers speakers of fourteen contiguous Salishan languages, sometimes extended to Tillamook and Nuxalk. A 2012 estimate put the population at a minimum of 56,590: 28,406 Status Indians registered to Coast Salish bands in British Columbia and 28,284 enrolled members of federally recognized tribes in Washington State. In folk-culture terms they matter for a weaving and carving complex — wool robes, spindle whorls, imbricated basketry, house posts — that is deliberately more minimalist than the art of their northern neighbours.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

Coast Salish art divides into two major forms: flat design and carving, and basketry and weaving. Historically these followed gendered roles, men making figurative sculpture and painting depicting crests, shamanic beings and spirits, women producing baskets and textiles most often decorated with abstract designs.

**Mountain-goat and woolly-dog wool weaving** — Wool from the mountain goat and from the now-extinct Salish Woolly Dog was used for woven mats, blankets, clothing and robes. The wool was mixed with a diatomaceous earth that removed oils and added a white colour, then wetted and twisted between palm and thigh into a loose strand before spinning. Weaving was done on a loom of two upright bars carrying two horizontal rollers; some loom poles were themselves carved with supernatural characters or family history. Smaller textiles were functional, while many larger robes served as indicators of wealth.

**Spindle whorl** — Whorls were set on the shafts of wooden spindles to spin the loose strands. Some are plain; others carry elaborate designs and depicted beings, and the whorl is one of the principal supports of the flat-design idiom alongside house posts, welcome figures, combs, bentwood boxes and canoes.

**Imbricated coiled slat basketry** — The best-documented pattern-bearing form in the objects shown here: circular trays and rectangular slat baskets coiled from cedar or hemlock roots, decorated with imbricated designs in plain and black-dyed prunus bark, sometimes finished with an undulating decorative edge. Preparation tools included specially designed combs; a separate tool pushed the weft during weaving.

**Cedar-bark work** — Cedar bark was both a basketry fibre and a sheet material. A basket in the Museum of Ethnography collection is made of red cedar-bark fibre with a handle wrapped in a decorative band of probably red-dyed cedar-bark fibre; the same collection holds an *öskar*, a cedar-bark bailer of a type used to clear unwanted water from canoes on rivers, lakes and the sea.

**Carex twine and reed matting** — Coast Salish people use over 100 species of plants, among them the leaves of *Carex* for baskets and twine. Woven reed mats were made into the mattresses and cushions of the longhouse.

**Motif vocabulary.** Imbrication in plain and black-dyed prunus bark (the standard basketry surface pattern); crest figures, shamanic beings and spirits in men's figurative work; abstract design in women's weaving and basketry; animal features worked onto bowl surfaces, extended on more elaborate pieces into head, body, wings and limbs; the seated human figure intertwined with animals; and on a mountain-goat horn bracelet, groups of four or five scratched parallel lines separated by lines of three circles.

### Clothing & dress

Wool from mountain goat and woolly dog supplied blankets, clothing and robes, the larger robes doubling as public statements of wealth. A photographic postcard of three Northwest Coast men shows the Coast Salish sitter in a cloth cap with a feather, wearing a blanket over a shirt and a second blanket around the waist with leggings and footwear, while his Haida and Tlingit companions wear carved frontlet headdresses with shell, ermine tails and sea-lion whiskers — a useful contrast in ceremonial headgear. Trade blankets and ornamentation were among the luxuries Coast Salish traders took from the Hudson's Bay Company posts. Ceremonial dress for the *sxwayxwey* mask society is distinct from daily wear: regalia covered with feathers, and leggings hung with hoof rattles. Nineteenth-century studio and field photographs show the Euro-American clothing of the period — the Songhees chief James Sqwameyuks in jacket, floral-patterned waistcoat, shirt and trousers; a Sechelt woman in a shirt and long skirt, her child in a cap, long-sleeved top, trousers, socks and shoes. Many Coast Salish mothers shaped the heads of free-born babies, binding them with cradle boards long enough to produce a steeply sloping forehead; a British Museum model of a cradle demonstrates the stages of the practice.

### Architecture

Villages consisted of shed-roofed cedar longhouses built of western red cedar split planks and beams over an earthen floor, housing forty or more people, usually a related extended family. Interior walls were lined with sleeping platforms standing three or four feet above the ground, with storage shelves above them for baskets, tools and clothing and firewood stowed beneath; food hung drying from the ceiling, partitions separated families, and interior fires vented through roof slats used as chimneys. Large beams at the sides, called house posts, were carved or painted with ancestors, family history or supernatural beings. The wealthy built on an extraordinary scale: Simon Fraser described a Sto:lo house 640 by 60 feet, a Squamish longhouse measured 200 by 60 feet and held eleven families numbering about a hundred people, and the Suquamish Oleman House (Old Man House) at what became the Port Madison Reservation ran 500 by 40–60 feet around 1850. The gambrel roof was unique to Puget Sound Coast Salish. Pit-houses, called *kekuli* in Chinook Jargon, were also used. Villages stood near navigable water for dugout canoe transport, sometimes stretching for miles along a river. In the Fraser Canyon, boulder walls were built in the fifteenth century; these Salish Defensive Sites, one excavated by Kisha Supernant at Yale, British Columbia in 2008, may have served for defence, as fishing platforms and as house terraces.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources describe no ceramic or metalworking tradition; the everyday repertoire is wood, bark, fibre and horn. Men carved house posts, grave monuments, masks and ritual paraphernalia including rattles — sheets of mountain-goat horn bent and sewn into volumetric triangles, originally hung with strands of mountain-goat wool. The same flat-design idiom carries onto combs (one British Museum comb is of wood, possibly yew), bentwood boxes, welcome figures and canoes. Carved bowls range from simple forms with animal features to the complex seated human figure bowl; one seated human figure bowl was used in a female puberty ritual in Secwépemc territory and was believed to aid women in giving birth. Northwest Coast groups have worked wood and fibre for over 10,500 years, and waterlogged wet sites preserve the perishable end of the kit: wedges, fishhooks, basketry, cordage and nets. Photographs of the Fraser River show salmon caches raised on stilts, large wooden drying racks, long salmon spears and dip nets on poles.

## Jewelry & body adornment

Adornment is thinly documented in these sources. The one object shown is a bracelet cut as a thin length of mountain-goat horn, its shouldered end tapering to a pointed hitch that slots into a hole in the other end, decorated with four groups of roughly scratched parallel lines and two lines of three circles each, and worn or polished very smooth inside and out. Ornamentation was among the luxury categories Coast Salish traders sought from European ships. The most consequential body practice recorded is not jewellery but head shaping: the careful binding of free-born infants' heads with cradle boards to produce a sloping forehead, a visible mark of rank in a society divided into upper class, lower class and slaves.

## Music & performance

Performance among the Coast Salish is bound to spirit power. Coast Salish people hold that through dances, masks and ceremonies they express the spiritual powers given to them, and that those powers define a community's success in leadership, bravery, healing or artistry. Spirit dancing ceremonies are common winter gatherings at which members show their powers through song and dance; people often come together on the longhouse floor, where each member's power is their own alone to display in various songs, and the powers sought individually through trials of isolation attach to spirit animals such as raven, woodpecker, bear or seal. In the central Coast Salish region the *sxwayxwey* mask ceremony is central: men from families holding the hereditary right are initiated into the society, wear the mask and dance, joined by women singers and a special song. Rattles of bent and sewn mountain-goat horn, and leggings strung with hoof rattles, are the percussion named in the sources. The potlatch, the great ceremonial display of wealth, was banned in Canada in 1885 and in the United States some years later; suppression ended in 1934 in the US and in 1951 in Canada, after which some potlatching became overt immediately. Gambling on *slahal*, a sleight-of-hand game, accompanied athletic contests as recreation.

## Dance & theatre

Two named dance traditions appear in the sources. The *sxwayxwey* (also *Sx̱wáýx̱way* or *Skwayskway*) mask dance is performed by hereditarily entitled men of the central Coast Salish, in masks with bulging cylindrical eyeballs, "horns" rendered as animal heads, and drooping tongues, crowned dynamically with large feathers; dancers wear feather-covered regalia and hoof-rattle leggings, and women sing. Winter spirit dancing, by contrast, is the collective but individually owned display of acquired spirit powers on the longhouse floor through song and dance. The sources used do not describe a theatrical or puppet tradition.

## Festivals & rituals

The ritual year turns on the winter spirit dances and on the potlatch, the public display of wealth — wealth here including land, food resources, household items and adornments, which could not buy status or power but could enhance it, and which was never meant to be hidden. Individual ritual life began with the vision quest: journeys involving other states of consciousness, varied and widely practised, through which guardian spirits were sought. Belief in guardian spirits and in shapeshifting between human and animal was widely shared, and conceptions of the soul and of the lands of the living and the dead were complex and mutable. The Duwamish had a soul recovery and journey ceremony. Of the people recorded near Port Townsend, shamans held that every being has five spiritual components — body, inner and outer soul, life force and ghost — that illness follows the soul's removal from the body and death follows its arrival in the underworld, and that the shaman's work is to travel to the underworld and recover the soul in transit. The journey there was described as a two-day walk along a trail through bushes and past a lake to a river-divided valley, and the afterlife closely resembled the life lived, with work, hunting and family. Spirits appeared only at night, so people travelled by day and stayed close to others. Life-cycle rites in the sources include the female puberty ritual in which a seated figure bowl was used, and the head-shaping of free-born infants.

## Foodways

Salmon was the dietary staple, supplemented by a rich variety of other seafoods and forage, especially among the southern Coast Salish in their more temperate territories. Shellfish were abundant; butter clams, horse clams and cockles were dried for trade. Kokanee, a freshwater fish, was taken in the Lake Washington and Lake Sammamish watersheds. Land management was deliberate: forest gardens on the northwest coast of Canada held crabapple, hazelnut, cranberry, wild plum and wild cherry, and there is documentation of the cultivation of great camas, Indian carrot and Columbia lily. Anthropogenic grasslands were maintained for game habitat and for vegetable sprouts, roots, bulbs, berries and nuts; the most important plant foods were probably bracken and camas, and wapato especially for the Duwamish. Many varieties of berries were gathered, some with comblike devices not reported elsewhere; salal is the source of multiple tinctures and teas, and its berries are often eaten during feasts. Acorns were relished but not widely available, and regional tribes travelled in autumn to the Nisqually Flats to harvest them. Hunting was specialized into what were probably the professions of sea hunter, land hunter and fowler, with waterfowl taken on moonless nights using strategic flares. The Muckleshoot Seasonal Rounds set the calendar: salmon on the river banks in January; salmonberry sprouts eaten with salmon eggs by May, while men hunted deer and elk and women gathered camas on the prairies and clams on the beaches; steelhead and king salmon in mass along the rivers in summer, with berries abundant in the forests.

## Oral tradition & literature

*Legends of Vancouver*, published in 1911 by the Canadian author E. Pauline Johnson (Tekahionwake) and now available online from the UPenn Digital Library, is a collection of Coast Salish "as told-to" narratives stemming from the author's relationship with the Squamish chief Joe Capilano. The narrative world it draws on is one of guardian spirits and of transformation between human and animal spirits. A later retelling for children, *The Adventures of Yoo-Lah-Teen: A Legend of the Salish Coastal Indians*, was published by Ellen Pugh and Laszlo Kubinyi in 1975. Oratory has its own modern landmark: Chief Dan George's 1967 speech on what had happened to his people, delivered at a Canadian Centennial ceremony in Vancouver's Empire Stadium, riveted its audience and touched off public awareness and Native activism in British Columbia and Canada. Language documentation includes the *Lushootseed Dictionary* of Dawn Bates, Thom Hess and Vi Hilbert. Coast Salish characters have also entered genre fiction, in the Victoria author Stanley Evans's mystery series featuring the investigator Silas Seaweed.

## Language & religion

The Coast Salish or Central Salish languages form a branch of the Salishan family, spoken around most of the Georgia and Puget Sound basins; the Tsamosan and Tillamook languages are often treated by linguists as independent branches of Salishan rather than part of this one, and the position of Nuxálk (Bella Coola) is unsettled — it shares at least one phonological change with Coast Salish but also resembles the Interior Salish languages. The name Salish comes from the Salish people of Montana, whose Montana Salish is the easternmost Salishan language. Languages and peoples named in the museum records and articles include Halkomelem, Lushootseed, Squamish, Snuneymuxw, Sechelt/Shishalh, Songhees and Sto:lo; from 1970, such self-designations began to replace older names conferred by anthropologists, linguists and governments. Catholic missionaries arrived in Puget Sound around 1839–1840 and Methodists worked there from 1840 to 1842 without success. The living religious practice described in these sources is the spirit-power complex: guardian spirits, vision quests, shamanic soul recovery and the winter spirit dances.

## Sources & further reading

- Pamela Amoss, *Coast Salish Spirit Dancing: The Survival of an Ancestral Religion*, University of Washington Press, 1978.
- Bruce Granville Miller, *Be of Good Mind: Essays on the Coast Salish*, UBC Press, 2011.
- Aldona Jonaitis, *Art of the Northwest Coast*, Douglas & McIntyre, 2006.
- Steven C. Brown, Rebecca Blanchard and Nancy Davenport, *Contemporary Coast Salish Art*, University of Washington Press, 2005.
- Hilary Stewart, *Cedar: Tree of Life to the Northwest Coast Indians*, Douglas & McIntyre, 1984 — cited in the Museum of Ethnography records for the cedar-bark bailer and basket.
- Wayne Suttles and Barbara Lane, "Southern Coast Salish," in *Handbook of North American Indians*, vol. 7: *Northwest Coast*, Smithsonian Institution, 1990.
- Seattle Art Museum, "S'abadeb—The Gifts: Pacific Coast Salish Art and Artists" (opened 24 October 2008), 75 works of traditional and contemporary art; Burke Museum, Coast Salish Art.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coast_Salish_peoples
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coast_Salish_art
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coast_Salish_language
- British Museum online collection: https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection
- No UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage element in the sources consulted concerns this group.

## At a glance
| | |
|---|---|
| Who | Coast Salish people, an ethnically and linguistically related Indigenous peoples |
| Where | British Columbia, Washington and Oregon, from Vancouver Island through the Lower Mainland and Puget Sound |
| How many | a minimum of 56,590 |
| Language | fourteen contiguous Salishan languages |
| Religion | spirit-power complex with guardian spirits, vision quests and shamanic practices |
| Known for | weaving mountain-goat and woolly-dog wool robes · carving house posts and masks · imbricated coiled slat basketry · spirit dancing ceremonies · potlatch wealth displays |

## Overview

The Coast Salish are Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast living in British Columbia and Washington and Oregon. They speak fourteen related Salishan languages and number at least 56,590 people. Their art emphasizes a minimalist approach compared to northern neighbours, dividing into flat design and carving by men, and basketry and weaving by women. They are known for wool textiles, carved wooden objects, and ceremonies tied to spiritual power.

## Material culture

Coast Salish material culture centres on wood, bark, fibre and horn, shaped through weaving, carving and basketry with little ceramic or metalworking tradition.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Wool from mountain goat and the extinct Salish Woolly Dog was spun, woven and used for blankets, mats, clothing and wealth-indicating robes.

- **Mountain-goat and woolly-dog wool weaving** — Wool was mixed with diatomaceous earth, wetted and twisted between palm and thigh before being woven on a loom of two upright bars carrying two horizontal rollers.
- **Spindle whorl** — Whorls set on wooden spindles spun loose strands, and some carried elaborate designs depicting beings as a principal support of flat-design idiom.
- **Imbricated coiled slat basketry** — Circular trays and rectangular baskets were coiled from cedar or hemlock roots and decorated with imbricated designs in plain and black-dyed prunus bark.
- **Cedar-bark work** — Cedar bark served as both basketry fibre and sheet material for baskets and bailing tools used to clear water from canoes.
- **Carex twine and reed matting** — Woven reed mats were made into the mattresses and cushions of the longhouse, while Carex leaves were used for baskets and twine.

### Clothing & dress

Wool blankets and robes served as both everyday wear and public statements of wealth, while ceremonial dress for mask societies included feather-covered regalia and hoof-rattle leggings.

- **Wool robes and blankets** — Larger robes doubled as indicators of wealth, while trade blankets from the Hudson's Bay Company were among luxuries Coast Salish traders sought.
- **Sxwayxwey regalia** (*sxwayxwey*) — Ceremonial dress for the mask society consisted of regalia covered with feathers and leggings hung with hoof rattles.
- **Head shaping with cradle boards** — Many Coast Salish mothers bound the heads of free-born babies with cradle boards long enough to produce a steeply sloping forehead as a visible mark of rank.

### Architecture

Villages consisted of large shed-roofed cedar longhouses built of western red cedar planks and beams, housing extended families and sometimes stretching for miles along rivers.

- **Cedar longhouse** — Shed-roofed structures built of western red cedar split planks and beams over an earthen floor housed forty or more people with interior sleeping platforms, storage shelves and interior fires venting through roof slats.
- **House posts** — Large beams at the sides were carved or painted with ancestors, family history or supernatural beings.
- **Oleman House** — The Suquamish Oleman House (Old Man House) at Port Madison Reservation ran 500 by 40–60 feet around 1850 and held about a hundred people.
- **Gambrel roof** — A roof form unique to Puget Sound Coast Salish.
- **Kekuli** — Pit-houses were also used for shelter.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources describe no ceramic or metalworking tradition; the everyday repertoire centres on wood, bark, fibre and horn carved into functional and ceremonial forms.

- **House posts** — Men carved house posts with ancestors, family history or supernatural beings as supports of flat-design idiom.
- **Carved bowls** — Bowls ranged from simple forms with animal features to complex seated human figure bowls used in female puberty rituals and believed to aid women in giving birth.
- **Bentwood boxes** — Boxes were carved and decorated in flat-design idiom for storage and display.
- **Welcome figures** — Carved wooden figures displayed flat-design decoration.
- **Mountain-goat horn rattles** — Sheets of mountain-goat horn bent and sewn into volumetric triangles were hung with strands of mountain-goat wool for ceremonial use.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Jewelry is thinly documented, with the primary body practice being head shaping of infants as a visible mark of rank rather than ornamentation.

- **Mountain-goat horn bracelet** — A thin bracelet cut from mountain-goat horn with a shouldered end tapering to a pointed hitch was decorated with groups of parallel lines and lines of circles, worn or polished smooth inside and out.

## Music & performance

Performance is bound to spirit power, expressed through dances, masks and ceremonies that display the spiritual powers given to individuals and communities.

- **Spirit dancing ceremonies** — Common winter gatherings at which members show their powers through song and dance on the longhouse floor, with powers attached to spirit animals such as raven, woodpecker, bear or seal.
- **Sxwayxwey mask ceremony** (*sxwayxwey*) — Central to the central Coast Salish region, men from families holding hereditary rights are initiated into the society, wear the mask and dance, joined by women singers.
- **Mountain-goat horn rattles** — Percussion instruments of bent and sewn mountain-goat horn used in ceremonial performance.
- **Slahal** — A sleight-of-hand game on which gambling accompanied athletic contests as recreation.

## Dance & theatre

Two named dance traditions appear: the sxwayxwey mask dance of hereditarily entitled men, and winter spirit dancing as collective but individually owned display of acquired powers.

- **Sxwayxwey mask dance** (*sxwayxwey*) — Performed by hereditarily entitled men of central Coast Salish in masks with bulging cylindrical eyeballs, animal heads as horns and drooping tongues, crowned with large feathers, dancers wearing feather-covered regalia and hoof-rattle leggings while women sing.
- **Winter spirit dancing** — Collective but individually owned display of acquired spirit powers on the longhouse floor through song and dance.

## Festivals & rituals

The ritual year turns on winter spirit dances and the potlatch, a public display of wealth that enhanced but did not buy status or power.

- **Vision quest** — Journeys involving other states of consciousness through which guardian spirits were sought, widely practised in individual ritual life.
- **Potlatch** — The great ceremonial display of wealth including land, food resources, household items and adornments, banned in Canada in 1885 and in the United States some years later, with suppression ending in 1934 in the US and in 1951 in Canada.
- **Soul recovery and journey ceremony** — The Duwamish held ceremonies in which shamans travelled to the underworld to recover souls in transit, described as a two-day walk along a trail through bushes and past a lake to a river-divided valley.
- **Female puberty ritual** — A life-cycle rite in which a seated figure bowl was used.

## Foodways

Salmon was the dietary staple, supplemented by a rich variety of seafoods, forage and cultivated plants managed through deliberate land management.

- **Salmon** — The dietary staple, taken in mass along rivers in summer and on river banks in January.
- **Shellfish** — Butter clams, horse clams and cockles were abundant and dried for trade.
- **Camas** — Among the most important plant foods, gathered on the prairies and also cultivated in forest gardens holding crabapple, hazelnut, cranberry, wild plum and wild cherry.
- **Wapato** — An important plant food especially for the Duwamish.
- **Muckleshoot Seasonal Rounds** — A calendar setting the year: salmon on river banks in January, salmonberry sprouts eaten with salmon eggs by May, steelhead and king salmon in mass in summer with berries abundant in forests.

## Oral tradition & literature

Coast Salish narrative traditions centre on guardian spirits and transformation between human and animal spirits, documented in published collections and modern oratory.

- **Legends of Vancouver** — Published in 1911 by Canadian author E. Pauline Johnson (Tekahionwake), a collection of Coast Salish as-told-to narratives from the author's relationship with Squamish chief Joe Capilano.
- **The Adventures of Yoo-Lah-Teen** — A later retelling for children published by Ellen Pugh and Laszlo Kubinyi in 1975.
- **Chief Dan George's 1967 speech** — Delivered at a Canadian Centennial ceremony in Vancouver's Empire Stadium, it riveted its audience and touched off public awareness and Native activism in British Columbia and Canada.
- **Lushootseed Dictionary** — Language documentation by Dawn Bates, Thom Hess and Vi Hilbert.

## Language & religion

Coast Salish languages form a branch of the Salishan family around most of the Georgia and Puget Sound basins, while the living religious practice is the spirit-power complex.

- **Halkomelem** — One of the named Coast Salish languages found in museum records and articles.
- **Lushootseed** — One of the named Coast Salish languages documented in the Lushootseed Dictionary.
- **Squamish** — One of the named Coast Salish languages.
- **Guardian spirits** — Spiritual powers sought through vision quests and attached to spirit animals, central to the living religious practice.
- **Winter spirit dances** — The survival of an ancestral religious practice in which members display their spiritual powers through song and dance.

## Glossary

- *sxwayxwey* — mask ceremony and dance tradition of hereditarily entitled central Coast Salish men
- *kekuli* — pit-house used for shelter
- *slahal* — sleight-of-hand gambling game
- *potlatch* — great ceremonial display of wealth including land, food, household items and adornments
- *vision quest* — journey involving other states of consciousness to seek guardian spirits
- *guardian spirits* — spiritual powers given to individuals through vision quests, attached to spirit animals
- *Halkomelem* — one of the fourteen contiguous Salishan languages
- *Lushootseed* — one of the fourteen contiguous Salishan languages, documented in dictionary
- *Squamish* — one of the fourteen contiguous Salishan languages
- *Duwamish* — one of the named Coast Salish peoples known for soul recovery ceremonies
- *Suquamish* — one of the named Coast Salish peoples
- *imbricated coiled slat basketry* — basketry technique using imbricated designs in plain and black-dyed prunus bark
- *spindle whorl* — disk set on wooden spindle shaft to spin wool strands, often decorated with elaborate designs
- *Carex* — plant whose leaves are used for baskets and twine
- *flat-design idiom* — abstract design tradition on bowls, combs, bentwood boxes, welcome figures and canoes
- *Salishan* — language family including Coast Salish and related peoples

title: "Odawa"
subtitle: "Canada"
region: "North America"
