## Overview

The Odawa — also written Ottawa or *Odaawaa*, and syncoped in their own speech to *Daawaa* — are an Indigenous people of the Eastern Woodlands, living today in southeastern Canada and the northeastern United States across a border that was drawn across their territory only in the 18th and 19th centuries. Their remembered homeland is Manitoulin Island, on the northern side of Lake Huron, and the Bruce Peninsula in Ontario; after the 17th century Odawa communities also formed along the Ottawa River, in Michigan's Lower Peninsula, in Wisconsin, and in northwest Ohio along the Maumee, Auglaize and Blanchard rivers. About 15,000 Odawa live in Ontario, Michigan and Oklahoma. They are one of the Anishinaabeg, distinct from but closely related to the Ojibwe and Potawatomi, with whom they formed the Council of Three Fires, and they speak a divergent dialect of Ojibwe within the Algonquian family. In folk-culture terms their defining role is commercial: their name derives from *adaawe*, "to trade", and neighbours knew them as the traders who moved cornmeal, sunflower oil, furs and skins, rugs and mats, tobacco, and medicinal roots and herbs between nations.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The objects this atlas shows are dominated by two techniques — glass beadwork on skin and cloth, and porcupine quillwork on birchbark — together with plaited mats.

**Floral glass beadwork** — Beadwork in floral arrangements worked on tanned deer skin, as on a pouch finished with tassels, and on the cloth garments worn in the Harbor Springs photographs: a beaded vest, beaded leggings and beaded moccasins.

**Beaded skin pouches** — A chief's pouch keeps the whole beaver skin with head, legs and tail intact; the tail is embroidered on one side with white beads laid on blue serge, and the bag is lined with pink patterned white calico. It is recorded as having belonged to the "Heathen Chief of the Spanish River Indians".

**Birchbark-and-sweetgrass quillwork** — Mats, baskets and a wall pocket built from birchbark with coiled sweetgrass edging and decorated with porcupine quillwork. The sequence of near-identical mats, baskets and wall pockets in the collection is catalogued as souvenir ware, that is, work made for sale rather than for the household.

**Rush matting** — A mat woven of rush, the plainest of the recorded floor and wall coverings, and consistent with the "rugs and mats" named among Odawa trade goods.

**Black ash basketry and birchbark biting** — Continued as living practices; Kelly Church (born 1967) is recorded as a black ash basket weaver and birch bark biter.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name only one pattern class by name: *floral*, on beadwork. Champlain's 1615 account adds, of bodies rather than cloth, tattooing "in many fashions and designs".

### Clothing & dress

The earliest description is Samuel de Champlain's, who in 1615 met 300 men near the mouth of the French River whom the French called *cheveux relevés* — "hair lifted, raised, rolled up". He recorded that they wore no breech clouts, that their bodies were tattooed in many fashions and designs, their faces painted and their noses pierced, and that their equipment was a bow and arrows, a buckler of boiled leather and a club. Nineteenth- and twentieth-century photographs in the collection show two very different registers of dress. For display and ceremony, an Odawa man at Harbor Springs, Michigan, poses in a feather headdress with a beaded and decorated tunic; in another Harbor Springs postcard, Frank Leo wears a feather headdress, face paint, a patterned cloth shirt, a beaded vest, a loin covering, beaded leggings and beaded moccasins, while the woman beside him wears a headband, several necklaces, a fringed dress and shoes. For dealings with the United States government, a seated studio portrait of the Ottawa chief John Wilson (Partee), made in Washington, D.C., shows him in shirt, vest, suit, tie and pocket watch. Cloth and blankets were among the goods the Odawa took in exchange for furs.

### Architecture

The sources used do not describe Odawa house forms. They do record one built feature of the homeland: the Saugeen complex people of the Bruce Peninsula, a Hopewell-influenced Middle Woodland group that may have developed into the Odawa, raised earthwork mounds for burials, a practice that ended about 250 CE; the Saugeen mounds have not been excavated.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Bark and wood dominate. A model canoe is made of birch bark, wood and gum, and belongs to a set with five paddles — the canoe being also the technology the Odawa held over inland partners who lacked it. Birchbark served equally for containers: baskets, mats and a wall pocket, all coiled with sweetgrass. Rush was woven into mats. Metal and manufactured goods entered the household through the fur trade rather than local workshops: hatchets, knives, kettles, traps, needles, fish hooks, and later firearms. The asymmetry of that trade is recorded bluntly — the Cree are said to have given the Odawa "all their beaver robes for old knives, blunted awls, wretched nets and kettles used until they were past service". Birchbark also carried writing, in the *Wiigwaasabak* scrolls that preserved the migration history.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Body ornament is documented mainly in early contact description and in later photographs. Champlain recorded tattooing in many designs, painted faces, pierced noses, and the raised, rolled hair that gave the people their French name. The twentieth-century photographs show a headband and multiple necklaces on an Odawa woman, and face paint on a man in a feather headdress. "Jewelry and decorative items" are listed among the European goods received for furs, and white glass beads are the medium of the embroidery on the beaver-skin chief's pouch. The sources name no individual ornament types.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not cover Odawa instruments, song genres or performance occasions.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not cover Odawa dance or dramatic traditions.

## Festivals & rituals

Odawa religion is described as the traditional Native American religion of the Odawa, practised in communities in both Canada and the United States, with no formal leadership or organizational structure and much internal variation; it is particularly close to that of the Ojibwe, and like other Native American religions has adapted to environmental change and contact with other communities. The sources record one body of sacred narrative in detail rather than a festival calendar: directed by the *miigis* (luminescent) beings, the Anishinaabe peoples moved inland along the Saint Lawrence River, and at the "Third Stopping Place" near the present Straits of Mackinac the southern Anishinaabeg divided into Ojibwe, Odawa and Potawatomi. Burial under earthwork mounds is attested archaeologically for the Saugeen complex. Christian practice arrived unevenly: Catholic missionaries, among them Frederic Baraga, worked in Michigan, Manitoulin Island converts divided between Catholic, Methodist and Anglican affiliation, and Enmegahbowh (c. 1807–1902) became the first Native American ordained an Episcopal priest. The sources used do not describe Odawa birth, coming-of-age, wedding or funeral rites.

## Foodways

The sources do not describe Odawa cooking or named dishes. What they document is the food economy. Cornmeal and sunflower oil head the list of goods the Odawa traded, alongside tobacco and medicinal roots and herbs, which indicates both horticulture and the processing of seed oil. Hunting supplied the trade in beaver — the most highly prized fur in Europe — and in deer, marten, raccoon, fox, otter and muskrat. Among the European goods taken in exchange, kettles, traps, needles and fish hooks all bear on getting and cooking food, as does the alcohol that entered later. One episode of ritual cannibalism is recorded in the sources, at the 1752 raid on Pickawillany, where the Miami chief Memeskia was killed, boiled and eaten in front of his warriors by the allied Odawa, Potawatomi and Ojibwe war party assembled by Charles Langlade.

## Oral tradition & literature

Anishinaabeg tradition, recorded in *Wiigwaasabak* birch bark scrolls, holds that the Odawa came from the eastern side of North America — Turtle Island — and from a region called Dawnland on the East Coast. Odawa literacy in their own language began on Manitoulin Island in the 19th century, where speakers wrote official letters and petitions, personal documents, band regulations, a proclamation and census statements between 1823 and 1910, and contributed articles to *Anishinabe Enamiad* ("the Praying Indian"), an Ojibwe newspaper published at Harbor Springs, Michigan, from 1896 to 1902. Andrew Blackbird (c. 1814/1817–1908) wrote a history of his people in English with an appended grammar, vocabulary lists and translations of the Ten Commandments and the Lord's Prayer. The major modern collection comes from Jane Willetts Ettawageshik, who spent about two years recording stories in the Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians community; Howard Webkamigada translated them into English as *Ottawa Stories from the Springs*. Basil Johnston is noted as a prominent Odawa author.

## Language & religion

Odawa is a dialect of Ojibwe within the Algonquian family, known to its speakers as *Nishnaabemwin*, "speaking the native language", or *Daawaamwin*, "speaking Ottawa". It is among the most changed of the Ojibwe dialects, above all through a pervasive vowel syncope that deletes short vowels and creates consonant clusters found nowhere else in Ojibwe; the third-person prefix /o-/ has been eliminated entirely, so that *jiimaan* means both "canoe" and "his/her canoe". Two subdialects, "Ottawa Ottawa" and "Chippewa Ottawa", reflect 19th-century in-migration by Southwestern Ojibwe and Potawatomi speakers who shifted to Odawa. Of roughly 5,000 ethnic Odawa and 10,000 more with Odawa ancestry, about 500 people in Ontario and Michigan speak the language, and the Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma has three fluent speakers; revitalization runs through second-language teaching in primary and secondary schools. There is no official orthography, but the Double Vowel system, attributed to Charles Fiero, is used in the 1985 dictionary and 2001 reference grammar. Religious life combines traditional Odawa practice, closely allied to Ojibwe practice, with the Catholic, Methodist and Anglican affiliations taken up from the 19th century.

## Overview

The Odawa are an Indigenous people whose name means "to trade", a role that defined them as merchants moving goods between nations across the Great Lakes region. One of the Anishinaabeg peoples closely related to the Ojibwe and Potawatomi, they speak a distinctive dialect of Ojibwe marked by vowel deletion and consonant clusters. Today about 15,000 Odawa live across Ontario, Michigan and Oklahoma, with revitalization efforts teaching the language in schools.

## Material culture

Odawa material culture centers on glass beadwork and porcupine quillwork on skin and birchbark, along with woven rush and birchbark containers and canoes.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Beadwork in floral patterns and porcupine quillwork on birchbark are the dominant techniques.

- **Floral glass beadwork** — Beads arranged in floral designs on tanned deer skin and cloth garments like vests, leggings and moccasins.
- **Beaded skin pouches** — Pouches made from whole beaver skins with head, legs and tail, embroidered with white beads on blue serge.
- **Birchbark quillwork** — Mats, baskets and wall pockets made from birchbark with sweetgrass edging, decorated with porcupine quills.
- **Black ash basketry** — Baskets woven from black ash, a practice that continues as a living tradition.
- **Rush matting** — Plain mats woven from rush for floor and wall coverings, part of Odawa trade goods.

### Clothing & dress

Odawa dress ranged from tattooed and painted bodies with raised hair in early times to beaded garments and feather headdresses in later periods.

- **Cheveux relevés** — Hair lifted, raised and rolled up, a distinctive style observed by Champlain in 1615.
- **Beaded tunic and leggings** — Decorated cloth tunics and leggings embroidered with glass beads, worn for display and ceremony.
- **Feather headdress** — Headdresses made of feathers worn with beaded garments for formal occasions.

### Architecture

No sources describe Odawa houses, but their Saugeen predecessors built earthwork mounds for burials.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Bark and wood dominate Odawa everyday objects, with metal and manufactured goods entering through the fur trade.

- **Birch bark canoe** — Model canoe made of birch bark, wood and gum, part of a set with five paddles.
- **Birchbark containers** — Baskets, mats and wall pockets made from birchbark and coiled with sweetgrass.
- **Wiigwaasabak scrolls** (*Wiigwaasabak*) — Birchbark scrolls that preserve the migration history of the Anishinaabeg peoples.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Odawa body ornament included tattooing, face paint, pierced noses and glass beads from European trade.

- **Tattooing** — Designs and fashions tattooed on the body, recorded by Champlain in 1615.
- **Face paint** — Paint applied to faces for body adornment and ceremony.
- **Glass beads** — White glass beads from European trade used to embroider ornaments and garments.

## Music & performance

No sources describe Odawa musical instruments, song genres or performance occasions.

## Dance & theatre

No sources describe Odawa dance or dramatic traditions.

## Festivals & rituals

Odawa religion combines traditional practice with Catholic, Methodist and Anglican affiliation, centered on the sacred narrative of Anishinaabeg migration.

- **Miigis migration** (*miigis*) — Luminescent beings directed the Anishinaabeg peoples inland along the Saint Lawrence River to the Straits of Mackinac.
- **Third Stopping Place** — The location near the Straits of Mackinac where Ojibwe, Odawa and Potawatomi divided from the southern Anishinaabeg.
- **Burial mounds** — Earthwork mounds used for burials by the Saugeen complex, a Hopewell-influenced group that may have developed into the Odawa.

## Foodways

Odawa foodways centered on cornmeal and sunflower oil production, hunting for furs, and European metal tools for processing food.

- **Cornmeal trade** — Cornmeal was a major good traded by the Odawa between nations.
- **Sunflower oil** — Oil pressed from sunflower seeds and traded as a major Odawa commodity.
- **Beaver hunting** — Beaver furs were the most highly prized trade good with Europeans.

## Oral tradition & literature

Odawa narrative tradition was recorded on Wiigwaasabak birch bark scrolls, and later in written texts by Odawa speakers and authors.

- **Wiigwaasabak scrolls** (*Wiigwaasabak*) — Birch bark scrolls recording the migration history and sacred narrative of the Anishinaabeg peoples from the Dawnland.
- **Anishinabe Enamiad** — An Ojibwe newspaper published at Harbor Springs, Michigan, from 1896 to 1902, with contributions from Odawa writers.
- **Andrew Blackbird's history** — A history of the Odawa people written in English with grammar, vocabulary and translations of Christian texts.
- **Ottawa Stories from the Springs** — Modern stories recorded from the Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians, translated by Howard Webkamigada.

## Language & religion

Odawa is a highly changed dialect of Ojibwe marked by vowel deletion, with about 500 speakers in Ontario and Michigan and three in Oklahoma.

- **Nishnaabemwin** — The Odawa name for their language, meaning "speaking the native language".
- **Daawaamwin** — An Odawa name for the language, meaning "speaking Ottawa".
- **Double Vowel orthography** (*Double Vowel*) — Writing system attributed to Charles Fiero, used in the 1985 dictionary and 2001 reference grammar.
- **Vowel syncope** — Pervasive deletion of short vowels and creation of consonant clusters unique to Odawa among Ojibwe dialects.

## Glossary

---
title: "Cowichan"
subtitle: "Canada"
region: "North America"
tags: [ethnography, north-america]
---

## Overview

The Cowichan — *Quwʼutsun* in Halkomelem — are a group of Coast Salish peoples of the Cowichan Valley on Vancouver Island, British Columbia. Their territory covered the whole valley, the country around Cowichan Lake and Shawnigan Lake, and extended into the Gulf Islands and to the Fraser River; the most heavily settled part was the lower valley from present-day Duncan down to Cowichan Bay, including the lower Koksilah River. Cowichan Tribes, the band government created under the Indian Act by amalgamating seven neighbouring peoples, has over 3,800 registered members and is the single largest First Nations band in British Columbia. The language is Halkomelem, a Salishan language of the Central Salish branch. In folk-culture terms the Cowichan are known above all for a distinctive type of knitting, most especially the Cowichan sweater, and for carved spindle whorls, horn rattles and spoons held in museum collections.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Cowichan knitting** — The sources identify the Cowichan with a distinctive type of knitting, most especially the *Cowichan sweater*; they do not describe its materials, technique or patterning, so nothing further can be said here from them.

**Spun-wool preparation and the spindle whorl** — The largest single class of Cowichan objects in the collection shown is the spindle whorl, the weighted disc that steadies a hand spindle. Those catalogued are cut from wood, several specifically of maple: roughly disc-shaped, often slightly convex or with a raised centre, pierced by an axial hole, and worked on the face with carving, engraving, openwork or red paint. One is worn smooth and well patinated around the axial hole from use; another appears unused. Wool is also attested as a finishing material on ceremonial objects — two horn rattles carry tassels or strips of wool threaded through holes along their edges.

**Cedar-bark construction** — Cedar bark worked as a flexible sheet is documented in a canoe bailer: a broad flat piece of cedar bark gently curved, its two ends turned up and gathered or pleated into vertical uprights, shaved down and bound with cherry (*Prunus*) bark onto an oval-sectioned horizontal handle, perhaps of cedar wood.

**Motif vocabulary.** The museum catalogue describes rather than names the designs; they include a nine-lobed flower-like circular design set immediately around a whorl's axial hole; a herring-bone pattern cut with a (crooked?) knife on a whorl's underside; a bird with outstretched wings, carved on the front of two whorls; twelve triangles spaced in pairs radiating from the central hole; openwork rays around the central hole; two concentric engraved lines; eight smaller holes spaced evenly around a central hole; a crest design on a horn spoon's bowl, a diamond form with a "U" form at the centre partly filled with crossed hatching and flukes or tail turned towards the handle; and a face flanked by trigons on a horn rattle.

### Clothing & dress

The sources document dress chiefly through three photographs. Two nearly identical carte-de-visite albumen prints show a seated studio portrait of a Cowichan woman on Vancouver Island wearing a woven brimmed Haida hat, a Hudson's Bay and Co. blanket over her shoulders, and a cloth shirt and skirt — an assemblage combining an imported trade blanket, a hat made by a neighbouring people, and settler-made cloth garments. A black-and-white postcard printed at Duncan shows three Quamichan men dancing in a clearing as part of a potlatch, dressed in ceremonial costume, with other Quamichan people gathered around watching; the caption does not itemise the costume, so its elements cannot be named from this source. Knitted garments — the Cowichan sweater above all — are the one dress form the sources attribute distinctively to the Cowichan. Beyond these, the sources used do not cover everyday or ceremonial dress, head coverings, belts or footwear.

### Architecture

The sources give almost nothing on built form. The potlatch postcard from Duncan shows wooden houses in the background of the dance ground, and the Halkomelem word *léləmʼ* "house" is recorded (in the Downriver dialect material), but no house type, framing method, roof form or carved or painted decoration is described. What the sources do document is settlement geography: seven traditional villages — Quamichan (*Kwaʼmutsun*), Comiaken (*Qwumʼyiqunʼ*), Koksilah (*Xwulqwʼselu*), Somena (*Sʼamunu*), Clemclemluts (*Lhumlhumulutsʼ*), Khenipsen (*Xinupsum*) and Cowichan Bay (*Tlʼulpalus*) — and nine reserves totalling 24 square kilometres (5,900 acres) within a core traditional territory of about 3,750 square kilometres (900,000 acres). The reserves lie along the Cowichan River and Cowichan Bay and include Theik 2, Kil-pah-las 3, Est-Patrolas 4, Tzart-lam 5, Kakalatza 6, and Skutz 7 and 8 at Skutz Canyon.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Wood and horn dominate the documented object repertoire. Besides the spindle whorls and the cedar-bark canoe bailer, the collection holds a wooden comb carved with a *xwe-xwe* mask figure; a spoon of mountain goat horn with a simple pointed handle and a fine, highly unusual engraved crest design on the bowl; a wooden salmon fish-lure; and a smoking pipe of wood and brass — the one object combining a worked metal element. Two rattles are made from horn: one from a circular piece folded in half into a semicircle and filled with unidentified material, with a wooden handle fixed to the lower edge; the other a length of horn with a handle carved as a bird's head, the far end steamed flat, folded over and sewn shut, and accented with abalone shell. No ceramics appear among the objects shown. In the present day, Cowichan Tribes owns Khowutzun Millwork & Joinery, a woodworking enterprise within its Khowutzun Development Corporation group.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used do not cover Cowichan jewelry, tattooing or hair practices; the only adornment material they name is the abalone shell used as an accent on a horn rattle.

## Music & performance

The sound-producing instruments in the collection are two horn rattles, both of mountain-goat-type horn worked by folding: one a semicircle with a face and trigons carved on each outer side, a wooden handle at the base and wool tassels threaded through holes along its lower edge; the other a horn length with a bird's-head handle, steamed flat and sewn shut at the opposite end, hung with strips of wool and accented with abalone. Both are filled with unidentified material or objects to produce the sound. The single documented performance context is a potlatch at Duncan, photographed for a printed postcard, at which three Quamichan men danced in ceremonial costume before an audience of other Quamichan people. The sources name no song genres, no further instruments, and no singers or song-keepers, and Canada has no UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscriptions, so there is no inscription to reference here.

## Dance & theatre

Two items touch on dance. The potlatch postcard records three Quamichan men dancing in a clearing in ceremonial costume as part of the potlatch, watched by a gathered crowd — the only dance event described. A wooden comb carries a figure of a *xwe-xwe* mask; the catalogue names the mask type but does not say how or when the mask itself was worn or danced, and the sources used offer no further account of masked or dramatic performance.

## Festivals & rituals

The potlatch is the one named ceremonial occasion in the sources, documented in the Duncan postcard as a gathering with dancing, ceremonial dress and a watching community. For life-cycle practice, the sources record that arranged marriages between children in different Halkomelem-speaking language areas were common, and that these marriages helped establish a regional social network across the Strait of Georgia–Puget Sound basin — part of the same pattern of movement by which Island people crossed the Strait of Georgia to camp along the Fraser River, in both the Downriver and Upriver areas, for the summer salmon runs. The sources also describe institutions that stood outside festival life: before and during early contact, Cowichan warriors travelled long distances in large war canoes to raid other villages, seize goods and take captives for enslavement or ransom, captives being incorporated into households, traded or used as labour, and slavery was a recognised social institution before European contact. Birth, coming-of-age and funeral rites, and any annual calendar of observances, are not covered by the sources used.

## Foodways

The sources do not name a single Cowichan dish, cooking method or ceremonial food, but they establish that the food economy turned on salmon. Island Halkomelem speakers crossed the Strait of Georgia each summer to camp along the Fraser River for the salmon runs; among the objects shown is a salmon fish-lure of wood, together with a cedar-bark canoe bailer for keeping a working canoe dry and a mountain goat horn spoon for eating or serving. The continuing legal weight of the fishery is recorded in the Cowichan Tribes v. Canada ruling of August 2025, in which the Supreme Court of British Columbia granted the Cowichan Tribes Aboriginal title over a portion of Lulu Island in Richmond, adjacent to the Fraser River, and fishing rights over a portion of the river itself. Beyond salmon fishing and the two utensils, the sources used do not cover staples, preparation or food ritual.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used contain no Cowichan folktales, epics, proverbs or riddles, and name no storytellers or storytelling occasions; what they document instead is language documentation and archiving — the FirstVoices website holds 1,754 archived words and 690 archived phrases of Halkomelem, delivered through an iPhone app released in 2011 and an Android version in 2016.

## Language & religion

Cowichan speak Halkomelem, a member of the Central Salish branch of the Salishan family; the other branches are Tsamosan, Interior Salish, Bella Coola and Tillamook, and speakers of Central and Tsamosan languages are usually identified in ethnographic literature as Coast Salish. The Island dialect, *Hulʼqumiʼnumʼ*, is also called "Cowichan" and is shared with the Snuneymuxw, Snaw-naw-as, Stzʼuminus, Lake Cowichan, Halalt, Lyackson, Penelakut and Lamalchi; tense, sharply articulated glottalized resonants are a key feature of Island speech. The Cowichan write the language in a cased Latin alphabet with modifier apostrophes and doubled letters for vowel length, using *ou* for the long [u] of French loanwords, *u* for schwa, and including the tetragraph *tthʼ*. The language is near extinction: fewer than twenty-five fluent speakers were estimated in 2000 and 263 reported in 2014, with 21 Head Start programs including a language-nest immersion preschool, and a language program at Cowichan First Nation. The sources used do not describe Cowichan religion, beyond noting that missionary influence helped suppress inter-tribal warfare and slavery in the mid-19th century.

## Sources & further reading

- Brent Galloway, *Dictionary of Upriver Halkomelem*, University of California Press, 2009 — the published dictionary for the Upriver dialect of the language.
- Wayne Suttles (2004), the Musqueam reference work cited throughout the Halkomelem phonology and morphology literature, and the source of the Downriver dialect data summarised above.
- FirstVoices Halkomelem archive and mobile apps (iPhone 2011, Android 2016): 1,754 words and 690 phrases.
- Cowichan Tribes official website; the Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development Canada First Nations Detail profile for Cowichan; the Hulʼqumiʼnum Treaty Group; and Khowutzun Development Corporation.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cowichan_Tribes
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cowichan_language
- British Museum online collection (https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection) — holds the Cowichan and Quamichan spindle whorls, horn rattles, horn spoon, *xwe-xwe* comb, cedar-bark bailer, fish-lure, smoking pipe and photographs described here.
- No UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage elements are inscribed for Canada, so no ICH identifier is cited.
